The PID \(k[t]\) is integrally closed: inserting a coprime fraction into a monic equation forces its denominator to divide a power of its coprime numerator, hence to be a unit. Consequently

\[ \overline A\ \subset\ \{z\in F:\operatorname{Tr}(ze_i)\in k[t]\text{ for every }i\} \ \subset\ d^{-1}\sum_i k[t]e_i \tag{RC3} \]

for one nonzero common denominator \(d\) of the inverse trace matrix. The right module is finite free over the Noetherian ring \(k[t]\); its submodule \(\overline A\) is finite. Integrality over \(A\) and over \(k[t]\) are equivalent here, by transitivity in one direction and the same monic equation in the other. This proves the assertion about the normalization of \(A\).

For a reduced affine ring, apply this construction to each of its finitely many minimal-prime quotients and take the product. Its total quotient ring is the product of their fraction fields. Explicitly, for each minimal prime choose an element in all the others and not in that prime; the product choices and their sum produce the corresponding orthogonal idempotents after inverting a nonzerodivisor. Fractions on each factor then give the asserted product. The product normalization is finite over the original ring. Integral closure commutes with localization: a monic equation after localization becomes an integral equation for a sufficiently large denominator multiple of its root, and the reverse inclusion is immediate. The affine normalizations therefore glue to a finite map (RC1).

The map is an isomorphism at every generic point. Its coherent cokernel consequently has zero-dimensional support, a finite set on a Noetherian curve. Finiteness also gives properness of \(D\) over \(k\).

For clarity, the local regularity needed next does not require a surface-resolution theorem. A normal one-dimensional Noetherian local domain \(B\) is a DVR. Choose \(0\ne x\) in its maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\). The only prime of \(B/(x)\) is its maximal ideal, which is nilpotent: a finite list of nilpotent generators has a zero sufficiently high product power. Thus \(\mathfrak m^n\subset(x)\) for some \(n\). If \(n=1\), the ideal \(\mathfrak m\) is already principal. Otherwise choose minimal \(n\) and \(y\in\mathfrak m^{n-1}\setminus(x)\). Then \(z=y/x\notin B\), while \(z\mathfrak m\subset B\). If \(z\mathfrak m\subset\mathfrak m\), a matrix for multiplication on finitely many generators of \(\mathfrak m\) and its characteristic determinant make \(z\) integral over \(B\); the nonzero ideal \(\mathfrak m\) is faithful, so its annihilating monic polynomial annihilates \(z\). This contradicts normality. Hence \(za\) is a unit for some \(a\in\mathfrak m\), and \(b/a=(zb)/(za)\in B\) for all \(b\in\mathfrak m\). Thus \(\mathfrak m=(a)\). DFR3 and DFR6 give the discrete valuation.

At a closed point of \(D_i\), its residue field is \(k\) and its cotangent space has dimension one. In an affine presentation choose independent linear parts for all but one coordinate, and lift them to defining equations. SF1–SF3 cut out a smooth curve through the point. Its local ring is a DVR and surjects onto the local ring of \(D_i\); the kernel is zero since a nonzero prime in a DVR has zero-dimensional quotient. The remaining defining ideal vanishes on a neighborhood, by finite generation. This proves smoothness. Finally a nonconstant rational function on \(D_i\) extends to a morphism to \(\mathbf P^1\): at each DVR either it or its inverse is regular. This proper nonconstant morphism has finite fibres, hence is finite by Lesson 3, §0F. The explicit finite-over-projective construction, Theorem 0F7 there, makes \(D_i\) projective. \(\square\)

2V.2. The conductor and the arithmetic genus

Let \(S\) be the finite set where \(\nu\) is not an isomorphism. For \(x\in S\) put

\[ A_x=\mathcal O_{Z,x},\quad B_x=(\nu_*\mathcal O_D)_x,\quad \delta_x=\dim_k(B_x/A_x),\quad b_x=\#\nu^{-1}(x). \tag{RC4} \]

The semilocal ring \(B_x\) has \(b_x\) maximal ideals, all with residue field \(k\). Let \(J_x\) be their intersection. The conductor is the common ideal

\[ I_x=\{a\in A_x:aB_x\subset A_x\},\qquad C_x=B_x/I_x,\quad E_x=A_x/I_x. \tag{RC5} \]

RC2. The rings \(C_x,E_x\) are finite-dimensional \(k\)-algebras, the latter is local, and \(I_x\subset J_x\). Writing \(M_x=\operatorname{rad}C_x\) and \(N_x=\operatorname{rad}E_x\), we have

\[ \delta_x=(b_x-1)+\epsilon_x,\qquad \epsilon_x=\dim_kM_x-\dim_kN_x\ge0. \tag{RC6} \]

If \(g_i=\dim_kH^1(D_i,\mathcal O_{D_i})\), \(b=\sum_i g_i\), and \(g=\dim_kH^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)\), then

\[ g=b+\sum_{x\in S}\delta_x-c+1. \tag{RC7} \]

Proof. The finite module \(B_x/A_x\) is supported only at the closed point, so some power of the maximal ideal annihilates it. That power lies in \(I_x\); thus both quotients in (RC5) are finite-dimensional. The conductor is an ideal of both rings. If it were not in a maximal ideal of \(B_x\), its image in the local ring \(A_x\) would contain an element outside the maximal ideal after contraction, or, equivalently, \(B_x/I_x\) would omit that branch. More directly, any element of \(I_x\) outside a maximal ideal of \(B_x\) has nonzero residue in \(k\), and as an element of \(A_x\) has that same residue at every branch. It is a unit of \(A_x\); then \(I_x=A_x\), forcing \(B_x=A_x\), contrary to \(x\in S\). This proves \(I_x\subset J_x\).

The reduced quotient of \(C_x\) is \(k^{b_x}\), by the Chinese remainder theorem; that of \(E_x\) is the diagonal \(k\). Its nilradical embeds in \(M_x\). Since \(B_x/A_x=C_x/E_x\) additively, their dimensions give (RC6).

Here is the cohomology calculation. The normalization sequence is exact:

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Z\longrightarrow\nu_*\mathcal O_D \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{x\in S}(B_x/A_x)_x \longrightarrow0 . \tag{RC8} \]

Its last sheaf is a finite sum of skyscraper sheaves and has no positive cohomology: every restriction between opens containing the supporting point is the identity, and the other restrictions are surjective. Cohomology of \(\nu_*\mathcal O_D\) equals that of \(\mathcal O_D\), since the inverse images of affine opens and their intersections are affine under a finite map; the SC11–SC12 Čech complexes agree.

Each \(D_i\) has constants \(k\) by FC20. Global functions on \(Z\) inject into \(k^c\), so form a finite reduced \(k\)-algebra. Such an algebra is a product of copies of \(k\); connectedness rules out nontrivial idempotents, leaving precisely \(k\). Taking the alternating dimensions in (RC8), or its cohomology sequence through degree one, now proves (RC7). \(\square\)

2V.3. Local units and unique prime-to-characteristic division

RC3. The local unit quotient is

\[ B_x^*/A_x^*\simeq (k^*)^{b_x}/k^*\ \times\ U_x,\qquad U_x=(1+M_x)/(1+N_x). \tag{RC9} \]

For every positive integer \(h\) invertible in \(k\), multiplication by \(h\) is bijective on \(U_x\).

Proof. Since \(I_x\) is in the Jacobson radicals, units lift from both quotients in (RC5). Their unit kernels agree, namely \(1+I_x\). Thus \(B_x^*/A_x^*=C_x^*/E_x^*\).

The Artinian product decomposition of \(C_x\), together with its \(k\)-algebra structure, gives a section \(k^{b_x}\to C_x\) of reduction: multiply scalars by the orthogonal local-factor idempotents. Every unit is uniquely a residue unit times an element of \(1+M_x\). In \(E_x\) the same statement uses the single diagonal copy of \(k\) and \(1+N_x\). This proves (RC9).

For any nilpotent ideal \(M\), filter \(1+M\) by \(1+M^j\). Successive quotients are the additive groups \(M^j/M^{j+1}\), and taking the \(h\)-th power induces multiplication by the unit \(h\). Lifting one layer at a time, correcting the error by \(h^{-1}\) times its leading term, proves existence and uniqueness of an \(h\)-th root in \(1+M\). The filtration is finite, so this is a finite argument, valid in positive characteristic without logarithms. It applies to both \(M_x\) and \(N_x\). The induced map on their quotient is surjective; if an element has \(h\)-th power in \(1+N_x\), the unique \(h\)-th root of that element of \(1+N_x\) is also its unique root in \(1+M_x\). This proves injectivity. \(\square\)

2V.4. Actual line bundles patched across the conductor

RC4. Pullback of line bundles is surjective and its kernel is

\[ 0\longrightarrow K_Z\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Z) \xrightarrow{\nu^*}\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Pic}(D_i) \longrightarrow0,\qquad K_Z=\frac{\prod_{x\in S}(B_x^*/A_x^*)} {\operatorname{im}((k^*)^c)} . \tag{RC10} \]

The componentwise constants in the denominator are restricted to their branches.

Proof. At each \(x\) the ring square is an actual fibre product:

\[ A_x=B_x\times_{C_x}E_x. \tag{RC11} \]

Indeed an element of \(B_x\) whose conductor residue belongs to \(E_x\) differs from an element of \(A_x\) by an element of \(I_x\), which is in \(A_x\).

A line bundle on \(D\) has a frame on a neighborhood of the finite set above each \(x\). To justify a simultaneous frame, its module over the semilocal ring \(B_x\) is free: choose one element with a prescribed nonzero basis residue at every maximal ideal, using the Chinese remainder theorem for the module; Nakayama makes it a generator everywhere, and the rank-one localizations make the map from the ring an isomorphism. Its finitely many denominators can be cleared on a neighborhood of these points.

Patch this frame with the free rank-one module over \(E_x\). The patching module consists of pairs whose residues agree under the chosen isomorphism over \(C_x\). It is rank-one free over \(A_x\). More generally, if the identification is multiplication by \(v\in C_x^*\), lift \(v\) to a unit \(\widetilde v\in B_x^*\); then \((\widetilde v,1)\) is a frame by (RC11). These modules agree with the original line bundle away from the conductor. All finite data spread to neighborhoods; on overlaps away from \(S\) they glue by the original line-bundle transition maps. This constructs a line bundle on \(Z\) pulling back to the prescribed bundle on \(D\), proving surjectivity.

If the pullback is trivial, choose its global frame on each \(D_i\). A local frame at each conductor point gives an identification over \(C_x\), classified by a unit modulo \(E_x^*\), equivalently \(B_x^*/A_x^*\). Changing the local frame changes exactly this denominator. Changing the global normalized frames changes exactly the restrictions of \((k^*)^c\), since these are all global units on \(D\). Conversely these changes give isomorphic patched bundles, and an isomorphism restricts to precisely such frame changes. This proves the kernel formula and exactness. The proof classifies actual line bundles; it has not replaced them by just their degrees or by an unconstructed Picard scheme. \(\square\)

2V.5. The incidence graph and the torsion rank

Make a bipartite graph \(\Delta\). Its vertices are the \(c\) normalized components and the points of \(S\); its edges are the branches above those points. Multiple branches on the same component give distinct edges. The graph is connected: a partition with no connecting edge would partition the components into two disjoint closed unions in \(Z\), hence two open and closed subsets. Set

\[ r=\#E(\Delta)-\#V(\Delta)+1 =\sum_{x\in S}(b_x-1)-c+1 . \tag{RC12} \]

When \(S\) is empty, connectedness gives \(c=1\), and \(\Delta\) is its single vertex, so \(r=0\).

RC5. There is an isomorphism of abelian groups

\[ K_Z\simeq(k^*)^r\times\prod_{x\in S}U_x. \tag{RC13} \]

The coordinates on its first factor depend on a spanning tree. For a prime \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\) there is an exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow(\mathbf Z/\ell)^r \longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell] \longrightarrow\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Pic}(D_i)[\ell] \longrightarrow0, \qquad \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell]=2b+r. \tag{RC14} \]

An identification of the first group with this displayed constant vector space includes a choice of primitive \(\ell\)-th root of unity.

Proof. The component constants in (RC10) have no nilpotent part in (RC9). Their quotient of the torus factor is the edge-unit group \((k^*)^{E(\Delta)}\) modulo vertex rescalings, with one ratio on each oriented edge. A spanning tree gauges every tree-edge value to one, successively from a root vertex. The common scalar at all vertices acts trivially, and each remaining edge has one unconstrained unit. There are exactly \(r\) remaining edges. This proves (RC13) integrally, with no division by a graph determinant and no finite hidden quotient.

The \(h\)-th power map on \(k^*\) is surjective since \(k\) is algebraically closed. For prime \(h=\ell\), its kernel has exactly \(\ell\) elements: \(T^\ell-1\) has nonzero derivative at its roots and splits over \(k\). RC3 therefore makes multiplication by \(\ell\) surjective on \(K_Z\), with kernel of dimension \(r\).

Given an \(\ell\)-torsion class on \(D\), choose any lift \(L\) through (RC10). Its \(\ell\)-th power belongs to \(K_Z\); divide that element by \(\ell\) inside \(K_Z\) and correct \(L\) by the inverse of the chosen quotient. The corrected lift is actual \(\ell\)-torsion. This proves the right surjectivity in (RC14); the other exactness assertions follow from (RC10). Each normalized component has a \(k\)-point. JC identifies its degree-zero line bundles with its Jacobian, and CU gives exactly \(2g_i\) dimensions of prime-to-characteristic torsion; torsion has degree zero since degrees take values in \(\mathbf Z\). Summing yields the last assertion. \(\square\)

2V.6. The bound and all equality conditions

RC6. For every prime \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\),

\[ \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell]\le g+b,\qquad g+b-\dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell] =\sum_{x\in S}\bigl(\delta_x-b_x+1\bigr). \tag{RC15} \]

Equality holds if and only if, for every \(x\in S\),

\[ A_x=k+J_x\ \subset B_x. \tag{RC16} \]

Proof. Subtract (RC14) from (RC7) plus \(b\), using (RC12). This gives the equality in (RC15). Every summand is nonnegative by (RC6), so equality is equivalent to \(\delta_x=b_x-1\) for all \(x\).

The residue map \(B_x\to k^{b_x}\) is surjective and sends \(A_x\) to the diagonal \(k\). Thus \(A_x\subset k+J_x\), with

\[ \dim_k B_x/(k+J_x)=b_x-1. \tag{RC17} \]

Equality of this dimension with \(\dim_kB_x/A_x\) forces (RC16), and (RC16) implies that dimension equality. This is an equality of actual local rings inside their finite normalization, not just a comparison of tangent dimensions. \(\square\)

2V.7. Completed multicross rings

RC7. Condition (RC16) is equivalent to a completed local-ring isomorphism

\[ \widehat A_x\simeq k[[X_1,\ldots,X_{b_x}]]/ (X_iX_j: i\ne j). \tag{RC18} \]

For a singular point satisfying this condition, \(b_x\ge2\). If \(b_x=2\), this is the node \(k[[X_1,X_2]]/(X_1X_2)\). For \(b_x>2\) it is called a multicross singularity and need not be a node.

Proof. Suppose (RC16). Its maximal ideal is exactly \(J_x\), an ideal also of \(B_x\). Completion of the finite module \(B_x\) with respect to this ideal gives the product of its completed DVRs. Indeed the distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, their intersection powers are their product powers, and the Chinese remainder theorem splits every quotient into the quotients at these branches. The completions are \(k[[t_i]]\): successively subtract the residue scalar and divide by a uniformizer; completeness and separatedness give unique convergent coefficients. Consequently

\[ \widehat A_x =k+\prod_{i=1}^{b_x}t_i k[[t_i]] \subset\prod_{i=1}^{b_x}k[[t_i]]. \tag{RC19} \]

This also follows by completing the exact finite-module sequence \(A_x\to B_x\to k^{b_x}/k\), using EA7. Map \(X_i\) to the tuple with entry \(t_i\) on its branch and zero elsewhere. Every power series modulo the mixed products has a unique constant plus one series with zero constant on each axis; hence this map gives precisely (RC18).

For the converse, let \(\mathfrak m\) be the maximal ideal of \(A_x\). Completion of \(0\to A_x\to B_x\to B_x/A_x\to0\) remains exact by EA7, and the finite-length quotient is unchanged. The completion of \(B_x\) is a product of branch DVR completions, as above; the \(\mathfrak mB_x\)-adic and branch-radical-adic topologies agree, since both ideals have the same radical and are finitely generated. It is also the integral closure of \(\widehat A_x\) in its total quotient ring. Here this last assertion has an elementary justification: a conductor nonzerodivisor remains a nonzerodivisor after completion by flatness; inverting it makes the completed finite inclusion an isomorphism. Thus both rings have the same total quotient ring. The product of DVRs is integrally closed by the valuation argument DFR7, and every element of it is integral over \(\widehat A_x\), since it is finite.

For the axes ring in (RC18), the product of the axis power-series rings is exactly its normalization: it is a finite module, it has the same total quotient ring after inverting \(X_1+\cdots+X_{b_x}\), and is integrally closed. Its quotient by the axes ring is the space of branch constants modulo their common constant, of dimension \(b_x-1\). Normalization is unique inside the total quotient ring, so the preceding exact completed sequence gives \(\delta_x=b_x-1\). RC6 then gives (RC16).

If \(b_x=1\), (RC16) says \(A_x=B_x\), which is a DVR by RC1, so the point was not singular. This proves the final assertions. \(\square\)

2V.8. Application to a supplied regular model and its limits

RC8. In the setting of VP, put \(Z=(X_k)_{\mathrm{red}}\). It is a connected reduced projective curve, so RC1–RC7 apply. For \(\ell\) prime to \(\operatorname{char}k\) and to \(d=\gcd_i m_i\),

\[ \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(C)[\ell] -\dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\Phi_X[\ell] \ \le\ 2b+r\ \le\ g_Z+b,\qquad g_Z=\dim_kH^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z). \tag{RC20} \]

Every map preceding the dimension calculation is compatible with supplied automorphisms of the curve or model.

Proof. The first inequality is the actual specialization and generic torsion obstruction of VP6–VP7, with RC5 evaluating the special group. The second is RC6. An automorphism transports integral elements, the conductor, local units and the patched line bundles, and permutes the branches and components. It therefore respects (RC8), (RC10) and their torsion sequences. Coordinates from a spanning tree need not respect it; no equivariant splitting of (RC14) is asserted.

Equality in the second inequality determines precisely the multicross condition (RC18). It does not eliminate the possibility \(b_x>2\). Nor does (RC20) prove existence of a regular model, minimalization, a uniform bound on \(\Phi_X[\ell]\), reducedness of the original special fibre, or the extra local condition that reduces multicross points to nodes. These remain separate inputs for general semistable reduction. The nonminimal blowup example in Exercise 2U still prevents inferring reducedness from a maximal special torsion rank alone. \(\square\)

2V.9. Graded exercise: branch conditions and missing torsion

Exercise 2V (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. In characteristic two consider \(A=k[t^2,t^3]\). Explain why \(t^2\) alone is not a separating parameter. Apply the construction in RC1 with the integral element \(b=t^3\), its equation over \(k[t^2]\), and the power \(q=4\). Exhibit the resulting separating parameter and a monic equation making \(t^2\) integral over its polynomial ring.
  2. For a normal one-dimensional Noetherian local domain, fill in the determinant step in RC1 and the argument that \(z\mathfrak m\not\subset\mathfrak m\) makes the maximal ideal principal. Identify the use of normality.
  3. Compute \(\delta\), the branch number, the conductor and the unit quotient for the completed cusp ring \(k[[t^2,t^3]]\subset k[[t]]\). Prove directly that the extra unit group contributes no \(\ell\)-torsion when \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\).
  4. Over any algebraically closed field, describe the image of\[ k[[x,y]]/(xy(x-y))\longrightarrow k[[t]]^3,\qquad f\longmapsto(f(t,0),f(0,t),f(t,t)). \tag{RCX1} \] Compute its conductor, \(\delta\), branch number, local unit quotient and \(\epsilon\). Explain why this ordinary plane triple point is not the three-axis multicross ring.
  5. In the two-branch ring of pairs \((f(t),g(s))\) satisfying \(f(0)=g(0)\) and \(f'(0)=g'(0)\), compute the conductor, \(\delta\), \(\epsilon\), and the unit quotient. Compare with pairs satisfying only equality of the constants. Derivatives here mean the first formal coefficients, in every characteristic.
  6. An incidence graph has three component vertices, two singular vertices of valencies three and two, and is connected. The normalization genera are \(1,0,2\); the two \(\delta\)-invariants are \(3,1\). Compute \(b,r,g\), the prime-to-characteristic Picard-torsion dimension, and the defect in RC15. State which singularity fails the equality criterion.
  7. Prove the integral spanning-tree gauge count in RC5, including a component joined twice to the same singular vertex. Show why one common vertex scalar is the entire kernel and why there is no finite quotient omitted by the rank calculation.
  8. Give the explicit correction of a lift \(L\) of a normalized \(\ell\)-torsion bundle when \(L^{\otimes\ell}\) corresponds to \((a_1,\ldots,a_r,u)\) under (RC13). Distinguish uniqueness of division on the nilpotent factor from division on the torus.
  9. For a rational cuspidal curve and a rational nodal curve, each with just the indicated singularity and normalization \(\mathbf P^1\), compute \(g,b,r\) and the prime-to-characteristic torsion dimensions. In characteristic \(p>0\), compute the \(p\)-torsion of the cusp's additive factor and explain the restriction on \(\ell\).
  10. For the \(n\)-axis complete local ring \(A_n\), \(n\ge2\), put \(s=X_1+\cdots+X_n\). Prove \(s\) is a nonzerodivisor, calculate the entire ring \(A_n/(s)\), and compute its socle. State exactly what this calculation establishes before a Gorenstein criterion has been proved.

Complete solution.

  1. Write \(v=t^2\). Then \(dv=0\), and \(k(t)/k(v)\) is inseparable of degree two. The element \(b=t^3\) satisfies \(b^2-v^3=0\), while \(db=t^2dt\ne0\). RC1 gives \(u=v^4+b=t^8+t^3\). In characteristic two, substitution yields

    \[ v^8+v^3+u^2=0,\qquad du=t^2dt\ne0. \tag{RCX2} \]

    This is monic in \(v\); it makes \(v\) integral over \(k[u]\). Since \(b=u-v^4\), the whole ring \(A\) is finite over \(k[u]\), and the field extension is separable. The construction uses characteristic-two differentiation rather than a characteristic-zero separability assumption.

  2. Choose generators \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) of \(\mathfrak m\). If \(z\mathfrak m\subset\mathfrak m\), write \(za_i=\sum_jc_{ij}a_j\), with \(c_{ij}\in B\). The adjugate identity for \(zI-C\) gives \(\det(zI-C)a_i=0\) for every \(i\). At least one \(a_i\ne0\) and the ambient fraction ring is a field, so this monic determinant vanishes at \(z\). Normality forces \(z\in B\), contradicting its construction. Thus some \(a\in\mathfrak m\) has \(za\) outside \(\mathfrak m\), hence a unit. For every \(b\in\mathfrak m\), \(zb\in B\) and \(b/a=(zb)/(za)\in B\); consequently \(\mathfrak m=(a)\). Normality was used precisely to forbid the integral fraction outside \(B\).

  3. The cusp ring consists of all series whose coefficient of \(t\) is zero. Its quotient in \(k[[t]]\) is spanned by \(t\), so \(\delta=1\), \(b_x=1\) and \(\epsilon=1\). Its conductor is \(t^2k[[t]]\): every order-at-least-two series stays in the ring after multiplication by any series, while a conductor element with a nonzero constant would multiply \(t\) to a forbidden first coefficient. Modulo this conductor the two rings are \(k[t]/t^2\) and \(k\). Thus

    \[ B^*/A^*\simeq 1+kt\simeq(k,+),\qquad (1+at)(1+bt)=1+(a+b)t . \tag{RCX3} \]

    Multiplication by \(\ell\) is multiplication by its nonzero scalar on \(k\), hence bijective and has zero kernel.

  4. The map is injective. In \(k[[x,y]]\), the intersection of the three principal ideals \((x),(y),(x-y)\) is their product: divisibility by each of the distinct prime factors forces divisibility by their product. Its image consists of triples with one common constant and first coefficients \((a,b,a+b)\); all higher coefficients can be prescribed independently. Indeed the polynomials \(x(x-y)\), \(y(y-x)\) and \(xy\) isolate respectively a nonzero quadratic coefficient on each branch. Multiplication by a series in its branch parameter produces all series of order at least two on that branch. This proves both necessity and sufficiency of the stated conditions.

    The conductor is \((t^2k[[t]])^3\). It contains this ideal by the preceding isolation. Conversely a conductor element must stay in the image after multiplication by each branch idempotent in the normalization. This first kills its constant and then kills each of its first coefficients by the linear relation above. The Artin normalization has dimension six; the image has one constant and two independent linear coefficients, hence dimension three. Therefore

    \[ b_x=3,\quad\delta=3,\quad\epsilon=1,\qquad B^*/A^*\simeq(k^*)^2\times(k,+). \tag{RCX4} \]

    The nilpotent quotient is \(k^3/\{(a,b,a+b)\}\), an additive one-dimensional space. The three-axis ring has \(\delta=2\) and independent first coefficients, so these completed rings differ even though both have three smooth branches with distinct tangent directions in their respective ambient spaces.

  5. The conductor is \(t^2k[[t]]\times s^2k[[s]]\). The same branch-idempotent test kills constants and first coefficients, while every pair of order at least two belongs to the conductor. The normalization modulo it has dimension four; the subring is the diagonal dual-number algebra, of dimension two. Thus \(\delta=2,b_x=2,\epsilon=1\). Units split into their two nonzero constants and their two linear coefficients; quotienting the diagonal subring gives \(k^*\times(k,+)\). With only the common-constant condition, the conductor is \(tk[[t]]\times sk[[s]]\), \(\delta=1,\epsilon=0\), and the unit quotient is just \(k^*\). The lost first-coefficient freedom accounts for exactly the extra genus contribution.

  6. There are five graph edges and five vertices, so \(r=1\). Also \(b=3\) and \(\sum\delta_x=4\), giving

    \[ g=3+4-3+1=5,\qquad \dim\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell]=2\cdot3+1=7,\qquad g+b-7=1. \tag{RCX5} \]

    At the valency-three point \(\delta-(b_x-1)=3-2=1\); at the valency-two point it is \(1-1=0\). Precisely the first fails RC16. These computations are conditional on the stated curve data; they do not assert an unspecified geometric realization of every incidence pattern.

  7. Orient the edges, choose a root vertex and set its scalar to one. Moving outward along the tree, there is exactly one scalar at each new vertex that sends its incoming tree-edge value to one. All vertices are reached once and no constraint remains, since a tree has no cycle. Every non-tree edge then has an arbitrary unit; changing these units changes the class. A vertex rescaling fixing all edges must have equal scalars at the two ends of every edge and hence the same scalar everywhere, by connectedness. This is the whole kernel. If two branches join the same pair of vertices, one can be a tree edge and the other supplies a free cycle coordinate. The construction is an explicit quotient isomorphism for unit groups, so an unobserved finite cokernel cannot be introduced by rational rank reasoning.

  8. Choose \(q_i\in k^*\) with \(q_i^\ell=a_i\). Let \(v\) be the unique element of the nilpotent quotient with \(v^\ell=u\), whose existence and uniqueness were proved by the finite filtration in RC3. Let \(Q\in K_Z\) be the class \((q_1,\ldots,q_r,v)\). Then \(L\otimes Q^{-1}\) has trivial \(\ell\)-th power and the same pullback to \(D\). Each \(q_i\) has \(\ell\) choices, differing by \(\mu_\ell(k)\); these account for \(K_Z[\ell]\). Division on the nilpotent factor has a single answer. Neither property implies a preferred splitting of the torsion sequence or compatibility of arbitrary root choices with automorphisms.

  9. For the cusp, \(c=1,b=0,\delta=1,b_x=1\), so \(g=1,r=0\), and the prime-to-characteristic torsion dimension is zero. Its Picard kernel is additive by part 3, and \(\mathbf P^1\) has no torsion in its Picard group. For the node, \(c=1,b=0,\delta=1,b_x=2\), so \(g=1,r=1\) and the dimension is one. Its kernel is \(k^*\). In characteristic \(p\), every element of the additive group is killed by \(p\). Since \(k\) is algebraically closed, its dimension over \(\mathbf F_p\) is infinite (it contains finite subfields of arbitrarily large degree). Thus substituting \(\ell=p\) into the prime-to-characteristic formula would fail. This does not contradict the earlier unique division, which required an invertible integer.

  10. Use the embedding \(A_n=k+\prod_iX_i k[[X_i]]\) from RC19. The element \(s\) has value \(X_i\) on branch \(i\), so multiplication by \(s\) is injective on every branch and therefore on \(A_n\). In the quotient its linear relation is \(\sum_iX_i=0\). Multiplying it by \(X_i\) gives \(X_i^2=0\), since mixed products already vanish. There are no further linear relations, and all products in the maximal ideal vanish. Hence

\[ A_n/(s)=k\oplus V,\qquad V=\bigl(\bigoplus_i kX_i\bigr)/k\!\left(\sum_iX_i\right), \quad V^2=0,\quad \operatorname{Soc}(A_n/(s))=V,\quad\dim_kV=n-1. \tag{RCX6} \]

The socle consists of the elements annihilated by the maximal ideal. Since \(V\ne0\) for \(n\ge2\), a nonzero scalar does not lie in it, whereas every element of \(V\) does. This establishes the exact Artin quotient and its socle dimension. Converting that calculation into a Gorenstein criterion, and transferring the criterion from a regular-model fibre to its completed local ring, still requires proof.

2W. Cartier curve singularities and the node criterion

The equality in RC15 gives a multicross completed local ring. A multicross with three or more branches is a possible reduced curve singularity, but it cannot be a Cartier curve in a regular surface. We prove this through local duality and also check it directly on cotangent spaces. The argument applies to the reduced special fibre even when the original fibre has multiplicities.

Our free comparisons are the Stacks project's Cartier-divisor Gorenstein statement, multicross criterion, Artinian duality, and quotient by a nonzerodivisor. The necessary homological and duality statements are proved below. In particular, a general dualizing-complex theorem is not an unproved input.

2W.1. Free resolutions, scalar actions and completion

For finite modules \(M,N\) over a Noetherian ring \(A\), define \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,N)\) by applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,N)\) to a free resolution of \(M\). Every term can be chosen finite free, since all successive kernels are finite.

CN1. This construction is independent of the resolution, has the long exact sequence in the first variable, and satisfies flat base change

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,N)\otimes_A B \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^i_B(M\otimes_A B,N\otimes_A B) \quad(B/A\text{ flat}). \tag{CN1} \]

If \(aM=0\), multiplication by \(a\) on every such Ext group is zero. For a local ring with residue field \(\kappa\), completion therefore preserves the \(\kappa\)-vector spaces \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(\kappa,A)\).

Proof. A map of modules lifts to free resolutions: lift the images of the generators in degree zero; in the next degree their boundary errors lie in the kernel and hence in the image of the next differential. Continue by projectivity. Two lifts of the same map are homotopic. In degree zero lift their difference into the first boundary; subtract its homotopy boundary and repeat in the next degree. Thus comparison maps between two resolutions are inverse up to homotopy. Applying Hom proves independence and functoriality.

For a short exact sequence of modules, choose resolutions of its first and third terms. Lift the degree-zero free generators of the third to the middle module and add the free generators of the first. Its kernel is an extension of the two corresponding first kernels: projection gives the map to the third kernel, and subtraction of a chosen lift leaves exactly the first kernel. Repeat. This constructs a degreewise split short exact sequence of resolutions. Applying Hom leaves it degreewise exact. Taking cocycles, lifting them, and taking their differential gives the usual connecting map; its kernel and image follow by lifting and subtracting boundaries. This proves the long exact sequence.

The scalar \(a\) on a free resolution lifts the zero map of \(M\) when \(aM=0\), so the preceding homotopy makes its action on cohomology zero. Multiplication on the target equals precomposition by this scalar on each Hom module, which proves the stated assertion.

For (CN1), tensor the resolution with \(B\). Flatness preserves its exactness, and finite freeness identifies each Hom term after tensoring with the Hom term over \(B\). Flatness also preserves kernels and images of the differentials, hence cohomology. EA7 proves that Noetherian local completion is flat and faithfully flat and has the same residue field. Since the maximal ideal kills \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(\kappa,A)\), its tensor product with the completion is that same vector space. \(\square\)

2W.2. The change of rings for a Cartier equation

CN2. Let \(S\) be Noetherian, let \(f\) be a nonzerodivisor, and put \(A=S/(f)\). For every finite \(A\)-module \(M\) there are natural isomorphisms

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^{i+1}_S(M,S) \simeq\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,A)\qquad(i\ge0). \tag{CN2} \]

Proof. First \(\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,S)=0\), since \(fM=0\) and multiplication by \(f\) is injective on \(S\). Apply Hom from \(M\) to \(0\to S\xrightarrow fS\to A\to0\). The long exact sequence, obtained by the same degreewise Hom construction in the second variable, starts with an isomorphism

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A) \simeq\operatorname{Ext}^1_S(M,S): \tag{CN3} \]

the following multiplication by \(f\) is zero by CN1. The second-variable long exact sequence exists because every term of the chosen resolution is free, so Hom from that term preserves the short exact sequence.

For a finite free \(A\)-module \(P\), its two-term \(S\)-free resolution gives

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^1_S(P,S)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,A), \qquad \operatorname{Ext}^j_S(P,S)=0\quad(j\ne1). \tag{CN4} \]

Choose a finite free \(A\)-cover \(P\to M\), with kernel \(M'\). The \(S\)-Ext sequence and (CN3) identify \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_S(M,S)\) with the cokernel of \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(M',A)\). The \(A\)-Ext sequence identifies this very cokernel with \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(M,A)\). For \(i\ge2\), both sides of (CN2) shift to their preceding degree for \(M'\), using (CN4) on the \(S\)-side and freeness of \(P\) on the \(A\)-side. Induction proves every degree. Comparison of free covers and the homotopy argument CN1 make these identifications natural. \(\square\)

2W.3. A Cartier curve in a regular surface has type one

For a one-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay local ring \(A\), with residue field \(\kappa\), its type means

\[ \tau(A)=\dim_\kappa\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(\kappa,A). \tag{CN5} \]

In dimension one, Cohen–Macaulay means that some element of the maximal ideal is a nonzerodivisor; we will exhibit one in the rings where this terminology is used.

CN3. Let \((S,\mathfrak n,\kappa)\) be a regular local ring of dimension two and let \(0\ne f\in\mathfrak n\). Then \(A=S/(f)\) has dimension one, is Cohen–Macaulay, and

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^i_A(\kappa,A)= \begin{cases}\kappa&i=1,\\0&i\ne1.\end{cases} \qquad\text{In particular }\tau(A)=1. \tag{CN6} \]

Proof. NM1 in Lesson 8 proves that a regular parameter pair \(u,v\) is a regular sequence and that its Koszul complex resolves \(\kappa\). Its dual is the same complex in reversed degrees, with a harmless sign change. Explicitly, if \(-va+ub=0\), regularity of \(v\) modulo \(u\) gives \(a=uc\) and then \(b=vc\). The degree-zero kernel is zero and the degree-two cokernel is \(S/(u,v)=\kappa\). Thus the \(S\)-Ext groups are \(\kappa\) in degree two and zero elsewhere. CN2 proves (CN6).

Here are the dimension and nonzerodivisor assertions as well. NM1–NM2 make \(S\) a factorial domain. Write \(f\) as a unit times a product of powers of distinct primes \(p_j\). Every prime minimal over \((f)\) is one of the height-one ideals \((p_j)\), by the principal height bound and factorization. Their strict inclusion in \(\mathfrak n\) gives dimension one for \(A\); a longer chain would give a chain of length at least three in \(S\).

Choose \(g\in\mathfrak n\) outside all \((p_j)\). The elementary finite prime-avoidance argument here is explicit. For each \(j\), choose \(a_j\in\mathfrak n\setminus(p_j)\) and \(b_j\) in all the other \((p_i)\) but not in \((p_j)\), taking a product of choices from \((p_i)\setminus(p_j)\). Then \(\sum_j a_jb_j\) avoids every \((p_j)\). This also works with the empty product when there is just one prime. Factorization shows that \(gh\in(f)\) implies \(h\in(f)\), so \(g\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(A\). The ideal \((f,g)\) is primary to \(\mathfrak n\): its only possible containing prime is \(\mathfrak n\), since a height-one prime containing \(f\) is one of the excluded factors. A power of the finitely generated maximal ideal therefore lies in \((f,g)\). This completes the assertions. \(\square\)

2W.4. Artinian duality and the socle

Let \(Q\) be a finite-dimensional local \(k\)-algebra with residue field \(k\), maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_Q\), and socle

\[ \operatorname{Soc}(Q)=\{q\in Q:\mathfrak m_Qq=0\}. \tag{CN7} \]

For a finite \(Q\)-module put \(D_k(M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,k)\), with \(Q\)-action \((a\lambda)(m)=\lambda(am)\).

CN4. This is an exact duality on finite modules, and \(D_k(Q)\) is injective. Moreover

\[ D_k(Q)/\mathfrak m_QD_k(Q) \simeq D_k(\operatorname{Soc}(Q)),\qquad D_k(Q)\simeq Q\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \dim_k\operatorname{Soc}(Q)=1. \tag{CN8} \]

The first isomorphism is restriction of functionals. In the last isomorphism the modules are \(Q\)-modules.

Proof. Vector-space duality is exact and its double dual is the original finite vector space, compatibly with the \(Q\)-action. The formula

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_Q(M,D_k(Q)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,k),\quad \phi\longmapsto[m\mapsto\phi(m)(1)] \tag{CN9} \]

has inverse \(\lambda\mapsto[m\mapsto(a\mapsto\lambda(am))]\). It holds for arbitrary modules. Since a functional extends across an inclusion of vector spaces by extending a basis, the right functor is exact. This proves injectivity.

Under the perfect vector-space pairing between \(Q\) and \(D_k(Q)\), the annihilator of \(\mathfrak m_QD_k(Q)\) is precisely \(\operatorname{Soc}(Q)\): it consists of the \(q\) with \(\lambda(aq)=0\) for every \(a\in\mathfrak m_Q\) and every functional \(\lambda\). Taking the dual annihilator proves the first assertion in (CN8), including its kernel.

If the socle is one-dimensional, Nakayama makes \(D_k(Q)\) cyclic; a surjection \(Q\to D_k(Q)\) is an isomorphism by equality of their \(k\)-dimensions. Conversely a free rank-one dual has a one-dimensional reduction modulo \(\mathfrak m_Q\), so the socle has dimension one. Equivalently, choose a functional \(\lambda\) nonzero on the socle. Every nonzero ideal meets the socle, by multiplying it by a last nonzero power of the nilpotent maximal ideal. Hence no nonzero ideal can lie in \(\ker\lambda\), and

\[ Q\times Q\longrightarrow k,\qquad(a,b)\longmapsto\lambda(ab) \tag{CN10} \]

is a perfect pairing. This also gives the explicit isomorphism \(a\mapsto a\lambda\). \(\square\)

2W.5. A canonical module for a complete local curve

Let \(A\) be a complete one-dimensional Noetherian local \(k\)-algebra with residue field \(k\). Suppose \(t\) is a nonzerodivisor in its maximal ideal and \(Q=A/tA\) is finite-dimensional. Put \(D=k[[t]]\), \(F=k((t))\).

CN5. The ring \(A\) is finite free over \(D\), and

\[ \omega_A=\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,D),\qquad \omega_A/t\omega_A\simeq D_k(Q). \tag{CN11} \]

This module has a length-one injective resolution, and

\[ A\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_A(\omega_A,\omega_A), \qquad \operatorname{Ext}^i_A(\omega_A,\omega_A)=0\quad(i>0). \tag{CN12} \]

It is therefore an actual dualizing module; this term here refers to a finite module with finite injective dimension and the homothety and Ext properties (CN12).

Proof. Since \(tA\) is primary to the maximal ideal, the \(t\)-adic and maximal-ideal-adic topologies agree: some \(\mathfrak m^a\subset tA\), while \(tA\subset\mathfrak m\), and taking powers gives the two bounds. A basis of \(Q\) lifts to elements \(e_1,\ldots,e_N\) of \(A\). Successively express the residue modulo \(t\), subtract it, and divide by \(t\). Completeness writes every element as \(\sum_j e_jf_j(t)\), with \(f_j\in D\). A relation between these elements can be divided by the smallest power of \(t\) among its nonzero coefficients, since \(t\) is regular. Its reduction modulo \(t\) contradicts the chosen basis. Thus these elements are a \(D\)-basis. The map \(D\to A\) is injective as well: a nonzero series is a power of \(t\) times a unit. Dualizing this basis proves (CN11), including its \(Q\)-action.

For every \(A\)-module \(M\), evaluation at one and its inverse from (CN9) give the adjunction

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(M,\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,I)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_D(M,I). \tag{CN13} \]

The modules \(F\) and \(F/D\) are divisible over the PID \(D\), hence injective. Here is the extension argument: for a map on a submodule, extend it maximally by Zorn's lemma. To add an element \(x\), its annihilator modulo the old submodule is an ideal \(aD\). Choose an image \(y\) satisfying \(ay\) equal to the prescribed image of \(ax\), using divisibility; if the ideal is zero there is no constraint. The formula on the old submodule plus \(Dx\) is then well-defined. Maximality forces extension to the entire module.

Apply \(\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,-)\) to \(0\to D\to F\to F/D\to0\). Freeness of \(A\) preserves exactness, and (CN13) makes both resulting right modules injective over \(A\). This is the asserted injective resolution of \(\omega_A\).

A free \(A\)-resolution of a finite module is also a \(D\)-free resolution. Applying (CN13) degreewise therefore identifies its Ext into \(\omega_A\) with its \(D\)-Ext into \(D\). For \(M=\omega_A\), which is \(D\)-free, the positive groups vanish. In degree zero the adjunction gives the double \(D\)-dual of \(A\), namely \(A\). Under it, multiplication by \(a\) evaluates a functional at \(a\), exactly the double-dual evaluation. Thus the isomorphism is the homothety map in (CN12). \(\square\)

2W.6. Type, canonical freeness and the Gorenstein condition

We use the standard local definition: a Noetherian local ring is Gorenstein when it has finite injective dimension as a module over itself. The following criterion proves the connection to the concrete canonical module just constructed.

CN6. For \(A,t,Q\) as in CN5,

\[ \tau(A)=\dim_k\operatorname{Soc}(Q),\qquad A\text{ Gorenstein} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \omega_A\simeq A \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \tau(A)=1. \tag{CN14} \]

The integer and the criterion do not depend on the parameter \(t\).

Proof. Apply CN2 to \(A\to Q=A/(t)\) and \(M=k\). It gives \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(k,A)=\operatorname{Hom}_Q(k,Q)=\operatorname{Soc}(Q)\). CN11 and CN4 show that \(\tau(A)=1\) exactly when \(\omega_A/t\omega_A\) is a free rank-one \(Q\)-module. Lift its generator. Nakayama gives a surjection \(A\to\omega_A\); both sides are free \(D\)-modules of the same finite rank, so this is an isomorphism. Indeed a surjective square matrix over the local ring \(D\) has invertible reduction and hence unit determinant. Conversely freeness of \(\omega_A\) gives the asserted freeness after reduction. CN5 then makes \(A\) have injective dimension at most one.

For completeness we prove the converse from finite injective dimension, rather than using a canonical-module uniqueness theorem. If \(A\) has finite injective dimension, CN2 implies that \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_Q(M,Q)=0\) in all sufficiently large degrees for every finite \(Q\)-module \(M\), with a single degree bound independent of \(M\).

Every finite \(Q\)-module \(N\) embeds into a finite sum of copies of \(D_k(Q)\): dualize a finite free cover of \(D_k(N)\), using CN4. Iterate on the finite cokernel. After sufficiently many steps the last cokernel is injective. To justify this last inference, dimension shifting gives zero \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_Q(Q/I,-)\) for every ideal \(I\). The sequence \(0\to I\to Q\to Q/I\to0\) says that every map from \(I\) extends to \(Q\). This is the injectivity criterion, whose proof is the same maximal-extension argument used in CN5: the ideal of coefficients carrying a newly adjoined element into the old domain supplies exactly the map to be extended. All ideals are finite, so the available vanishing suffices. Thus \(Q\) has a finite resolution by finite injective modules.

The dual of a finite injective \(Q\)-module is finite projective. Exact duality CN4 transforms its lifting problem against a surjection of finite modules into the extension problem for the injective. In particular a finite free cover of that dual splits; the kernel and Nakayama show that a finite projective module over a local ring is free. Dualizing the finite injective resolution consequently gives a finite free resolution of \(D_k(Q)\).

A finite module of finite projective dimension over an Artinian local ring is free. To verify this, take a minimal free resolution, choosing a basis modulo the maximal ideal for each kernel. Every differential has entries in that ideal. If its last nonzero degree were positive, multiply a basis vector in that last free module by a nonzero socle element of \(Q\). This is a nonzero vector killed by its differential, contradicting injectivity of the last differential. The socle is nonzero because a last nonzero power of the nilpotent maximal ideal is annihilated by the ideal (and for a field the socle is the whole field). A finite free resolution can be made minimal by cancelling each unit matrix entry and its two-term identity summand. Hence the minimal resolution is finite, so the argument applies.

It follows that \(D_k(Q)\) is free. Its \(k\)-dimension equals that of \(Q\), forcing rank one. CN4 gives a one-dimensional socle, and the first part gives \(\omega_A\simeq A\). This proves all equivalences. Their intrinsic Ext description proves parameter independence. \(\square\)

2W.7. The exact type of a multicross point

For \(n\ge2\) let

\[ A_n=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]/(X_iX_j:i\ne j), \qquad B_n=\prod_{i=1}^nk[[X_i]]. \tag{CN15} \]

CN7. This is a one-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay complete local ring, and

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^1_{A_n}(k,A_n)\simeq B_n/A_n \simeq k^n/k,\qquad \tau(A_n)=n-1. \tag{CN16} \]

It is Gorenstein if and only if \(n=2\), in which case it is the node. For \(n=1\) the ring is the smooth DVR and has type one.

Proof. RC19 embeds \(A_n\) as the tuples with a common constant. The element \(s=\sum_iX_i\) is a nonzerodivisor, because its value on each branch is that branch's parameter. RCX6 computed its finite Artin quotient:

\[ A_n/(s)=k\oplus V,\qquad V^2=0,\qquad \dim_kV=n-1,\qquad\operatorname{Soc}(A_n/(s))=V. \tag{CN17} \]

That proof uses only \(X_iX_j=0\) and \(\sum_iX_i=0\): multiplication by \(X_i\) gives \(X_i^2=0\), and there is just one linear relation. Thus CN5–CN6 apply and already give the type and Gorenstein assertions.

We also identify the Ext group itself. The maximal ideal is the direct sum of the cyclic branch ideals \(I_i=X_ik[[X_i]]\). An \(A_n\)-linear map from \(I_i\) to \(A_n\) must have image in \(I_i\): all the other branch ideals annihilate the source, and their common annihilator in \(A_n\) is \(I_i\). Conversely any image \(X_ih_i(X_i)\) of its generator defines such a map. Consequently

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\mathfrak m_{A_n},A_n)=B_n. \tag{CN18} \]

Apply Hom to \(0\to\mathfrak m_{A_n}\to A_n\to k\to0\). Its first Hom from \(k\) is zero, since \(s\) is regular. Its last Ext from the free module \(A_n\) is zero. It identifies \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(k,A_n)\) with the cokernel of \(A_n\to B_n\), whose map is actual multiplication. Branch constants modulo their common constant give (CN16). For \(n=1\) the two-term DVR resolution of \(k\) gives \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(k,A_1)=k\); the annihilator argument above was explicitly for \(n\ge2\). \(\square\)

2W.8. The reduced fibre of a regular model

CN8. Let \(R,X,C,k\) satisfy VP's hypotheses, and put \(Y=X_k\), \(Z=Y_{\mathrm{red}}\). At every closed point, each of \(Y\), \(Z\), and any reduced union of special-fibre components has a one-dimensional Gorenstein local ring of type one. In particular, if

\[ \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell] =\dim_kH^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)+ \sum_i\dim_kH^1(D_i,\mathcal O_{D_i}) \quad(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k), \tag{CN19} \]

then every singularity of \(Z\) is a node. If the original special fibre is also reduced, the actual algebraic node charts of NE and their intrinsic resolution of NS are available for the model.

Proof. At a closed point \(x\), the ring \(S=\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is regular of dimension two. The dimension assertion is the relative-curve dimension calculation used in VP and NS: flatness gives the base prime chain below a one-dimensional fibre chain, while the dimension bound gives at most two. VP1 and NM2 factor the special equation locally as

\[ \pi=\varepsilon\prod_{j=1}^a f_j^{m_j},\qquad \mathcal O_{Y,x}=S/(\pi),\qquad \mathcal O_{Z,x}=S/\Big(\prod_{j=1}^a f_j\Big). \tag{CN20} \]

Here the \(f_j\) are nonassociate prime local equations for exactly the components through \(x\). The radical of \((\pi)\) is their product ideal: an element in every \((f_j)\) is divisible by their product in the factorial ring, and the reverse inclusion is immediate. A chosen reduced union uses the corresponding subproduct. Every such equation is a nonzero nonunit in \(S\). CN3 gives type one and a regular parameter for each quotient.

These curve rings contain \(k\), with residue field \(k\). Their completions retain a regular parameter and a finite-dimensional parameter quotient by EA7 and flatness. CN1 gives the same type after completion; CN5–CN6 make each completed ring Gorenstein, with injective dimension at most one. This also proves the assertion for the uncompleted local ring \(A\). Indeed (CN1) for every finite module \(M\) and faithful flatness give \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,A)=0\) for \(i\ge2\), since the completed target has that injective bound. The ideal-extension criterion proved in CN6 then gives injective dimension at most one over \(A\). Existence of an initial injective embedding can be taken from the general construction: every module embeds in a product of modules \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(A,\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z)\), using enough additive characters to separate its nonzero elements. Divisibility makes \(\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z\) injective over \(\mathbf Z\) by CN5's PID argument, and adjunction makes each coinduced module and their product injective. A nonzero additive element is detected by a character on its cyclic group, extended to the whole additive group by that injectivity. Thus the criterion does not assume injective resolutions without constructing them.

Finally RC6–RC7 turn (CN19) into the multicross description of every completed singular local ring, with \(n=b_x\ge2\). CN1 and CN3 give its type one, while CN7 gives type \(n-1\); hence \(n=2\). There is also a direct cotangent check:

\[ \dim_k\mathfrak m_{S/(f)}/\mathfrak m_{S/(f)}^2 =\dim_k\mathfrak n/(\mathfrak n^2+(f))\le2,\qquad \dim_k\mathfrak m_{A_n}/\mathfrak m_{A_n}^2=n. \tag{CN21} \]

The two independent linear parameters of the regular surface give the first bound, and the axes relations have degree two, giving the second equality. Both arguments exclude \(n>2\). If \(Y=Z\), NE applies to the split completed nodes of the actual special fibre and supplies pointed étale algebraic charts; NS resolves their positive thicknesses under its stated model hypotheses.

This conclusion concerns the reduced fibre. It does not force the original multiplicities \(m_j\) in (CN20) to be one. Regular-model existence, minimalization, uniform numerical bounds and the remaining genus inequalities still enter the general semistable-reduction argument. No analytic period covering or whole semiabelian lift follows just from the local criterion. \(\square\)

2W.9. Graded exercise: local duality and the nodal boundary

Exercise 2W (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. For \(A=k[[u,v]]/(uv)\), compute every \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(k,A)\). Explain why their vanishing above degree one does not say that the ring is regular or that \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(k,k)\) vanishes there.
  2. Prove the flat-completion comparison of CN1 directly from a finite-rank free resolution. Explain why it preserves the scalar action and the exact type, even if the resolution is infinite.
  3. For \(Q=k[e]/e^m\), \(m\ge2\), give a functional whose product pairing is perfect, compute its matrix and determinant, and identify the socle. Do the same for \(k[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)\).
  4. For \(Q=k[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^2)\), compute the socle and the minimum number of generators of \(D_k(Q)\). Prove that no functional gives a perfect product pairing.
  5. Regard the node as a finite free algebra over \(D=k[[s]]\), with \(s=x+y\). Give a basis and its multiplication table. Construct an explicit generator of its canonical module and verify that the associated \(D\)-valued pairing is perfect in every characteristic.
  6. For the three-axis ring over \(D=k[[s]]\), \(s=x_1+x_2+x_3\), give a basis. For a functional with values \(a,b,c\) on that basis, compute its product-pairing determinant. Compare its divisibility with the exact canonical-module generator count and with the branch-projection calculation of Ext.
  7. In the formal regular surface \(k[[x,y]]\), put \(\pi=x^2y\), giving a local map \(k[[\pi]]\to k[[x,y]]\). Compute the original and reduced special fibres, their component multiplicities and their local types. State why a nodal reduced fibre does not prove semistable reduction of this model.
  8. Compute \(\delta,b_x,\tau\) for the cusp \(k[[x,y]]/(y^2-x^3)\). Identify exactly which hypothesis of the multicross node criterion fails. Explain why Gorenstein does not mean smooth or nodal.
  9. Suppose a supplied regular model of a genus-\(g\) curve satisfies VP's torsion hypotheses, with \(\ell\) prime to the residue characteristic and to \(d=\gcd_i m_i\). Assume \(\dim\operatorname{Pic}(C)[\ell]=2g\), the VP obstruction has dimension at most the incidence rank \(r\), and \(g\ge g_Z=\dim H^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)\). Use the proved formulas to force the exact equalities and nodality of \(Z\). Identify the separate assertions still needed for a general existence theorem.
  10. For the ordinary plane triple point \(k[[x,y]]/(xy(x-y))\), compute its type, its conductor defect and its prime-to-characteristic local unit factors. Compare it with the three-axis multicross and verify the cotangent-space obstruction.

Complete solution.

  1. The ring \(S=k[[u,v]]\) is regular local of dimension two, with its displayed regular parameters. The equation \(uv\) is a nonzero nonunit, so CN3 gives

    \[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(k,A)=0,\quad \operatorname{Ext}^1_A(k,A)=k,\quad \operatorname{Ext}^i_A(k,A)=0\ (i\ge2). \tag{CNX1} \]

    The maximal ideal of \(A\) needs two generators, while the dimension is one; it is not regular. These Ext groups have target \(A\), so their vanishing expresses an injective property of \(A\). The regularity argument NM1 instead involves free resolutions and Tor, or Ext with residue-field target. Changing the target changes the Hom complex; no vanishing for the latter groups follows from (CNX1).

  2. Write a free resolution with finite free terms \(P_i\). Termwise finite freeness identifies \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(P_i,A)\otimes_A\widehat A\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat A}(P_i\otimes_A\widehat A,\widehat A)\). Flatness preserves both the resolution and the kernel and image in every fixed degree, giving the stated comparison. A fixed degree uses only two adjacent differentials, so no infinite product or sum is interchanged with tensoring. Multiplication by an element acts by the same scalar on each compared term. For \(M=k\), CN1's homotopy makes the maximal ideal act by zero on Ext; tensoring with the completion therefore gives that same \(k\)-vector space, with unchanged dimension.

  3. Let \(\lambda\) extract the coefficient of \(e^{m-1}\). In the ordered basis \(1,e,\ldots,e^{m-1}\), the product-pairing matrix has ones on the antidiagonal and zeros elsewhere:

    \[ G_{ij}= \begin{cases}1&i+j=m-1,\\0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \quad(0\le i,j<m),\qquad \det G=(-1)^{m(m-1)/2}. \tag{CNX2} \]

    The socle is \(ke^{m-1}\). For \(k[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)\), let \(\lambda\) extract \(xy\). In the basis \(1,x,y,xy\), its matrix is the antidiagonal permutation matrix of size four, with determinant one. Its socle is \(kxy\): multiplying a general element by \(x\) and \(y\) kills exactly all coefficients except the \(xy\) coefficient. All determinants stay nonzero in characteristic two.

  4. The maximal ideal is \(kx\oplus ky\), its square is zero, and it is exactly the socle. Thus \(D_k(Q)\) needs two generators by CN8 and Nakayama. More explicitly any functional gives the matrix

    \[ \begin{pmatrix} \lambda(1)&\lambda(x)&\lambda(y)\\ \lambda(x)&0&0\\ \lambda(y)&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \tag{CNX3} \]

    with determinant zero. Its last two rows are linearly dependent, including when one or both of their displayed entries vanish. This agrees with the socle obstruction.

  5. The basis is \(1,x\), with \(y=s-x\) and \(x^2=sx\). Every branch series reduces to this form by the common-constant description, or by CN5 and the two-dimensional quotient modulo \(s\). Let \(\lambda(1)=0,\lambda(x)=1\). Then

    \[ \bigl(\lambda(e_ie_j)\bigr)_{e=(1,x)} =\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&s\end{pmatrix}, \qquad\det=-1. \tag{CNX4} \]

    Thus \(a\mapsto[b\mapsto\lambda(ab)]\) identifies \(A\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,D)\). This is an actual canonical-module generator and a unimodular pairing, including in characteristic two.

  6. Use \(1,x_1,x_2\), with \(x_3=s-x_1-x_2\), \(x_i^2=sx_i\), and \(x_1x_2=0\). These span: a higher power on a branch is \(s^{j-1}x_i\), and \(x_3\) is eliminated by its displayed relation. Independence follows by restriction first to branch three, then to branches one and two. The product-pairing matrix and its determinant are

    \[ G=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\b&sb&0\\c&0&sc\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det G=sbc(sa-b-c). \tag{CNX5} \]

    Every determinant is divisible by \(s\), so none is a unit of \(D\). Reduction modulo \(s\) gives the ring in part 4; its dual needs two generators. The same is therefore true of the canonical module by CN11 and Nakayama. In (CN18), projection to branches one and two gives independent classes modulo the diagonal constants; the three projections sum to the image of one. Thus \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(k,A_3)=k^3/k\) has dimension two. The determinant, minimal-generator and Ext calculations agree.

  7. The local map is injective: a nonzero series in \(\pi\) becomes a nonzero series in \(x^2y\), with distinct monomials. The original special fibre is \(k[[x,y]]/(x^2y)\), with multiplicities \(2,1\) on \(x=0,y=0\). Its reduced fibre is \(k[[x,y]]/(xy)\). Both equations are nonzerodivisors in the regular surface, so CN3 gives type one for both rings. The reduced curve is a node, but the original fibre is nonreduced; for example the nonzero class \(xy\) has square zero. A semistable special fibre must itself be reduced. This is a local example and does not assert that this formal surface is already a global proper curve model.

  8. Its normalization is \(k[[t]]\), with \(x=t^2,y=t^3\). The quotient is spanned by \(t\), so \(\delta=1,b_x=1\). The equation is a nonzero nonunit in a regular two-dimensional ring, hence \(\tau=1\) by CN3. But

    \[ \delta-b_x+1=1,\qquad \widehat A\ne k[[X_1,\ldots,X_{b_x}]]/ (X_iX_j:i\ne j). \tag{CNX6} \]

    For one branch the right ring would be a smooth DVR, whereas the cusp has a missing first coefficient. It fails the multicross hypothesis, equivalently the equality in RC15. Gorenstein controls its canonical module, not the number or shape of its branches by itself.

  9. VP and the assumed obstruction bound give \(2g-r\le\dim\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell]=2b+r\), hence \(g\le b+r\). RC7 and RC12 give \(g_Z=b+r+\sum_x\epsilon_x\ge b+r\). Together with the supplied inequality,

    \[ b+r\le g_Z\le g\le b+r. \tag{CNX7} \]

    All are equal, so every \(\epsilon_x=0\). RC6–RC7 give multicross points; CN8 makes them nodes. The assumptions include the actual generic torsion rank, the hypotheses needed for VP's torsion map, and a bound on the numerical obstruction for this same model. Establishing them uniformly after finite extension, producing and minimalizing a regular model, and proving reducedness of the original fibre still require their own arguments. The equality chain alone does not change the multiplicities or construct an analytic covering.

  10. CN3 gives type one because the ring is a hypersurface in the regular plane. RCX4 gives \(b_x=3,\delta=3,\epsilon=1\), with local unit quotient \((k^*)^2\times(k,+)\). Its cotangent dimension is two, since its defining equation has degree three and imposes no linear relation. The three-axis multicross has \(b_x=3,\delta=2,\epsilon=0\), local quotient \((k^*)^2\), and type two by CN7. Its cotangent dimension is three, since all its defining relations are quadratic. It therefore cannot be a Cartier curve in a regular surface with cotangent dimension two. A plane point with three distinct branch tangents is not automatically the multicross ring used in the equality theorem.

2X. Fibre cycles, genus inequalities and multiplicities

The reduced-fibre torsion bound and local node criterion do not by themselves eliminate multiplicities. We now prove the cohomology and intersection inequalities that do so on a supplied regular model with numerically minimal component data. The proof uses actual component-addition exact sequences, including the cases with repeated components.

Keep VP's hypotheses: \(R\) is a complete DVR with algebraically closed residue field \(k\), and \(X/R\) is an integral regular flat projective relative curve with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre \(C\), of genus \(g\). Write

\[ Y=X_k=\sum_{i=1}^s m_iC_i,\quad Z=Y_{\mathrm{red}}=\sum_iC_i,\quad d=\gcd_i m_i,\quad n_i=m_i/d,\quad D=\sum_i n_iC_i . \tag{MG1} \]

The \(C_i\) are integral proper curves. Put \(p_i=\dim_kH^1(C_i,\mathcal O_{C_i})\), and let \(Q_{ij}=C_i\cdot C_j\) be VP's actual intersection matrix. Let \(b_i\) be the genus of the normalization of \(C_i\), and put \(b=\sum_i b_i\).

The free comparisons are the Stacks project's primitive-fibre construction, Euler-characteristic relation, strict genus comparison, component-graph inequality, and numerical minimality criterion. The proofs needed here follow explicitly.

2X.1. Adding a component, with its full cohomology sequence

For an effective vertical Cartier divisor \(A=\sum_i a_iC_i\), write \(\chi(A)=\chi(A,\mathcal O_A)\), and use the zero divisor as the empty scheme, with Euler characteristic zero.

MG1. For every \(i\) there is an exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(-A)|_{C_i} \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{A+C_i} \longrightarrow\mathcal O_A\longrightarrow0,\qquad \chi(A+C_i)-\chi(A)=1-p_i-(Qa)_i . \tag{MG2} \]

The line in this sequence has no global section when \((Qa)_i>0\). All the sheaves in (MG2) have zero cohomology in degrees at least two.

Proof. Locally let \(u\) and \(v\) be equations for \(A\) and \(C_i\) in the regular local domain of \(X\). The kernel of \(S/(uv)\to S/(u)\) is \(uS/(uv)\); multiplication by \(u\) identifies it with \(S/(v)\), since \(u\) is a nonzerodivisor. Changing the equation \(u\) changes this identification by exactly the transition unit of \(\mathcal O_X(-A)\). Thus it is the indicated line on \(C_i\), even when \(C_i\) already occurs in \(A\).

Its degree is \(-A\cdot C_i=-(Qa)_i\), by VP3 and degree additivity CE1. The constants of \(C_i\) are \(k\): RC1's finite normalization injects them into the constants \(k\) of its smooth integral projective normalization, and the constant functions give the reverse inclusion. Hence \(\chi(C_i,\mathcal O_{C_i})=1-p_i\). The degree definition and additivity of Euler characteristics prove (MG2).

A nonzero section of a line on an integral proper curve gives an injection of the structure sheaf into that line. Its cokernel has finite support, since the section is nonzero at the generic point. Its Euler characteristic is its nonnegative \(k\)-length. Thus a line of negative degree has no nonzero global section.

We also justify the cohomological dimension being used. For any line \(L\) on \(C_i\), tensor its finite normalization sequence with \(L\). It is an injection into the finite pushforward of its pullback, with a finite-support cokernel. Finite pushforward has the same affine Čech complex, and a finite-support sheaf has no positive cohomology, as in RC2. The smooth normalized curve has no cohomology above degree one by the two-affine curve calculation DC5. Hence \(H^j(C_i,L)=0\) for \(j\ge2\); the same argument gives finiteness in degrees zero and one. Starting with the empty divisor and adding its finitely many components with repetitions, (MG2) now gives these assertions for \(\mathcal O_A\) as well. \(\square\)

2X.2. The primitive component-addition sequence and its constants

MG2. There exists a finite sequence

\[ Z=A_0\subset A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_N=D,\qquad A_{j+1}=A_j+C_{i_j},\qquad N=\sum_i(n_i-1), \tag{MG3} \]

such that \(A_j\cdot C_{i_j}>0\) at every step. Every \(A_j\) has global constants exactly \(k\), and every restriction on \(H^1\) in this sequence is surjective.

Proof. The vector \(n=(n_i)\) is primitive and satisfies \(Qn=0\). Suppose \(A\) has coefficient vector \(a\), with \(1\le a_i\le n_i\), and \(a\ne n\). The negative-form identity VP4 gives \(a^TQa<0\). Indeed its only rational kernel is the line through \(n\). If \(a=tn\), a Bézout combination of the primitive entries \(n_i\) shows \(t\) is an integer; the inequalities force \(t=1\), contrary to \(a\ne n\). Consequently

\[ \sum_i(n_i-a_i)(Qa)_i=(n-a)^TQa=-a^TQa>0. \tag{MG4} \]

Some deficient index \(i\), with \(a_i<n_i\), therefore has \((Qa)_i>0\). Add that component. Each step decreases \(\sum_i(n_i-a_i)\) by one, so it stops at \(D\), with exactly the length stated in (MG3).

VP1 gives \(\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)=k\). At each step the kernel line in (MG2) has negative degree and hence zero \(H^0\). Restriction therefore injects \(\Gamma(A+C_i,\mathcal O)\) into \(\Gamma(A,\mathcal O)=k\), and the constant functions show it is exactly \(k\). The \(H^0\) restriction is consequently an isomorphism. The full long exact sequence and MG1 now give

\[ 0\longrightarrow H^1(C_i,\mathcal O_X(-A)|_{C_i}) \longrightarrow H^1(A+C_i,\mathcal O) \longrightarrow H^1(A,\mathcal O)\longrightarrow0. \tag{MG5} \]

This proves all assertions, not just equality of Euler characteristics. \(\square\)

2X.3. Generic genus, the gcd and the primitive fibre

Put \(g_D=\dim_kH^1(D,\mathcal O_D)\) and \(g_Z=\dim_kH^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)\).

MG3. One has

\[ 1-g=d(1-g_D). \tag{MG6} \]

In particular, \(d\) divides \(g-1\). If \(d=1\), then \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=k\), \(\dim_kH^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=g\), and

\[ H^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\twoheadrightarrow H^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z), \qquad g\ge g_Z . \tag{MG7} \]

A supplied \(K\)-point of \(C\) ensures \(d=1\) by VP7.

Proof. The line \(T=\mathcal O_X(D)\) has torsion order \(d\) by VP2–VP5: its \(d\)-th power is the principal fibre line, and the vertical Picard lattice gives its exact order. Its restriction to \(D\) is therefore torsion, so has degree zero, using CE1's additive degree on the possibly nonreduced proper curve \(D\).

For each integer \(r\ge1\), the same local multiplication proof as MG1 gives

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(-rD)|_D \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{(r+1)D} \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{rD}\longrightarrow0 . \tag{MG8} \]

The kernel line has degree zero because it is a power of \(T|_D\). Thus its Euler characteristic is \(\chi(D)\), and induction gives \(\chi(rD)=r\chi(D)\). Since \(Y=dD\), this yields \(\chi(Y)=d\chi(D)\). The flat Euler-characteristic theorem CE3 gives \(\chi(Y)=\chi(C)=1-g\), and MG2 gives \(\chi(D)=1-g_D\). This proves (MG6).

When \(d=1\), \(D=Y\), so its constants and \(H^1\) assertion follow from MG2 and the Euler identity. Composing the actual surjections (MG5) proves (MG7). No unjustified \(H^0\) base-change isomorphism is being assumed. \(\square\)

2X.4. The Euler polynomial and the numerical genus budget

Call the component data numerically minimal if no index has both \(p_i=0\) and \(Q_{ii}=-1\).

MG4. For every effective vertical cycle \(A=\sum_i a_iC_i\),

\[ \chi(A)=\sum_i a_i(1-p_i) -\frac12\left(a^TQa-\sum_i a_iQ_{ii}\right). \tag{MG9} \]

In particular,

\[ 2g-2=\sum_i m_iq_i,\qquad q_i=2p_i-2-Q_{ii}. \tag{MG10} \]

For numerically minimal data and \(g\ge2\), every \(q_i\ge0\). Every index with \(q_i>0\) satisfies \(m_iq_i\le2g-2\), and there are at most \(2g-2\) such indices.

Proof. The right side of (MG9) vanishes at \(a=0\) and changes by \(1-p_i-(Qa)_i\) when \(a\) changes to \(a+e_i\), exactly (MG2). Induction on the sum of the coefficients proves the formula for every ordering. The expression is integral, since

\[ a^TQa-\sum_i a_iQ_{ii} =\sum_i a_i(a_i-1)Q_{ii} +2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_jQ_{ij} \tag{MG11} \]

is even. Insert \(a=m\), use \(Qm=0\) and \(\chi(Y)=1-g\), to obtain (MG10).

If \(s>1\), connectedness of the intersection graph and \(Qm=0\) imply \(Q_{ii}<0\) for every \(i\). For \(p_i=0\), numerical minimality therefore forces \(Q_{ii}\le-2\), giving \(q_i\ge0\). For \(p_i\ge1\), one has \(q_i\ge1\). If \(s=1\), then \(Q_{11}=0\), \(D=C_1\), and (MG6) reads \(g-1=d(p_1-1)\). The assumption \(g\ge2\) forces \(p_1\ge2\), again giving \(q_1>0\). All positive summands in (MG10) are positive integers, which proves the bounds.

For \(s>1\), the zero-budget components are precisely \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-2\). Their multiplicities obey the exact harmonic equation

\[ 2m_i=\sum_{j\ne i}Q_{ij}m_j . \tag{MG12} \]

The genus budget alone does not bound the number of these components or the length of their chains; a uniform numerical-type argument must still control them. \(\square\)

2X.5. The component graph, its genus and the exact defect

Let \(\Gamma\) be the simple graph with one vertex for each \(C_i\) and one edge for each unordered pair with \(Q_{ij}>0\), regardless of the size of that intersection number. It is connected. Write \(e\) for its edge count and

\[ t=e-s+1 . \tag{MG13} \]

This is not the branch-incidence graph of RC5; its rank need not equal \(r\) there.

MG5. There are exact formulas

\[ g_Z=\sum_i p_i+\sum_{i<j}Q_{ij}-s+1,\qquad g_Z-(b+t)=\sum_i(p_i-b_i) +\sum_{\substack{i<j\\Q_{ij}>0}}(Q_{ij}-1)\ge0 . \tag{MG14} \]

Equality holds if and only if every \(C_i\) is smooth and every meeting pair has total intersection number one.

Proof. Apply (MG9) to \(a=(1,\ldots,1)\); its diagonal terms cancel. Since \(Z\) has constants \(k\), this gives the first formula. Subtract \(b+t\) to get the second. For the integral component \(C_i\), RC1–RC2 give

\[ p_i-b_i=\sum_{x\in C_i} \dim_k\bigl((\nu_{i*}\mathcal O_{D_i})_x/\mathcal O_{C_i,x}\bigr)\ge0 . \tag{MG15} \]

Equality means that the finite normalization is an isomorphism, hence \(C_i\) is smooth. Each positive \(Q_{ij}\) is an integer, a sum of positive local intersection lengths over \(k\), by VP3. Thus the other summands are nonnegative and vanish precisely as stated.

When \(Q_{ij}=1\), there is exactly one intersection point and its local quotient \(S/(f_i,f_j)\) has length one. Thus \((f_i,f_j)\) is the maximal ideal of the regular surface local ring; the equations are regular parameters and the two curves meet transversely. Three distinct components can still pass through the same point with pairwise transverse intersections. Consequently the equality in (MG14) alone does not assert that the whole reduced curve is nodal. RC's separate torsion equality and CN's local criterion are still needed. \(\square\)

2X.6. Strict loss of genus for a nonreduced primitive cycle

MG6. Assume numerical minimality. Then

\[ g_D\ge g_Z,\qquad g_D=g_Z\ \Longleftrightarrow\ D=Z . \tag{MG16} \]

In particular, when \(d=1\),

\[ g=g_Z\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Y=Z \ \Longleftrightarrow\ m_i=1\text{ for every }i . \tag{MG17} \]

Proof. Every step of (MG3) has the exact cohomology sequence (MG5). The kernel has dimension

\[ h^1(C_i,\mathcal O_X(-A)|_{C_i}) =p_i-1+(Qa)_i , \tag{MG18} \]

since the line has zero \(H^0\) and Euler characteristic \(1-p_i-(Qa)_i\). Summing gives \(g_D-g_Z\ge0\).

If \(D\ne Z\), consider the last step \(D=A+C_i\). Then \(Qn=0\) gives \((Qa)_i=-Q_{ii}\), so its kernel has dimension \(p_i-1-Q_{ii}\). There must be more than one component, because for \(s=1\) the primitive coefficient is one and \(D=Z\). Thus \(Q_{ii}\le-1\). If \(p_i\ge1\), this kernel has positive dimension. If \(p_i=0\), numerical minimality gives \(Q_{ii}\le-2\), with the same conclusion. The last step alone therefore makes \(g_D>g_Z\). Conversely \(D=Z\) gives equality. For \(d=1\), MG3 gives \(g_D=g\) and \(D=Y\), proving (MG17). \(\square\)

2X.7. What numerical minimality means geometrically

MG7. The excluded numerical pair \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\) is equivalent to

\[ C_i\simeq\mathbf P^1_k,\qquad \mathcal O_X(C_i)|_{C_i}\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1}(-1). \tag{MG19} \]

Thus numerical minimality is exactly the absence of vertical curves of the first kind, where this term means the pair of properties in (MG19).

Proof. If \(p_i=0\), (MG15) and nonnegativity force the normalization genus and every normalization defect to vanish. Hence \(C_i\) is a smooth projective genus-zero curve. Choose a \(k\)-point \(P\), which exists over algebraically closed \(k\). Riemann–Roch SD gives \(\chi(\mathcal O(P))=2\), so it has at least two independent sections. Their ratio supplies a nonconstant rational function with pole divisor bounded by \(P\), choosing the constant section as denominator in the rational-function description of sections. It defines a proper map \(C_i\to\mathbf P^1\), finite by Lesson 3, §0F. Its degree is the pole-divisor degree, at most one and positive, by DC's finite-pullback degree calculation; it is therefore one. A finite degree-one map to the normal curve \(\mathbf P^1\) is an isomorphism: on affine charts its finite integral algebra lies in the same function field, and integral closedness leaves just the target algebra.

Every line on \(\mathbf P^1_k\) is \(\mathcal O(a)\), with \(a\) its degree. Indeed DC1–DC4 identify lines with divisors; a degree-zero divisor is principal by products of linear factors and the corresponding order at infinity. The normal line of the Cartier component is \(\mathcal O_X(C_i)|_{C_i}\), whose degree is \(Q_{ii}\) by VP3. Thus \(Q_{ii}=-1\) gives (MG19). Conversely that pair plainly has \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\).

This identifies the geometric configuration excluded by the hypothesis. It does not construct a contraction, prove that a succession of contractions terminates in a regular model, or establish regular-model existence. Those are separate geometric tasks; numerical minimality here is an explicit condition on a supplied model. \(\square\)

2X.8. The conditional semistable-fibre criterion

MG8. Suppose the supplied regular model has numerically minimal data and \(d=1\). Let \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\) be a prime for which the following two assertions hold for this same model and generic curve:

\[ \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(C)[\ell]=2g, \qquad \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\Phi_X[\ell]\le t . \tag{MG20} \]

Then \(Y\) is reduced and nodal; every \(C_i\) is smooth, and each meeting pair intersects once and transversely. In particular the actual algebraic node charts and intrinsic resolution from NE–NS apply to the original model.

Proof. The actual VP torsion obstruction, followed by RC's bound, gives

\[ 2g-t\le\dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell] \le g_Z+b . \tag{MG21} \]

MG3 and MG5 give \(g\ge g_Z\ge t+b\). Combining all three inequalities in the direction that controls equality yields

\[ 2g\le t+g_Z+b\le2g_Z\le2g . \tag{MG22} \]

Every inequality is an equality. Thus \(g=g_Z\), so MG6 forces \(Y=Z\) and all multiplicities one. Also \(g_Z=t+b\), so MG5 makes the components smooth and their pairwise intersections single transverse points. Finally (MG21) is equality in RC15. RC7 gives multicross completed singularities, and CN8 makes them nodes. As \(Y=Z\), these are now the actual special-fibre nodes to which NE applies, followed by NS's intrinsic construction under its stated hypotheses.

This is a criterion for a supplied model, with both assertions (MG20) specified at its actual field and numerical group. To obtain a general existence theorem, one still has to construct a regular model, reach the stated minimality condition and establish a uniform numerical bound that proves the second assertion after the finite extension used for the first. Choosing a prime after splitting its torsion without controlling the new model would not establish (MG20). The whole semiabelian lift and initial analytic period cover remain further constructions. \(\square\)

2X.9. Graded exercise: primitive cycles and genus loss

Exercise 2X (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. In \(S=k[[x,y]]\), take \(A=2C_1+C_2\), with \(C_1=(x)\), \(C_2=(y)\). Write the exact local sequence for adding \(C_1\), its kernel map, and its cancellation proof. Explain which line bundle supplies the global transition factors.
  2. Let\[ m=(1,2,1),\qquad Q=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1&0\\1&-1&1\\0&1&-2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad p_1=p_2=p_3=0 . \tag{MGX1} \] Find the primitive component-addition sequence, every kernel degree and \(H^1\)-dimension, the generic genus from MG10, and the reduced-fibre genus. Identify the missing hypothesis for a strict drop.
  3. Treat the following as numerical data, without assuming a geometric realization:\[ m=(1,2,3),\quad Q=\begin{pmatrix}-13&2&3\\2&-10&6\\3&6&-5\end{pmatrix}, \qquad p_i=0 . \tag{MGX2} \] Find a positive component-addition sequence from \((1,1,1)\) to \(m\). Compute its kernel dimensions, both genera and the full genus budget.
  4. For the numerical data \(m=(3,6)\), \(Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-4&2\\2&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \((p_1,p_2)=(0,1)\), compute \(d,n,g_D,g,g_Z\), the primitive sequence and its cohomology kernel. Check both the gcd formula and the full-fibre Euler formula; no geometric realization is assumed.
  5. For two components with genera \(p_1,p_2\), self-intersections \(u,v\), and intersection number \(a>0\), derive \(\chi(rC_1+sC_2)\) for all nonnegative integers \(r,s\). Verify its two first differences and the connected reduced-union genus.
  6. Two smooth rational components meet transversely at two distinct points and nowhere else. Compute the simple component-graph rank \(t\), the branch-incidence rank \(r\), the reduced genus, and both genus defects. Explain why the two graph ranks cannot be interchanged in MG20.
  7. Let \(Z\subset\mathbf P^2_k\) be three distinct concurrent lines. Compute \(p_i,b,t,r,g_Z\), the defect in MG14 and the defect in RC15. Explain precisely why equality in the component-graph bound does not rule out this point.
