  8. Prove the geometric characterization (MG19), including the use of a rational point and the normal-line degree. Identify the additional theorem needed to turn this characterization into a construction of a model without such curves.
  9. Assume MG8's hypotheses with \(g=3,b=1,t=2\). Compute the forced reduced genus and Picard-torsion dimension. Prove reducedness, the component intersection conclusions and actual nodality, listing the separate equality argument for each.
  10. Using only \(1-g=d(1-g_D)\), determine the possible positive integers \(d\) for \(g=0,1,2,3\). Explain what these arithmetic possibilities do and do not establish about curve models.

Complete solution.

  1. The sequence is

    \[ 0\longrightarrow S/(x) \xrightarrow{\ h\mapsto x^2yh\ }S/(x^3y) \longrightarrow S/(x^2y)\longrightarrow0 . \tag{MGX3} \]

    If \(x^2yh\in(x^3y)\), cancellation in the domain gives \(h\in(x)\); this proves injectivity. Its image is exactly the ideal generated by \(x^2y\) in the middle quotient, which is the kernel of restriction. Replacing \(x^2y\) by a unit times it changes the kernel frame by that unit. Thus the global kernel is \(\mathcal O_X(-A)|_{C_1}\), not a globally chosen trivial line on the component. The computation remains valid although \(C_1\) already occurred twice.

  2. One has \(Qm=0\), \(d=1\), and

    \[ Q(1,1,1)^T=(-1,1,-1)^T . \tag{MGX4} \]

    Add the middle component, reaching \(m\) in one step. Its kernel line has degree \(-1\); on the rational genus-zero component its Euler characteristic is zero and its \(H^0\) is zero, so \(h^1=0\). MG10 gives \(2g-2=0+2(-1)+0=-2\), hence \(g=0\). MG14 gives \(g_Z=0+(1+1)-3+1=0\). The middle component has \(p_2=0,Q_{22}=-1\), violating numerical minimality. Thus this numerical equality is exactly consistent with the exception in the strict-drop proof. The data also occur by starting with \(\mathbf P^1_R\), blowing up a smooth fibre point and then the intersection of its two reduced fibre components; the NS charts give the resulting multiplicity-two middle component. This realization does not satisfy the minimality hypothesis.

  3. The successive coefficient vectors and selected intersection degrees are

    \[ (1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\ i=3\ }(1,1,2) \xrightarrow{\ i=2\ }(1,2,2) \xrightarrow{\ i=3\ }(1,2,3),\qquad (Qa)_i=4,4,5 . \tag{MGX5} \]

    For verification the three matrix products before addition are \((-8,-2,4)\), \((-5,4,-1)\), and \((-3,-6,5)\). The kernel lines have degrees \(-4,-4,-5\) and, by MG18 with \(p_i=0\), \(H^1\)-dimensions \(3,3,4\). MG14 gives \(g_Z=2+3+6-3+1=9\). The budget coefficients are \(q=(11,8,3)\), so

    \[ 2g-2=1\cdot11+2\cdot8+3\cdot3=36,\qquad g=19. \tag{MGX6} \]

    The genus drop is \(19-9=10=3+3+4\), as required. Every diagonal is at most \(-2\), so the numerical data have no excluded genus-zero \((-1)\)-component. All these statements are conditional numerical checks; a realization has not been constructed.

  4. Here \(d=3,n=(1,2)\). The primitive sequence is \((1,1)\to(1,2)\), adding the second component, since \(Q(1,1)^T=(-2,1)^T\). Its line has degree \(-1\), zero \(H^0\) and \(h^1=1-1+1=1\). The reduced genus is \(g_Z=0+1+2-2+1=2\), so \(g_D=3\). The gcd relation gives \(1-g=3(1-3)=-6\), hence \(g=7\). Independently \(q=(2,1)\) and

    \[ \sum_i m_iq_i=3\cdot2+6\cdot1=12=2\cdot7-2. \tag{MGX7} \]

    Thus \(\chi(D)=-2\) and \(\chi(Y)=-6=3\chi(D)\). The component of self-intersection \(-1\) has genus one, so it does not violate the specified numerical minimality.

  5. Substitute the two coefficients in (MG9):

    \[ \chi(rC_1+sC_2)=r(1-p_1)+s(1-p_2) -\binom r2u-\binom s2v-rsa . \tag{MGX8} \]

    The first differences are \(1-p_1-ru-sa\) and \(1-p_2-ra-sv\), precisely \(1-p_i-A\cdot C_i\). At \(r=s=1\), the constants of the connected reduced union are \(k\), giving genus \(p_1+p_2+a-1\). The binomial terms also explain directly why the half-integral-looking expression in (MG9) is integral.

  6. The simple graph has two vertices and one edge, so \(t=0\). The branch-incidence graph has two component vertices, two singular vertices and four edges, so \(r=4-4+1=1\). The normalization genus is \(b=0\), and \(g_Z=0+2-2+1=1\). The defect in MG14 is \(Q_{12}-1=1\); the defect in RC15 is zero, since both singularities are nodes. Accordingly the actual special Picard-torsion dimension is one. MG20 bounds a numerical obstruction by the simple-graph rank, which is zero here; replacing it by the incidence rank would weaken a hypothesis and would not justify MG8's same equality chain or its single-intersection-per-pair conclusion.

  7. Each component is \(\mathbf P^1\), so \(p_i=0\), \(b=0\). Every component pair has one transverse intersection, all at the common point. Thus \(e=3,s=3,t=1\), and MG14's calculation gives \(g_Z=1\) with defect zero. The normalization has three preimages of the single singular point, so its incidence graph has four vertices and three edges, giving \(r=0\). RCX4 gives \(\delta=3,b_x=3\), hence RC15's defect is one and the Picard-torsion dimension is zero. Therefore equality in MG14 makes the components smooth and each pair transverse, but allows their intersections to coincide. The separate torsion equality excludes that additional local coefficient condition. This is a plane curve example, not an assertion that its projective-plane self-intersections are the intersection matrix of a DVR fibre.

  8. From \(p_i=0\), normalization gives \(p_i=b_i+\sum_x\delta_{i,x}\); all terms are nonnegative, so the component is smooth of genus zero. Algebraic closedness provides a point \(P\). Riemann–Roch supplies a nonconstant function with at most a simple pole at \(P\), giving a finite degree-one map to \(\mathbf P^1\), hence an isomorphism by integral closedness of the target. The normal line is \(\mathcal O_X(C_i)|_{C_i}\), with degree \(Q_{ii}=-1\); the degree classification of lines on \(\mathbf P^1\) gives \(\mathcal O(-1)\). Conversely this curve and normal line have the stated numerical pair. To produce a model without them one still needs an actual contraction theorem, preservation of regularity and projectivity in the required setting, and a termination argument. The numerical characterization alone proves none of these construction assertions.

  9. MG21 gives \(4\le\dim\operatorname{Pic}(Z)[\ell]\le g_Z+1\), so \(g_Z\ge3\). MG3 gives \(g_Z\le3\); hence \(g_Z=3\) and the torsion dimension is four. MG6's strict equality criterion forces \(Y=Z\), giving all multiplicities one. Equality \(g_Z=b+t=3\) in MG14 makes every component smooth and every meeting pair intersect once transversely. Equality in RC15 gives the completed multicross rings, and CN8 reduces them to nodes. The earlier reducedness conclusion is what permits NE's actual algebraic charts for the model. The graph equality and the torsion equality have distinct jobs.

  10. The identity says \(g-1=d(g_D-1)\), with \(g_D\) a nonnegative integer. If \(g=0\), the product equals \(-1\), forcing \(d=1,g_D=0\). If \(g=1\), it is zero, allowing any positive \(d\) with \(g_D=1\). If \(g=2\), it equals one, forcing \(d=1,g_D=2\). If \(g=3\), it equals two, so the arithmetic possibilities are \(d=1,g_D=3\) and \(d=2,g_D=2\). This is a divisibility constraint and a list of compatible integers, not an existence proof for multiple fibres or curve models. In particular the genus-one identity alone cannot establish the gcd-one hypothesis of MG8.

2Y. A uniform bound for the model torsion obstruction

MG8 reduces the special-fibre argument to a bound on the finite numerical group of the actual model after torsion splitting. Its order can acquire arbitrarily large prime factors. What is needed is a bound on the dimension of its prime torsion, in terms of the component graph, valid uniformly for a prime chosen from the genus.

Keep the regular-model hypotheses of VP and MG, including algebraically closed residue field \(k\). Assume \(g\ge2\) and numerical minimality. Thus \(Q\) is the actual intersection matrix, \(m_i>0\) are the fibre multiplicities, and \(p_i\) are the arithmetic genera of the integral components. Set

\[ \beta_i=-Q_{ii},\quad q_i=2p_i-2+\beta_i,\quad J=\{i:q_i>0\},\quad B=6(g-1),\quad M=768(g-1). \tag{UB1} \]

For \(s>1\), every \(\beta_i\) is positive; the sum of normalization genera will be written \(b_{\mathrm{geom}}\) when needed. The simple component graph has rank \(t=e-s+1\), as in MG5.

Free comparisons are the Stacks project's positive-budget bound, uniform numerical estimate, graph torsion bound, and torsion proposition. We give the complete argument needed in the present algebraically closed residue-field setting, including the graph classification and the long path and fork cases.

2Y.1. The positive-budget components and their boundary

UB1. If \(s>1\), \(J\ne\varnothing\), \(\#J\le2g-2\), and

\[ m_j\beta_j\le B\quad(j\in J),\qquad m_iQ_{ij}\le m_j\beta_j\le B \quad(j\in J,\ i\ne j). \tag{UB2} \]

Every index outside \(J\) has \(p_i=0,\beta_i=2\).

Proof. MG4 gives \(\sum_i m_iq_i=2g-2>0\), with every \(q_i\ge0\), and proves the asserted zero-budget characterization and count. If \(p_j\ge1\), then \(\beta_j\le q_j\), so \(m_j\beta_j\le2g-2\). Otherwise \(p_j=0\), numerical minimality and \(q_j>0\) give \(\beta_j\ge3\), and

\[ \frac{\beta_j}{q_j}=\frac{\beta_j}{\beta_j-2}\le3. \tag{UB3} \]

The same genus budget gives \(m_j\beta_j\le6(g-1)=B\). Finally \(Qm=0\) says \(m_j\beta_j=\sum_{i\ne j}Q_{ij}m_i\), a sum of nonnegative integers, proving (UB2).

In particular, any zero-budget vertex meeting \(J\) has \(m_i\le B\), since the relevant positive integer \(Q_{ij}\) is at least one. This bounds the boundary values of each connected zero-budget subgraph, but not yet its interior. \(\square\)

2Y.2. Classification of the zero-budget subgraphs

UB2. A connected component \(I\) of the graph on the zero-budget vertices is one of the following:

  • a path \(A_n\), including a single vertex;
  • a fork \(D_n\), with three arm lengths \(1,1,n-3\), \(n\ge4\);
  • a fork with arm lengths \((1,2,2),(1,2,3)\), or \((1,2,4)\), called \(E_6,E_7,E_8\).

Arm length means the number of vertices after the central vertex. Every edge within \(I\) has intersection number one.

Proof. The principal matrix \(-Q_I\) is positive definite. A nonzero vector supported in the proper subset \(I\) cannot lie in VP4's kernel line spanned by the everywhere-positive vector \(m\). The diagonal entries of this matrix are two. For a pair joined by an edge of weight \(a\), evaluation at \((1,1)\) gives \(4-2a>0\); hence the positive integer \(a\) is one.

There is no cycle: the vector equal to one on a cycle and zero elsewhere has energy at most \(2n-2n=0\). There is no vertex with four neighbors: give that vertex coefficient two and four of its neighbors coefficient one; its energy is at most zero. Thus the graph is a tree of maximum degree three.

There cannot be two trivalent vertices. Take the path joining two of them, give every vertex on it coefficient two, and give coefficient one to the first two off-path neighbors at each end. These four neighbors are distinct, and there are no extra edges among the selected vertices because the graph is a tree. If the path has \(a\) edges, the energy is

\[ 2\bigl(4(a+1)+4\bigr)-2(4a+8)=0, \tag{UB4} \]

again a contradiction. A tree without a trivalent vertex is a path. With one such vertex it has three path arms.

For completeness, the positive-definiteness test determines all possible arm lengths. The path matrix \(L_a\), with diagonal two and adjacent entries minus one, has

\[ x^TL_ax=\sum_{j=0}^{a}(x_{j+1}-x_j)^2,\quad x_0=x_{a+1}=0,\qquad (L_a^{-1})_{11}=\frac a{a+1}. \tag{UB5} \]

The energy identity is expansion. The vector \(h_j=(a+1-j)/(a+1)\) satisfies \(L_ah=e_1\), proving the inverse entry. For a central coefficient \(z\), write the arm vector as \(zh+y\); its contribution \(x^TL_ax-2zx_1\) becomes \(y^TL_ay-z^2a/(a+1)\). The entire fork is therefore positive definite exactly when

\[ \frac1{a+1}+\frac1{b+1}+\frac1{c+1}>1, \qquad 1\le a\le b\le c . \tag{UB6} \]

If \(a\ge2\), the left side is at most one. Thus \(a=1\). If \(b=1\), any \(c\ge1\) works. If \(b=2\), strictness gives \(c<5\), hence \(c=2,3,4\). If \(b\ge3\), the last two terms sum to at most one half and strictness fails. These are exactly the listed graphs. This proves the classification, including sufficiency. \(\square\)

2Y.3. Arbitrarily long paths and forks

For \(i\in I\), put

\[ h_i=\sum_{j\in J}Q_{ij}m_j\ge0,\qquad 2m_i=\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\j\sim i}}m_j+h_i. \tag{UB7} \]

Every vertex with \(h_i>0\) meets \(J\), and therefore has \(m_i\le B\) by UB1. At least one such vertex exists, since the whole graph is connected.

UB3. The multiplicities on a path component satisfy \(m_i\le B\). On a \(D_n\)-component they satisfy \(m_i\le2B\), independently of its length.

Proof. On a path, take a maximal interval of vertices whose value is the maximum \(H\). An end of that interval has either a missing path neighbor or a neighbor with value less than \(H\). Equation (UB7) then gives \(h_i>0\) at that maximum vertex. Hence \(H\le B\).

The same maximum argument on a single arm, with the center treated as a fixed endpoint, shows that all values on that arm are at most the maximum of the center value and the values at attached vertices of the arm. A larger maximum would have a plateau end away from the center with positive \(h_i\), contradicting its being larger than all attached values.

Now let \(I=D_n\), with center value \(z\), two short-arm leaf values \(u,v\), and a third arm of arbitrary length. If either short leaf is attached to \(J\), its equation gives \(z\le2u\) or \(z\le2v\), so \(z\le2B\). If the center is attached, \(z\le B\). In either case the arm maximum argument and the other leaf equations bound every value by \(2B\).

It remains to handle the case where neither short leaf nor the center is attached. Then \(u=v=z/2\), and the center equation forces the first value on the long arm to be \(z\). Along the long arm, (UB7) says that successive differences are nonincreasing:

\[ m_{r+1}-m_r=(m_r-m_{r-1})-h_r . \tag{UB8} \]

Before the first attachment those differences are zero, so its value is still \(z\). Such an attachment must exist: otherwise the values would stay \(z\) to the terminal leaf, whose equation \(2z=z\) is impossible. Thus \(z\le B\). The values along the arm are nonincreasing from \(z\), and both short leaves are \(z/2\). This finishes the last case and the proof. \(\square\)

2Y.4. The uniform entry bound

UB4. For every numerically minimal model in the standing setting with \(g\ge2\),

\[ m_i|Q_{ij}|\le M=768(g-1)\quad\text{for all }i,j, \qquad m_i\le M . \tag{UB9} \]

No bound on the number of components is asserted.

Proof. Suppose \(s>1\). On an \(E\)-component, the longest distance between two vertices is at most six: its two longest arms have lengths at most four and two. Choose a vertex meeting \(J\), with multiplicity at most \(B\). Along an internal edge, (UB7) gives \(m_{j}\le2m_i\). Propagating along a shortest path therefore gives

\[ 2m_i\le2^7B=768(g-1) \quad(i\text{ in an }E\text{-component}). \tag{UB10} \]

UB3 gives the sharper bounds \(2m_i\le2B\) for paths and \(2m_i\le4B\) for \(D\)-components. UB1 bounds \(m_i\beta_i\) on \(J\) by \(B\). Since \(\beta_i=2\) elsewhere, all diagonal products \(m_i\beta_i\) are bounded by \(M\). For an off-diagonal entry, the row identity gives

\[ m_iQ_{ij}\le m_j\beta_j\le M . \tag{UB11} \]

Also every \(\beta_i\ge1\), so \(m_i\le m_i\beta_i\le M\).

If \(s=1\), then \(Q_{11}=0\) and MG3 gives \(g-1=m_1(p_1-1)\). Since \(g\ge2\), \(p_1\ge2\), so \(m_1\le g-1\). This proves (UB9) in that case as well. \(\square\)

2Y.5. The obstruction as a finite-field graph radical

This part is a general integer-matrix statement. Let \(Q\) be connected, symmetric, with nonnegative off-diagonal entries and positive integer kernel vector \(m\), as in VP4. Put \(d=\gcd_i m_i\), \(m^0=m/d\), and

\[ \Phi_Q=\ker((m^0)^T:\mathbf Z^s\to\mathbf Z)/Q\mathbf Z^s . \tag{UB12} \]

For each edge choose an orientation and set \(c_{ij}=m_im_jQ_{ij}\). Let \(\partial:\mathbf F_\ell^E\to\mathbf F_\ell^V\) be the signed incidence map, let \(C_E=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)\), and write \(W=\ker\partial\).

UB5. If \(\ell\) divides none of the \(m_i\) or positive \(Q_{ij}\), then

\[ \Phi_Q[\ell]\simeq \operatorname{rad}\bigl((z,w)\mapsto z^TC_E^{-1}w \text{ on }W\bigr),\qquad \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\Phi_Q[\ell]\le e-s+1=t . \tag{UB13} \]

The isomorphism includes the canonical integer Bockstein below; changing edge orientations changes its edge coordinates compatibly.

Proof. VP4 proves that the integral kernel of \(Q\) is \(\mathbf Zm^0\). For a vector \(\bar a\in\ker(Q\bmod\ell)\), choose an integral lift \(a\) and send it to the class of \(Qa/\ell\) in \(\Phi_Q\). It has zero pairing with \(m^0\), is killed by \(\ell\), and changing the lift adds an element of \(Q\mathbf Z^s\). This gives

\[ \ker(Q\bmod\ell)/\mathbf F_\ell m^0 \xrightarrow{\sim}\Phi_Q[\ell]. \tag{UB14} \]

Indeed, if \(Qa/\ell=Qv\), then \(a-\ell v\) is an integral multiple of \(m^0\), proving the kernel assertion. Conversely, a class represented by \(b\) killed by \(\ell\) has \(\ell b=Qa\) for some integral \(a\), proving surjectivity.

Let \(N=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)\). Direct expansion of the off-diagonal and diagonal entries, using \(Qm=0\), gives

\[ -NQN=\partial C_E\partial^T . \tag{UB15} \]

All indicated diagonal matrices are invertible over \(\mathbf F_\ell\). The substitution \(a=Nx\) carries \(\ker(Q\bmod\ell)\) to the kernel of the right side. The line spanned by \(m^0\) becomes the line of constant vertex vectors, since \(N^{-1}m^0=d^{-1}\mathbf1\).

Connectedness gives \(\ker\partial^T=\mathbf F_\ell\mathbf1\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\partial=s-1\): equality of the values at the two ends of every edge propagates through the graph, in any characteristic. Hence \(\dim W=e-s+1\).

For \(x\) in the kernel of (UB15), set \(z=C_E\partial^Tx\). Then \(z\in W\). Moreover \(C_E^{-1}z=\partial^Tx\) is orthogonal to \(W\) for the standard dot product, so \(z\) is in the displayed radical. Its kernel on vertex vectors is exactly the constant line. Conversely a radical vector \(z\in W\) has \(C_E^{-1}z\in W^\perp=\operatorname{im}\partial^T\). The last equality follows from inclusion and the dimensions \(s-1\) on both sides in the nondegenerate standard dot product. Thus \(z=C_E\partial^Tx\) for some \(x\), and \(z\in W\) puts \(x\) in the kernel of (UB15). Together with (UB14), this proves the isomorphism and its dimension bound. \(\square\)

2Y.6. A prime chosen uniformly from the genus

UB6. In the standing regular-model setting, numerical minimality and \(g\ge2\) imply

\[ \ell>768(g-1),\quad \ell\ne\operatorname{char}k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dim_{\mathbf F_\ell}\Phi_X[\ell]\le t . \tag{UB16} \]

If the actual generic Picard group has \(\ell\)-torsion dimension \(2g\) and \(d=1\), then the original special fibre is reduced and nodal, with all conclusions of MG8.

Proof. UB4 bounds every \(m_i\) and every positive \(Q_{ij}\) by \(M\), so the prime \(\ell>M\) divides none of them. UB5 applies to the actual \(\Phi_X=\Phi_Q\). For \(s=1\), that group is zero and \(t=0\), giving the same conclusion directly. The stated extra generic rank and \(d=1\) are now exactly the other hypotheses of MG8. This proves the assertion. \(\square\)

2Y.7. Torsion splitting before choosing a new model

UB7. Let \(R\) be a complete DVR with algebraically closed residue field and fraction field \(K\), and let \(C/K\) be smooth projective geometrically integral of genus \(g\ge2\). Choose a prime \(\ell>768(g-1)\) different from the residue characteristic. There is a finite separable extension \(K'/K\), with a complete DVR \(R'\) finite over \(R\) and residue field \(k\), such that \(C(K')\ne\varnothing\) and

\[ \operatorname{Pic}(C_{K'})[\ell]\simeq (\mathbf Z/\ell)^{2g}. \tag{UB17} \]

Consequently, if a regular projective model with numerically minimal data for \(C_{K'}\) is supplied over \(R'\), its special fibre is reduced and nodal.

Proof. First produce a separable point. A nonempty standard smooth curve chart has an étale coordinate map to \(\mathbf A^1_K\), by SF1–SF3. Its image contains a nonempty open set by EA14. The field \(K\) is infinite, since the powers of a uniformizer are distinct; choose a \(K\)-point of that open set. The nonempty fibre of the chart is an étale finite-type scheme over \(K\). An affine part of it has coordinate algebra a nonzero product of finite separable fields by EA10. One of those residue fields supplies a point after a finite separable extension \(K_1/K\).

The pointed Jacobian over \(K_1\) is constructed in JC. Its \(\ell\)-torsion is finite étale of rank \(\ell^{2g}\) by CU and FF. Its affine algebra splits into separable fields by EA10, so a finite separable extension splitting those finitely many fields makes all its geometric torsion points rational. Take a finite normal closure containing these fields and \(K_1\), using Lesson 1, §0B. JC's pointed line-bundle interpretation gives the actual Picard group equality (UB17). Cohomology commutes with field extension by the finite affine Čech or FC9 calculation, so the genus remains \(g\).

We justify the complete DVR assertion without applying the finite-residue-field hypothesis of Lesson 1's Proposition 0E.1 to the present residue field. Its trace-lattice construction itself has no such hypothesis. An integral \(K\)-basis of \(K'\) exists by scaling a basis by powers of the uniformizer. Nondegeneracy of the separable trace pairing puts the integral closure \(S\) of \(R\) between that lattice and its finite trace-dual lattice; the proof in §0E and the DVR submodule argument §0A make \(S\) finite free over \(R\). It is a complete normal domain with fraction field \(K'\).

Every maximal ideal of \(S\) contracts to the maximal ideal of \(R\), by the integral inverse argument EA5. The algebra \(S/\pi S\) is finite-dimensional over \(k\), hence Artinian. To spell out the needed localness step, it has finitely many maximal ideals: the Chinese remainder theorem for any list of distinct maximal ideals bounds their number by its \(k\)-dimension. Their intersection has a power which stabilizes by finite dimension; Nakayama makes that power zero. Powers of distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, so Chinese remaindering gives a nontrivial idempotent if there is more than one maximal ideal. Such an idempotent lifts uniquely to \(S\) by Hensel's simple-root argument for \(T^2-T\), with derivative a unit even in characteristic two. The domain \(S\) has no nontrivial idempotent, so \(S\) is local.

Finite integral incomparability in EA5 shows that this local domain has dimension one: contractions of a strict prime chain are strict, and \(R\) has dimension one; the chain from zero to its nonzero maximal ideal gives the reverse bound. RC1's normal one-dimensional Noetherian local-ring argument now makes \(S\) a DVR, without any residue-finiteness assumption. Write \(\pi=u\varpi^e\). Its two adic topologies agree, so this DVR is complete. Its residue field is finite over the algebraically closed field \(k\), hence is \(k\). Set \(R'=S\).

For the supplied new model, the \(K'\)-point makes \(d=1\) by VP7, and (UB17) gives the full generic rank. UB6 proves the numerical obstruction bound for this model, using the unchanged genus and the prime already chosen. MG8 therefore gives the claimed reduced nodal fibre. This does not assume that the numerical obstruction group remained the same under the field extension.

Regular-model existence and the construction of contractions reaching numerical minimality are still required. The present uniform estimate and finite-extension argument use the standing algebraically closed residue field; extending the reduction proof to a general residue field requires a proved descent or the corresponding weighted numerical argument. No whole semiabelian lift or analytic period cover is claimed here. \(\square\)

2Y.8. Large obstruction orders and finite actions

UB8. The uniform rank bound does not bound the prime divisors of \(|\Phi_X|\). As an integer numerical example of genus two, take a cycle with \(n\ge3\) rational vertices and attach one genus-one leaf to one cycle vertex. Give every vertex multiplicity one and let \(Q\) be the negative graph Laplacian. Then

\[ g=2,\quad t=1,\quad \max_{i,j}|Q_{ij}|=3,\quad \Phi_Q\simeq\mathbf Z/n . \tag{UB18} \]

This statement is about the numerical matrix; it asserts no unconstructed regular-model realization. The maps in UB5 and all bounds are compatible with supplied component-permuting actions preserving the model data.

Proof. Every rational cycle vertex has diagonal \(-2\), except the attachment vertex, whose diagonal is \(-3\). The genus-one leaf has diagonal \(-1\). Thus the two positive genus-budget contributions are one each, and (MG10) gives \(2g-2=2\); the data are numerically minimal, since the \((-1)\)-vertex has positive genus. Adding a leaf and its edge preserves \(t=1\).

For the integral matrix, change coordinates by writing the old leaf coordinate as the sum of the attachment coordinate and a new leaf coordinate, keeping every cycle coordinate. This is an integral unimodular change. The bridge energy becomes just the square of the new leaf coordinate, and the cycle energy is unchanged. The matrix is therefore integrally congruent to the cycle Laplacian with a separate \((-1)\)-block. VP's integral cycle computation gives its torsion cokernel \(\mathbf Z/n\), proving (UB18).

In particular, primes dividing \(n\) can be arbitrarily large while the genus and entry bound stay fixed. Their torsion dimension is one, consistent with \(t=1\). The use of a uniform rank bound in UB7 is therefore essential; a claim that a large prime avoids the order of every new obstruction group would be false.

A supplied action permutes vertices and branches, preserves \(m,Q\), and changes an oriented edge by the appropriate sign when it reverses that orientation. The integer lift \(a\mapsto Qa/\ell\), the incidence identity and the cycle pairing transform by these same maps. They are consequently equivariant; the rank bounds need no division by the action-group order or choice of an equivariant spanning tree. \(\square\)

2Y.9. Graded exercise: graph bounds and torsion radicals

Exercise 2Y (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. From the genus budget, prove \(m_j\beta_j\le6(g-1)\) on every positive-budget component. Explain both the positive-genus case and the rational case, and derive the boundary multiplicity bound.
  2. Prove all three forbidden-subgraph tests in UB2: a cycle, a four-leaf star, and two trivalent vertices joined by a path. Specify the entire test vector and compute its energy.
  3. For a three-arm fork, derive the Schur-complement inequality by completing the square on each arm. List every ordered arm triple \(a\le b\le c\) giving a positive definite matrix, and compute the diameters of \(E_6,E_7,E_8\).
  4. Prove the long-path multiplicity maximum argument, including a one-vertex path. Then prove the \(D_n\) bound in the case where only a short leaf is attached to the positive-budget graph; account for every other arm value.
  5. For \(E_8\), start with an attached vertex of multiplicity at most \(B\). Derive the precise factor \(2^7B\) on \(2m_i\). Explain why this does not assert that the number of rational \((-2)\)-components is bounded.
  6. For the unweighted \(n\)-cycle, calculate the cycle-space pairing over \(\mathbf F_\ell\), its radical, and \(\Phi_Q[\ell]\). Relate this calculation to the integral group \(\mathbf Z/n\).
  7. Let\[ Q=\begin{pmatrix}-3&3\\3&-3\end{pmatrix},\qquad m=(1,1). \tag{UBX1} \] Compute \(t,\Phi_Q\) and its \(3\)-torsion. Identify exactly which hypothesis of UB5 fails and why no edge-weight inverse can be used.
  8. Give the Bockstein isomorphism (UB14), proving its kernel, surjectivity and independence of the integer lift. Explain its conversion to the graph radical and how orientation reversal acts.
  9. For the genus-two numerical leafed cycle in UB8, perform the integral coordinate change and compute \(\Phi_Q\) for \(n=5\) and \(n=769\). Compare torsion order, torsion rank, entry size and the bound \(M\).
  10. Describe the full order of choices in UB7, from the prime to the finite separable extension and then the new model. Prove why the integral closure remains a complete DVR with algebraically closed residue field. Identify the geometric and residue-field inputs still required for general semistable reduction.

Complete solution.

  1. Write \(q_j=2p_j-2+\beta_j\). If \(p_j\ge1\), then \(q_j\ge \beta_j\) and \(m_j\beta_j\le2g-2\). If \(p_j=0\) and \(q_j>0\), numerical minimality gives \(\beta_j\ge3\), and \(\beta_j/(\beta_j-2)\le3\). Thus \(m_j\beta_j\le3(2g-2)=6(g-1)\). The row identity \(m_j\beta_j=\sum_{i\ne j}Q_{ij}m_i\) bounds each positive summand. If \(Q_{ij}>0\), it is at least one, so the adjacent multiplicity \(m_i\le B\).

  2. For a cycle of length \(n\), put one on its vertices and zero elsewhere; with diagonal two and edge entries minus one its energy is at most \(2n-2n=0\). For a four-leaf star, put two at the center and one at its four leaves; the energy is \(2(4+4)-2\cdot8=0\), with any extra selected edges decreasing it. For two trivalent vertices joined by a path of \(a\) edges, put two on every path vertex and one on the two off-path neighbors at each end. After the cycle exclusion these four neighbors are distinct and have no extra edges. The energy is \(2(4(a+1)+4)-2(4a+8)=0\). All vectors are nonzero, contradicting positive definiteness. Thus at most one trivalent vertex remains.

  3. On an arm of length \(a\), the solution to \(L_ah=e_1\) is \(h_j=(a+1-j)/(a+1)\). For central coefficient \(z\), write \(x=zh+y\). The arm energy is \(y^TL_ay-z^2a/(a+1)\). Summing and adding the center gives

    \[ \sum_{\mathrm{arms}}y^TL_ay+ z^2\left(\frac1{a+1}+\frac1{b+1}+\frac1{c+1}-1\right). \tag{UBX2} \]

    The positive triples are exactly \((1,1,c)\), \(c\ge1\), and \((1,2,2),(1,2,3),(1,2,4)\). If the smallest arm were at least two the reciprocal sum would be at most one; with the smallest one, the remaining cases follow from the strict half-sum inequality. The two longest arms give diameters \(4,5,6\) for \(E_6,E_7,E_8\).

  4. At an end of a maximum plateau on a path, the inside-neighbor sum is strictly below twice the maximum, either because a neighbor is missing or because one is smaller. Equation (UB7) gives a positive attachment there, bounding the maximum by \(B\). A one-vertex path has neighbor sum zero, so \(h=2m>0\) and the same conclusion. For a \(D_n\)-component attached at a short leaf, its equation gives center value at most twice that leaf's value, hence at most \(2B\). Every other short leaf is either attached, with value at most \(B\), or unattached, with value half the center. The long arm cannot exceed the maximum of the center and its attached values, by the plateau argument with the center as fixed endpoint. Thus every value is at most \(2B\), even if there are further attachments.

  5. Every internal edge satisfies \(m_{\mathrm{next}}\le2m_{\mathrm{previous}}\). The largest distance from the chosen attached vertex to any other \(E_8\)-vertex is at most its diameter six. Thus \(m_i\le2^6B\), and \(2m_i\le2^7B=768(g-1)\). This uses a diameter bound only for the finite \(E\)-graphs. Paths and \(D_n\)-forks may have arbitrarily many vertices; their independent maximum arguments control values without bounding length.

  6. Orient the cycle consistently and give its one-dimensional cycle space the vector \(z\) equal to one on every edge. Since all \(m_i=1,Q_{ij}=1\) on edges, \(C_E=I\), and the restricted pairing is

    \[ (az,bz)\longmapsto nab\quad\text{in }\mathbf F_\ell. \tag{UBX3} \]

    Its radical is the full line when \(\ell\mid n\), and zero otherwise. UB5 therefore gives torsion dimension one or zero respectively. This agrees exactly with the integral calculation \(\Phi_Q=\mathbf Z/n\); a cyclic group has one-dimensional \(\ell\)-torsion precisely when \(\ell\) divides its order.

  7. The simple graph has two vertices and one edge, so \(t=0\). A column generates the sublattice \(3\mathbf Z(1,-1)\) in the primitive degree-zero lattice \(\mathbf Z(1,-1)\); hence

    \[ \Phi_Q=\mathbf Z/3,\qquad \dim_{\mathbf F_3}\Phi_Q[3]=1>t. \tag{UBX4} \]

    The positive off-diagonal entry is divisible by three. The edge weight \(c_e=3\) vanishes in \(\mathbf F_3\), so \(C_E^{-1}\) does not exist and UB5's hypothesis fails. The real or rational rank of \(Q\) does not repair that failure modulo three.

  8. For \(\bar a\in\ker(Q\bmod\ell)\), choose \(a\in\mathbf Z^s\) and set \(b=Qa/\ell\). Then \((m^0)^Tb=0\), and \(\ell[b]=0\) in the quotient by \(Q\mathbf Z^s\). Replacing \(a\) by \(a+\ell v\) adds \(Qv\) to \(b\), so the class is independent of the lift. It vanishes exactly when \(Qa/\ell=Qv\), or \(a-\ell v\in\mathbf Zm^0\), giving the stated kernel. Any killed class has a representative \(b\) with \(\ell b=Qa\), giving surjectivity. With \(a=Nx\), the vector \(C_E\partial^Tx\) is a cycle and is orthogonal to every cycle for the inverse-weight pairing. The converse follows from \(W^\perp=\operatorname{im}\partial^T\). Reversing an edge changes its incidence coordinate and cycle coordinate by minus one; the paired construction and all equations transform accordingly, also in characteristic two where the sign is unchanged.

  9. Write the old leaf variable as the old attachment variable plus a new leaf variable. This integral triangular substitution has determinant one. The bridge square becomes the square of the new leaf variable, so the negative Laplacian is congruent to

    \[ Q_{\mathrm{cycle}}\oplus(-1). \tag{UBX5} \]

    Thus \(\Phi_Q=\mathbf Z/5\) or \(\mathbf Z/769\), respectively. Both examples have \(g=2,t=1\), entry size at most three, and \(M=768\). The prime \(769\) is larger than \(M\), yet its obstruction torsion is a nonzero line, allowed by \(t=1\). To check primality, it has no prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{769}<28\): division by \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) leaves nonzero remainders. The order and its prime factors are unbounded as the cycle length varies; the torsion rank stays at most one. These are numerical examples, not unproved geometric realizations.

  10. First fix the genus and choose \(\ell>768(g-1)\) away from the residue characteristic. Next choose a separable point using a nonempty étale coordinate chart and an element of the infinite fraction field in its open image. Over its finite separable residue extension, form the pointed Jacobian, then take a finite separable normal extension splitting the finite étale \(\ell\)-torsion algebra. Only then consider a regular projective model of the resulting curve and impose the stated numerical minimality.

For the valuation ring, separable trace nondegeneracy places the integral closure between a finite integral lattice and its trace dual, so it is finite free and complete over \(R\). Its residue algebra modulo the original uniformizer is finite-dimensional and Artinian, not necessarily a finite set. Multiple maximal ideals would give a nontrivial residue idempotent, which Hensel lifts to a contradiction in the domain. The local normal finite integral algebra has dimension one and hence is a DVR by RC1; its uniformizer-adic topology agrees with the original one. Its residue field is finite over algebraically closed \(k\), so remains \(k\). The unchanged genus makes the fixed prime satisfy UB6 for the new model, regardless of changes in its numerical group. Construction of regular models,contractions reaching minimality,and a proved descent or weighted argument for general residue fields remain required. Semiabelian lifting and the initial analytic covering are additional steps after the curve reduction argument.

2Z. Contracting exceptional components and reaching minimality

The uniform estimate UB applies to a numerically minimal regular model. We now construct the contractions needed to reach that condition, starting with a supplied regular projective model. The construction produces a scheme, proves its regularity and projectivity, identifies the original surface as its blowup, and permits supplied finite actions to descend.

Except for the local statements EC1–EC2, keep the standing complete DVR \(R\) with algebraically closed residue field \(k\), and an integral regular flat projective relative curve \(X/R\) with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre \(C\). An exceptional component means an actual component

\[ E\simeq\mathbf P^1_k,\qquad \mathcal O_X(E)|_E\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1}(-1). \tag{EC1} \]

MG7 proves that these are precisely the components with \(p_E=0,Q_{EE}=-1\). The free comparisons are the Stacks project's exceptional formal neighborhood, contraction criterion, and Picard sequence. The formal-functions theorem used below is proved in Lesson 3, §0.F.2, including FFR1–FFR9 and NF7; its free comparison is 02OC.

2Z.1. Dimension and completion tests used in the construction

EC1. A Noetherian local ring whose maximal ideal has \(r\) generators has dimension at most \(r\). Suppose \(B\) is a Noetherian local domain and its completion has associated graded ring \(\kappa[U,V]\), where \(\kappa=B/\mathfrak m_B\). Then \(B\) is regular of dimension two.

Proof. We give the dimension estimate rather than using an unproved height bound. Put

\[ \lambda_A(n)=\operatorname{length}_A(A/\mathfrak m_A^n). \tag{EC2} \]

These lengths are finite: finitely many maximal-ideal generators give finite spanning lists of monomials for each successive quotient.

A strict prime chain of length \(d\) forces \(\lambda_A(n)\ge c n^d\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some \(c>0\). First quotient by its first prime; lengths cannot increase under that quotient, and the quotient is a local domain with a chain

\[ 0=P_0\subsetneq P_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq P_d=\mathfrak m. \tag{EC3} \]

One may append the maximal ideal if necessary. Induct on \(d\). For \(d=0\), length is at least one. For \(d\ge1\), choose \(0\ne a\in P_1\). Artin–Rees for \((a)\subset A\), proved in Lesson 3, DFR1, gives an integer \(c_0\ge1\) such that

\[ (a)\cap\mathfrak m^n\subset a\mathfrak m^{n-c_0} \quad(n\ge c_0). \tag{EC4} \]

Since \(A\) is a domain, the first term of the exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow (a)/((a)\cap\mathfrak m^n) \longrightarrow A/\mathfrak m^n \longrightarrow A/((a)+\mathfrak m^n)\longrightarrow0 \tag{EC5} \]

has length at least \(\lambda_A(n-c_0)\). The last term surjects onto \(A/(P_1+\mathfrak m^n)\), whose length is at least \(c_1n^{d-1}\) by induction on the remaining chain in \(A/P_1\). Thus

\[ \lambda_A(n)\ge\lambda_A(n-c_0)+c_1n^{d-1}. \tag{EC6} \]

Iterate for at least a fixed positive multiple of \(n\) indices between \(n/2\) and \(n\). This proves the asserted lower bound. If the maximal ideal has \(r\) generators, its degree-\(j\) quotient is spanned by the \(\binom{j+r-1}{r-1}\) degree-\(j\) monomials. Hence

\[ \lambda_A(n)\le\binom{n+r-1}{r}=O(n^r) \tag{EC7} \]

for \(r>0\); for \(r=0\) the ring is a field. Comparing the two bounds proves \(\dim A\le r\).

For the completion assertion, EA7 identifies \(B/\mathfrak m_B^n\) with the corresponding completed quotient, so

\[ \lambda_B(n)=\frac{n(n+1)}2,\qquad \dim_\kappa\mathfrak m_B/\mathfrak m_B^2=2. \tag{EC8} \]

Nakayama makes two lifts generate \(\mathfrak m_B\), so the first assertion gives dimension at most two. Dimension zero would make this local domain a field. If its dimension were one, any nonzero \(a\in\mathfrak m_B\) would have radical \(\mathfrak m_B\): every nonzero prime is then maximal. Finite generation gives \(\mathfrak m_B^c\subset(a)\), so \(B/(a)\) has finite length. Cancellation by \(a\) identifies each successive quotient \((a^j)/(a^{j+1})\) with \(B/(a)\). Since \((a^n)\subset\mathfrak m_B^n\),

\[ \lambda_B(n)\le\operatorname{length}(B/(a^n)) =n\operatorname{length}(B/(a)), \tag{EC9} \]

contradicting (EC8). Its dimension is therefore two, equal to its embedding dimension, as required. \(\square\)

2Z.2. The ring of an exceptional formal neighborhood

EC2. Let \(E\) be an effective Cartier divisor on a Noetherian scheme, with \(E\simeq\mathbf P^1_F\) and \(\mathcal O_E(-E)\simeq\mathcal O(1)\), for any field \(F\). Set \(E_n=nE\). The ring

\[ A=\varprojlim_n\Gamma(E_n,\mathcal O_{E_n}) \tag{EC10} \]

is a complete Noetherian regular local domain of dimension two. Its residue field is \(F\), and

\[ \ker(A\to\Gamma(E_n,\mathcal O_{E_n}))=\mathfrak m_A^n, \qquad \operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_A}A=F[U,V]. \tag{EC11} \]

This does not assert an isomorphism with \(F[[U,V]]\) in mixed characteristic.

Proof. Write \(J=\mathcal O_X(-E)\). For \(d\ge0\) there are exact sequences

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_E(d+n) \longrightarrow J^d/J^{d+n+1} \longrightarrow J^d/J^{d+n}\longrightarrow0. \tag{EC12} \]

They follow by dividing consecutive powers of the invertible ideal \(J\). Lesson 3's projective-line Čech calculation PF5 gives \(H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(d+n))=0\), and all higher groups vanish. It follows by induction that these twisted thickenings have zero positive cohomology and surjective section transitions.

Put \(I_d=\ker(A\to\Gamma(E_d,\mathcal O_{E_d}))\), with \(I_0=A\). Taking successive lifts in the surjective systems identifies \(I_d\) with the limit of the sections of the twisted quotients in (EC12). In particular,

\[ I_d/I_{d+1}=H^0(\mathbf P^1_F,\mathcal O(d)),\qquad I_dI_e\subset I_{d+e}. \tag{EC13} \]

The multiplication is ordinary multiplication of homogeneous polynomials. Choose \(x,y\in I_1\) lifting a basis of \(H^0(\mathcal O(1))\). Their degree-\(d\) monomials form the basis in (EC13).

The ring \(A\) is separated and complete for the \(I_d\)-topology by its inverse-limit definition and surjectivity. Every element with nonzero residue in \(F\) is a unit: lift a residue inverse and use the convergent geometric series for an element of \(I_1\). Thus it is local with maximal ideal \(I_1\).

For \(z\in I_d\), cancel its initial homogeneous part by a degree-\(d\) polynomial in \(x,y\), using arbitrary lifts of its finitely many residue coefficients. Cancel the next part and continue. At the step of order \(e\ge d\), every degree-\(e\) monomial is a degree-\(d\) monomial times one of degree \(e-d\). Collect coefficients of the finitely many degree-\(d\) monomials. Each coefficient sequence is Cauchy, since its new terms have order at least \(e-d\). The limits and separatedness give \(z\in(x,y)^d\). Hence \(I_d=(x,y)^d\), proving the first part of (EC11).

To check Noetherianity, for any ideal take its graded ideal of initial forms in \(F[U,V]\). Hilbert's basis theorem EA4 supplies finitely many homogeneous generators represented by actual ideal elements. Cancel initial forms successively as above, now collecting coefficients of these finitely many elements. Completeness and separatedness give an actual finite generating list for the ideal. Thus \(A\) is Noetherian. Nonzero initial forms have nonzero products in \(F[U,V]\), so \(A\) is a domain. Equations (EC8)–(EC9) and the height estimate just proved give dimension two; its maximal ideal has the two generators \(x,y\). This proves regularity and all assertions. \(\square\)

2Z.3. A projective map which collapses exactly the component

EC3. For an exceptional component \(E\subset X\), there is a projective morphism \(f:X\to Y_0\), with \(Y_0/R\) integral and projective, which maps \(E\) to one point and is an isomorphism away from that point.

Proof. Choose a relatively very ample line \(H\), and write \(H|_E=\mathcal O(a)\), \(a>0\). Put \(L=H(aE)\). Choose \(n\) so large that \(H^n\) is generated by finitely many global sections and gives a closed embedding, and \(H^1(X,H^n)=0\), by PF7–PF8. For \(1\le j\le na\),

\[ 0\longrightarrow H^n((j-1)E) \longrightarrow H^n(jE) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_E(na-j)\longrightarrow0. \tag{EC14} \]

All last terms have zero \(H^1\), so induction gives zero \(H^1\) for every middle term. At \(j=na\), this proves

\[ \Gamma(X,L^n)\longrightarrow H^0(E,\mathcal O_E)=k \quad\hbox{is surjective}. \tag{EC15} \]

The sections of \(H^n\), multiplied by the canonical section of \(\mathcal O(naE)\), generate \(L^n\) off \(E\); a section restricting to one generates on \(E\). Choose a finite generating list containing all these sections. It defines a morphism to a projective space over \(R\). Let \(Y_0\) be its scheme-theoretic image, defined on target charts by the kernel of restriction to \(X\). Those kernels are prime because nonempty open subsets of the integral \(X\) have domain section rings. Thus \(Y_0\) is integral, closed and projective. The morphism to it is projective: use its closed graph and the projective embedding of \(X/R\).

All coordinates restrict to constants on \(E\), so its image is one \(k\)-point \(y_0\). The chosen \(H^n\)-coordinates vanish on \(E\) and do not all vanish at any point off it. On the projective open where those coordinates do not all vanish, projection onto them recovers the closed embedding defined by \(H^n\). Including the additional coordinates is its graph in the corresponding affine-bundle charts. Consequently the restriction from \(X\setminus E\) is an immersion. It is also proper over that target open, as a base change of the projective map. Its image is therefore closed there, and the immersion is a closed immersion. The full image outside \(y_0\) is precisely this open image. It follows that \(f\) is an isomorphism there and \(f^{-1}(y_0)\) has underlying set \(E\). \(\square\)

2Z.4. The finite algebra factor and regularity at the new point

EC4. There is an integral regular flat projective \(R\)-scheme \(Y\) and a projective morphism \(h:X\to Y\), with

\[ h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y,\qquad h^{-1}(y)=E\ \hbox{set theoretically},\qquad X\setminus E\simeq Y\setminus\{y\}. \tag{EC16} \]

Moreover

\[ \widehat{\mathcal O}_{Y,y}\simeq \varprojlim_n\Gamma(E_n,\mathcal O_{E_n}). \tag{EC17} \]

Proof. Proper coherent finiteness, Lesson 3, Theorem 0.C.10 and Corollary 0.C.11, makes \(f_*\mathcal O_X\) a coherent algebra on \(Y_0\). Form

\[ Y=\operatorname{Spec}_{Y_0}(f_*\mathcal O_X). \tag{EC18} \]

This is finite over \(Y_0\), and evaluation defines \(h\). On an affine \(U\subset Y_0\), put \(B_U=\Gamma(f^{-1}U,\mathcal O_X)\). For \(b\in B_U\), a finite affine cover of \(f^{-1}U\), with affine intersections, shows

\[ \Gamma((f^{-1}U)_b,\mathcal O_X)=(B_U)_b: \tag{EC19} \]

localize the equalizer computing global sections; localization is exact and the cover is finite. This proves \(h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\) on all distinguished charts. The map \(h\) is projective by its closed graph into \(X\times_{Y_0}Y\). Its closed image is all of \(Y\); otherwise a point outside the image would have a zero direct-image stalk, contrary to (EC16). The rings \(B_U\) are domains, and all nonempty charts share the unchanged generic open, so \(Y\) is integral.

Outside \(y_0\), the algebra in (EC18) is \(\mathcal O_{Y_0}\), so \(h\) is an isomorphism there. The connected curve \(E\) maps into the finite fibre of \(Y\to Y_0\); a connected subset of that finite discrete space is one point \(y\). Surjectivity of \(h\) proves that there are no other points over \(y_0\). Its residue field is \(k\), since it is finite over the algebraically closed \(k\).

Localize at \(y\), writing \(B=\mathcal O_{Y,y}\). The ideal \(\mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X\) and the invertible ideal \(J=\mathcal O_X(-E)\) have the same radical near this fibre. Also \(\mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X\subset J\), since every maximal-ideal function vanishes on the reduced curve \(E\). Noetherianity and a finite cover give \(J^c\subset\mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X\) for some \(c\). Their powers are cofinal:

\[ J^{cn}\subset\mathfrak m_B^n\mathcal O_X\subset J^n. \tag{EC20} \]

Apply the actual stalk formal-functions isomorphism NF7 to \(h,\mathcal O_X,y\). It is valid without flatness of \(h\). Cofinality in (EC20) identifies its limit with (EC17). EC2 gives its polynomial associated graded ring. Since \(B\) is a local domain, EC1 now proves that \(B\) is regular of dimension two. Every other local ring of \(Y\) is that of \(X\). Hence \(Y\) is regular.

The finite map \(Y\to Y_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf P_R^N\) makes \(Y\) projective by Lesson 3, Theorem 0.F.7. Its generic fibre is \(C\). Its local coordinate rings are torsion-free over the DVR \(R\), since they are domains containing \(R\), and are therefore flat: each finite submodule is free by Lesson 1, §0A, and their filtered union preserves injections after tensoring. Thus \(Y/R\) is flat. This completes the construction. \(\square\)

2Z.5. The blowup and the universal property

EC5. The morphism \(h\) is the blowup of the regular closed point \(y\). Any scheme map from \(X\) that is constant on \(E\) factors uniquely through \(h\). In particular the contraction is unique up to unique isomorphism.

Proof. By (EC17), the images of two generators \(u,v\) of \(\mathfrak m_B\) in \(J/J^2\) form a basis of \(H^0(E,\mathcal O(1))\). To see this from \(B\), use EA7's unchanged quotients modulo powers of the maximal ideal and (EC11). Their two restrictions generate \(\mathcal O(1)\) at every point of \(E\). Thus

\[ \mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X+J^2=J. \tag{EC21} \]

Stalkwise Nakayama on \(J/\mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X\), at points of \(E\), gives \(\mathfrak m_B\mathcal O_X=J\). Both ideals are the unit ideal off the fibre. The blowup universal property, proved in NS2 using its actual Rees charts, therefore factors \(h\) as

\[ X\xrightarrow{q}\operatorname{Bl}_yY\xrightarrow{b}Y. \tag{EC22} \]

The blowup of a regular two-dimensional local ring at its maximal ideal has exceptional fibre \(\mathbf P^1_k\), with conormal line \(\mathcal O(1)\). Here are the required local checks. NM1 gives \(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_B}B=k[\bar u,\bar v]\). Its two charts are

\[ B[t]/(ut-v)=B[v/u],\qquad B[s]/(vs-u)=B[u/v]. \tag{EC23} \]

For the first equality, \(u\) is a nonzero divisor in the displayed quotient: reducing an equation \(uF=(ut-v)G\) modulo \(u\) forces \(G\) to be divisible by \(u\), since \(v\) is a nonzero divisor in \(B/(u)\); cancel \(u\). Localization at \(u\) then identifies the chart with its subring of the fraction field. The other chart is the same argument. Modulo \(u\), the first chart is \(k[t]\). A local ring at a closed point of this exceptional affine line has maximal ideal generated by \(u\) and a lift of its irreducible residue polynomial; it has the strict prime chain \(0\subsetneq(u)\subsetneq\mathfrak n\). EC1 gives dimension at most two, so it is regular. At the generic point of the exceptional line the same argument gives a one-dimensional regular local ring. Off that line the chart is an open of \(Y\). This proves regularity of the whole blowup, and NM2 gives normality. The transition of the local equations \(u,v\) gives the conormal line \(\mathcal O(1)\).

The restriction of \(q\) to \(E\) is the map to this projective line given by the full basis of \(H^0(\mathcal O(1))\), hence is an isomorphism. Away from \(E\), it is already an isomorphism. The map \(q\) is projective and has finite geometric fibres, so Theorem 0.F.1 makes it finite. It is birational to the integral normal blowup. On an affine chart, its finite coordinate algebra is an integral subalgebra of the same fraction field; normality of the target makes that algebra the target ring. Thus \(q\) is an isomorphism, proving the blowup assertion.

For the universal property, let \(w:X\to Z\) send \(E\) to one point. Choose an affine neighborhood \(V\) of that point. Properness of \(h\) shows that

\[ U=Y\setminus h(X\setminus w^{-1}V) \tag{EC24} \]

is an open neighborhood of \(y\), and \(h^{-1}U\) maps to \(V\). On any affine open in \(U\), its functions map to functions on the inverse image; (EC16) identifies those with functions on that affine open itself. The resulting morphisms to \(V\) agree on overlaps and give a map \(U\to V\). Off \(y\) use the inverse of the isomorphism in (EC16). These maps agree on their overlaps, since their pullbacks agree and (EC16) detects the relevant functions, so they glue to \(Y\to Z\). The same argument proves uniqueness. Apply it to two contractions to obtain their mutually inverse unique isomorphisms. \(\square\)

2Z.6. Picard groups and the actual numerical transformation

EC6. Number the contracted component by \(0\), and write

\[ Q=\begin{pmatrix}-1&v^T\\v&A_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad m=(m_0,\bar m). \tag{EC25} \]

If \(C_i'\) is the image of a remaining component \(C_i\), then

\[ h^*C_i'=C_i+v_iE,\qquad Q'=A_0+vv^T,\qquad m_0=v^T\bar m,\qquad p_i'=p_i+\frac{v_i(v_i-1)}2. \tag{EC26} \]

The gcd of the fibre multiplicities and the finite numerical obstruction group are unchanged. There is also a split exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\xrightarrow{h^*} \operatorname{Pic}(X)\xrightarrow{\deg_E}\mathbf Z \longrightarrow0,\qquad n\longmapsto\mathcal O_X(-nE) \tag{EC27} \]

for its splitting.

Proof. The integral curve \(C_i'\) is Cartier, since \(Y\) is regular and factorial locally by NM2. Its pullback has strict transform \(C_i\), and differs from that by \(a_iE\). The pullback of a line on \(Y\) has degree zero on the fibre \(E\). Intersecting with \(E\) gives \(0=v_i-a_i\), proving the first formula. Intersections of pullbacks and their restrictions give the next formula by expansion:

\[ (C_i+v_iE)(C_j+v_jE)=Q_{ij}+v_iv_j. \tag{EC28} \]

For instance their degree can be computed on the total transform using the additive degree formula CE1; on \(E\) it is zero, and on \(C_i\) it is the pullback degree from \(C_i'\), unchanged under the degree-one proper birational curve map by the normalization/divisor calculation DC7. Alternatively the same equality follows locally from the Cartier divisors and their finite intersection lengths. The multiplicities of the remaining components stay \(m_i\), because \(h\) is an isomorphism at their generic points. The first row of \(Qm=0\) gives \(m_0=v^T\bar m\), and proves the gcd assertion.

We justify the arithmetic-genus formula without assuming smooth images. For \(q>0\), NF7 and cofinality (EC20) identify the completion of \((R^qh_*\mathcal O_X)_y\) with \(\varprojlim H^q(E_n,\mathcal O_{E_n})=0\), by EC2. The stalk is finite; FFR9 makes it zero. Away from \(y\), \(h\) is an isomorphism. Thus every positive higher image is zero. A line pulled back from \(Y\) has the same property, as one sees after trivializing it on target opens, and its degree-zero image is that line.

Apply the natural higher-image sequences to

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(-h^*C_i') \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{C_i+v_iE}\longrightarrow0. \tag{EC29} \]

They give \(h_*\mathcal O_{C_i+v_iE}=\mathcal O_{C_i'}\) and zero positive higher images. SC15's proved collapse therefore identifies their coherent cohomology and Euler characteristics. Add \(E\) successively to \(C_i\), using MG1. At the step \(C_i+rE\), its intersection with \(E\) is \(v_i-r\), so the Euler increment is \(1-v_i+r\). Summing \(r=0,\ldots,v_i-1\) gives

\[ \chi(\mathcal O_{C_i'})=\chi(\mathcal O_{C_i}) -\frac{v_i(v_i-1)}2, \tag{EC30} \]

which is exactly the last formula of (EC26).

For the obstruction, the integral unimodular substitution \(x_0=y_0+v^T\bar x\) gives

\[ Q\ \sim_{\mathbf Z}\ (-1)\oplus Q'. \tag{EC31} \]

The torsion cokernel is unchanged. VP4 identifies it with the actual \(\Phi_X\) or \(\Phi_Y\), respectively. Notice that this is an invariance under the constructed contraction, not an assertion about arbitrary ramified base change.

Finally represent a line on integral \(X\) by a Cartier divisor, using a nonzero rational section. Push its prime-divisor coefficients other than \(E\) to their closures on \(Y\). These are Cartier by NM2, and pulling that divisor back differs from the original by an integer multiple of \(E\). A degree-zero restriction to \(E\) makes that integer zero, because \(E^2=-1\). This proves the kernel assertion in (EC27). Pullback is injective by \(h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\), applied after local trivializations. The displayed splitting has degree \(n\) on \(E\), proving surjectivity and the whole split sequence. \(\square\)

2Z.7. Termination and supplied finite actions

EC7. A supplied regular projective model in the standing setting can be transformed, by finitely many of the contractions above, into a regular flat projective numerically minimal model of the same generic curve. At most \(s-1\) components are contracted, where \(s\) is the initial number of special-fibre components. If \(g\ge2\), a supplied finite semilinear action on the model may be retained throughout, by contracting entire orbits.

Proof. Whenever a component has \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\), MG7 identifies it with (EC1). EC3–EC5 contract it and retain regularity, projectivity, flatness and the generic fibre. Each step removes exactly one special-fibre component: all other components have distinct dense open images under the isomorphism off \(E\). A single remaining component cannot have self-intersection \(-1\), because its row in \(Qm=0\) is zero. Thus the process stops in at most \(s-1\) steps, precisely at the required numerical minimality.

For the action statement, first prove disjointness of all exceptional components when \(g\ge2\). If distinct exceptional components \(E,F\) meet with intersection \(a>0\), VP4's negative form gives

\[ (e_E+e_F)^TQ(e_E+e_F)=-2+2a\le0. \tag{EC32} \]

The positive integer \(a\) must be one. Equality in VP4 forces \(e_E+e_F\) onto the kernel line of the everywhere-positive multiplicity vector. There are then only these two components and their multiplicities are equal. Both have arithmetic genus zero, so (MG10) gives

\[ 2g-2=-m_E-m_F<0, \tag{EC33} \]

contrary to \(g\ge2\). Hence every finite orbit of exceptional components consists of disjoint curves.

Contract such an orbit one curve at a time. The morphism is an isomorphism near each of the other disjoint curves, so they remain exceptional until contracted. The universal property EC5, applied successively, says that the composite is universal for maps constant on every curve in the orbit. Any two orders consequently give a unique isomorphism of the targets. A supplied action permuting these curves descends by the same property, and uniqueness proves its identity and composition laws. For a semilinear action apply this to the corresponding base twists. Repeat with an orbit on each resulting model. The component count still decreases, proving termination without averaging by the group order or requiring an invariant ordering. This constructs equivariant numerical minimalization from the supplied model. \(\square\)

2Z.8. The remaining curve-model existence input

EC8. Let \(C/K\) have genus \(g\ge2\) over the standing complete DVR with algebraically closed residue field. Choose \(\ell>768(g-1)\) away from the residue characteristic, and take the finite separable point-and-torsion splitting extension \(R'/R\) constructed in UB7. If a regular integral flat projective model of \(C_{K'}\) is supplied over \(R'\), then a regular projective model with reduced nodal special fibre can be constructed from it. Numerical minimality need not be supplied.

Proof. Apply EC7 to the supplied model over \(R'\). Its residue field is still \(k\), by UB7, and its generic curve, genus, point and full \(\ell\)-torsion are unchanged by the contractions. The resulting model has the precise numerical minimality required in UB6–UB7. VP7 gives \(d=1\); UB gives the obstruction-rank bound for this actual final model. MG8 therefore makes its special fibre reduced and nodal. NE supplies its actual algebraic node charts and NS the intrinsic resolution statements under their proved hypotheses. If the starting model carries a supplied finite action, EC7 preserves it.

This closes the contraction and termination step in the standing setting. Existence of a regular projective model for an arbitrary initial curve remains a separate construction. Reduction over a general residue field still needs the appropriate weighted argument or a proved residue-field passage. The whole integral/formal semiabelian lift, the initial genuine analytic period cover and its geometric pairing identification remain additional steps in the abelian-variety argument. \(\square\)

2Z.9. Graded exercise: a contraction from its formal and numerical data

Exercise 2Z (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. Prove the quadratic length obstruction in EC1 for a local domain with a strict chain \(0\subsetneq P\subsetneq\mathfrak m\). Explain why polynomial associated graded ring in two variables makes the contracted local domain regular, without assuming a dimension theorem for completion.
  2. For the exceptional formal neighborhood, calculate the successive kernel dimensions and \(\operatorname{length}(A/\mathfrak m^n)\). Prove \(I_d=\mathfrak m^d\) by convergent coefficient correction. Explain why no coefficient field or equal-characteristic power-series presentation was used.
  3. Set \(R=\mathbf Z_2\), \(B=R[[u]]\), and blow up \((2,u)\). Calculate its two charts, exceptional curve and conormal line. Compare \(B/(2,u)^2\) with \(\mathbf F_2[[x,y]]/(x,y)^2\) as rings.
  4. In EC3 take \(H|_E=\mathcal O(3)\) and an exponent \(n\) satisfying the stated Serre hypotheses. List the degrees of all successive quotients in (EC14). Explain generation both on and off \(E\), and why the resulting morphism contracts no additional point or curve.
  5. In EC4 prove \(h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\) on every distinguished chart, not just on the original target charts. Explain the two ideal containments and how formal functions identifies the actual completed local ring.
  6. Prove \(\mathfrak m_y\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_X(-E)\), the factorization through the blowup, and the finiteness and isomorphism of the intermediate map. Specify where the full basis of \(H^0(\mathcal O(1))\) is needed.
  7. For the following integer data, contract the first index:\[ Q=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&1\\2&-7&1\\1&1&-4\end{pmatrix}, \quad m=(3,1,1),\quad p=(0,1,1). \tag{ECX1} \] Compute the new matrix, multiplicities, component arithmetic genera, genus budget, gcd and numerical obstruction group. This is a numerical calculation; it does not ask for an unconstructed model realization.
  8. Prove the split Picard sequence by Cartier divisors, and compute the coefficient of \(E\) in a line whose degree on \(E\) is \(d\). Explain why a pullback has zero degree on \(E\).
  9. Prove that exceptional components are disjoint when \(g\ge2\), and that contracting a finite orbit permits its action to descend. Explain uniqueness, independence of contraction order and termination. Contrast this with the genus-zero model obtained by blowing up a smooth point of the special fibre of \(\mathbf P^1_R\).
  10. Give the full logical order from the genus and chosen prime to the finite extension, supplied regular model, contractions and nodal conclusion. Distinguish the now-constructed steps from initial regular-model existence, residue-field passage and the analytic covering still required.

Complete solution.

  1. Choose \(0\ne a\in P\). Artin–Rees gives \((a)\cap\mathfrak m^n\subset a\mathfrak m^{n-c}\). The first term of (EC5) has length at least \(\lambda(n-c)\). Since \(A/P\) is not Artinian, its maximal-ideal powers never stabilize: stabilization would give a zero power by Nakayama, forcing dimension zero. Every degree-\(j\) quotient of its maximal ideal is therefore nonzero, so \(\operatorname{length}(A/(P+\mathfrak m^n))\ge n\). Thus

    \[ \lambda(n)\ge\lambda(n-c)+n,\qquad \lambda(n)\ge c' n^2 \quad\hbox{for sufficiently large }n \tag{ECX2} \]

    with \(c'>0\). The same induction along longer prime chains proves the height estimate in EC1. For the contracted domain, its completion has degree-\(j\) graded dimension \(j+1\), so its length is \(n(n+1)/2\) and its embedding dimension is two. A zero-dimensional domain is a field; a one-dimensional local domain has \(\lambda(n)=O(n)\) by (EC9). Hence its dimension is exactly two, and it is regular.

  2. The kernel of the transition from \(E_{n+1}\) to \(E_n\) is \(H^0(\mathcal O(n))\), of dimension \(n+1\) over the residue field. Thus

    \[ \dim_F I_d/I_{d+1}=d+1,\qquad \operatorname{length}(A/\mathfrak m^n) =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(j+1)=\frac{n(n+1)}2. \tag{ECX3} \]

    Length, rather than a vector-space structure on the whole quotient, is the invariant in mixed characteristic. Choose lifts \(x,y\) of the degree-one basis. At order \(e\ge d\), express the remainder's initial form as a linear combination of degree-\(e\) monomials, then factor each monomial into a degree-\(d\) one and a degree-\(e-d\) one. The collected coefficients of the finitely many degree-\(d\) monomials change by elements of order at least \(e-d\), so converge. The remainder tends to zero by separatedness. Therefore every element of \(I_d\) belongs to \((x,y)^d\), and the reverse inclusion follows from the filtration product. Only residue coefficients were lifted individually; no ring section of the residue map was assumed.

  3. The charts are

    \[ B[t]/(2t-u)=B[u/2],\qquad B[s]/(us-2)=B[2/u]. \tag{ECX4} \]

    Cancellation and reduction by the first parameter prove these equalities as in (EC23). Their exceptional affine lines have coordinates \(t\) and \(s\), with \(s=t^{-1}\) on the overlap, so the exceptional curve is \(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf F_2}\). Its local ideal generators are \(2\) and \(u\), with \(u=t\,2\) on the overlap. Thus the ideal restricted to the exceptional curve is \(\mathcal O(1)\), and its normal line is \(\mathcal O(-1)\). In \(B/(2,u)^2\), the class of \(2\) is nonzero but \(4=0\); this ring has characteristic four. The comparison ring over \(\mathbf F_2\) has characteristic two. Both have length three and associated graded dimensions \(1,2\), but they are not isomorphic as rings. This local example lies outside the algebraically closed residue-field standing setting and illustrates the characteristic qualification in EC2.

  4. For \(j=1,\ldots,3n\), the quotient degree is \(3n-j\), so the list is \(3n-1,3n-2,\ldots,0\). Every term has zero \(H^1\) on \(\mathbf P^1\). Starting with \(H^1(X,H^n)=0\), the exact sequences give zero \(H^1\) up to \(H^n((3n-1)E)\), so a section restricting to one on \(E\) exists. The multiplied \(H^n\)-sections generate off \(E\), and this additional section generates on \(E\). The \(H^n\)-coordinates all vanish on \(E\) and not simultaneously anywhere else. On their common projective open, projection recovers the embedding by \(H^n\), and the additional coordinates give its graph. Thus every point outside \(E\) is retained scheme-theoretically, while \(E\) alone maps to the new point.

  5. On \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset Y_0\), put \(D=\Gamma(f^{-1}U,\mathcal O_X)\). A distinguished open of \(\operatorname{Spec}D\) is \(D(b)\). Cover \(f^{-1}U\) by finitely many affine opens with affine intersections, and localize its section equalizer at the global function \(b\). Exact localization gives \(\Gamma((f^{-1}U)_b,\mathcal O_X)=D_b\), so the direct-image equality holds on the distinguished basis and hence as a sheaf. The inverse-image fibre has underlying set \(E\); its ideal is contained in \(J=\mathcal O_X(-E)\) because functions vanishing at \(y\) vanish on the reduced \(E\). Equality of radicals and finite generation give \(J^c\subset\mathfrak m_y\mathcal O_X\). Taking powers yields (EC20). NF7 computes the completion using all infinitesimal fibres, and these cofinal ideal systems identify that limit with all \(E_n\), not just their reduced supports. EC2 therefore computes the actual completion.

  6. Choose \(u,v\) in the maximal ideal whose completed classes give its degree-one basis. In \(J/J^2=\mathcal O(1)\), their restrictions are the full two-dimensional space of linear sections; they have no common zero. Hence \(J=\mathfrak m_y\mathcal O_X+J^2\), and Nakayama on the quotient gives \(J=\mathfrak m_y\mathcal O_X\). It is invertible, so NS2 constructs the factorization through the blowup. On \(E\) the intermediate map is exactly the degree-one projective-line map given by that basis; it is an isomorphism. Off \(E\) it is an isomorphism as well. It is projective with finite geometric fibres, hence finite by Theorem 0.F.1. A finite birational algebra over a normal target, inside the same fraction field, is the target algebra. The regular chart calculation proves the needed normality and therefore the whole map is an isomorphism. A single nonzero section of \(\mathcal O(1)\) would have a zero and would not supply either the ideal equality or this degree-one exceptional map.

  7. Here \(v=(2,1)\) and

    \[ A_0=\begin{pmatrix}-7&1\\1&-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q'=A_0+vv^T= \begin{pmatrix}-3&3\\3&-3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad m'=(1,1),\quad p'=(2,1). \tag{ECX5} \]

    The original first row gives \(m_0=2\cdot1+1\cdot1=3\). The arithmetic-genus changes are \(\binom22=1\) and \(\binom12=0\). The original budget coefficients are \((-1,7,4)\), and their multiplicity-weighted sum is \(-3+7+4=8\). The new coefficients are \((5,3)\), with the same sum eight. Hence \(2g-2=8\), or \(g=5\), in both numerical data sets. Both gcds are one. The primitive degree-zero lattice for \(Q'\) is generated by \((1,-1)\), and the columns generate three times that lattice, so \(\Phi_{Q'}=\mathbf Z/3\). The determinant-one substitution \(x_0=y_0+2x_1+x_2\) gives

    \[ T^TQT=(-1)\oplus Q',\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{ECX6} \]

    Thus \(\Phi_Q=\mathbf Z/3\) as well. No model realization of these integer data has been presumed.

  8. Choose a nonzero rational section of a line \(M\) and take its Cartier divisor. Push its nonexceptional prime coefficients to \(Y\); regular local factoriality makes the resulting divisor Cartier. Its pullback differs from the original divisor by \(aE\). A pulled-back line restricts to the constant line from the point \(y\), so has degree zero on \(E\). Since \(E^2=-1\), the degree of \(\mathcal O(aE)|_E\) is \(-a\). Therefore

    \[ M\simeq h^*M'\otimes\mathcal O_X(-dE) \quad\hbox{when }\deg_E M=d. \tag{ECX7} \]

    In particular degree zero is exactly the image of pullback. Its injectivity follows from \(h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\) after trivializing on target opens. Finally \(\mathcal O(-nE)\) has degree \(n\), proving the splitting and the full sequence.

  9. Two distinct exceptional curves meeting with intersection \(a>0\) give energy \(-2+2a\le0\). Thus \(a=1\), and zero energy puts their sum on VP4's multiplicity kernel line. Every other component would have positive multiplicity but coefficient zero in that sum, so there are only these two curves and their multiplicities agree. Their rational \((-1)\)-budget is then \(2g-2=-m_E-m_F<0\), impossible for \(g\ge2\). Hence every exceptional orbit is disjoint. A contraction changes nothing near a disjoint remaining curve. Successive contractions are universal for maps constant on every curve of the orbit, so any two orders have unique mutually inverse target maps. An action permuting the orbit descends by this property, and the same uniqueness proves its group law, including base twists. Each step removes a component, and the final one-component fibre has self-intersection zero; termination takes at most the original \(s-1\) contractions.

    In contrast, blowing up a smooth point of the reduced special fibre of \(\mathbf P^1_R\) gives two rational components, each with self-intersection \(-1\), meeting once with multiplicities \((1,1)\). Their energy is zero, and their budget gives \(2g-2=-2\), exactly \(g=0\). The disjointness assertion deliberately requires \(g\ge2\); it would be false in this example.

  10. Fix \(g\ge2\), then choose \(\ell>768(g-1)\) different from the residue characteristic. UB7 produces a finite separable extension with a rational point and the actual full generic Picard \(\ell\)-torsion, and proves that its valuation ring is a complete DVR with the same algebraically closed residue field. Over it, start with a supplied regular projective model. EC3–EC7 construct the contractions and terminate at a numerically minimal regular flat projective model, preserving the generic curve and its point and torsion. Apply UB to this actual model; the genus bound controls its new obstruction group, without identifying it with a pre-extension group. VP7 gives gcd one. MG8 forces the original special fibre of the final model to be reduced and nodal. NE and NS then give their actual chart and resolution conclusions.

    The contractions, projectivity, regularity, finite-action descent and termination have now been proved. Existence of the starting regular projective model for an arbitrary curve is still required, as is the appropriate general-residue-field argument. The whole semiabelian lift, genuine initial analytic period cover and geometric pairing identification remain additional requirements for the abelian-variety theorem.

2AA. Passing from perfect residue fields to the split model criterion

The algebraically closed residue field in UB and EC can be replaced by a perfect residue field. The complete unramified extension will serve as a testing base for a model constructed over finite extensions beforehand. Thus the conclusion will still be a model over a finite extension of the original complete discrete valuation ring.

Let \(R\) be a complete DVR, with uniformizer \(\pi\), fraction field \(K\), and perfect residue field \(k\). Let \(C/K\) be smooth, projective and geometrically integral of genus \(g\ge2\). The initial regular-model construction remains an explicit input. Free comparisons are the Stacks project's finite splitting of geometric components, degree-one characterization of the projective line, and projective exceptional contraction. We supply the field and model passage, using the actual earlier Hensel, flatness, cohomology, contraction and torsion proofs.

2AA.1. Finite unramified lifts with prescribed residue embeddings

RB1. A finite separable extension \(l/k\) has a finite free complete DVR lift \(R_l/R\), with uniformizer \(\pi\), residue field \(l\), and

\[ [\operatorname{Frac}R_l:K]=[l:k]. \tag{RB1} \]

Given lifts and a specified residue embedding, there is exactly one compatible \(R\)-algebra embedding of the lifts. Finite étale \(R\)-algebras are determined by their residue algebras.

Proof. Write \(l=k[\alpha]\) with monic separable minimal polynomial \(\bar f\), by the primitive-element proof after EA5. Lift its coefficients to a monic \(f\in R[T]\), and put

\[ R_l=R[T]/(f). \tag{RB2} \]

Monic division gives a free \(R\)-basis \(1,T,\ldots,T^{d-1}\). It is complete and separated, and its quotient by \(\pi\) is the field \(l\). Every maximal ideal contracts to the maximal ideal of \(R\), by the finite integral inverse argument EA5; hence its maximal ideal is \(\pi R_l\). An element with nonzero residue is a unit by a lifted inverse and the convergent geometric series. Every nonzero element has a first nonzero \(\pi\)-adic coefficient, so is \(\pi^n\) times a unit. Orders of nonzero products add because \(l\) is a field. Thus it is a domain and a DVR; its rank gives (RB1). The derivative \(f'\) is a unit, so this is an actual square-Jacobian étale algebra by EA8–EA11.

In another lift with the prescribed residue embedding, Hensel's Newton proof EA7 gives a unique root of \(f\) lifting the image of \(\alpha\). It defines the required map. The map is injective by flatness over \(R\) and the field map after inverting \(\pi\). If the residue map is an isomorphism, reduction and Nakayama make the map surjective between free \(R\)-modules of equal rank, hence an isomorphism.

For completeness the same uniqueness applies to an arbitrary finite étale algebra \(A/R\). EA10 makes \(A/\pi A\) a finite product of separable fields. Its factor idempotents lift uniquely in the complete finite \(R\)-module \(A\), by the Newton formula for \(T^2-T\); they remain orthogonal and sum to one. In each factor, a lifted primitive residue generator gives a map from (RB2). It is surjective by Nakayama, and its kernel is zero: the finite étale factor is free over local \(R\), its rank is the residue degree, and both sides have that same rank. Combining the factors proves the assertion. This also proves compatibility with compositions of prescribed residue embeddings. \(\square\)

2AA.2. The complete unramified testing base and regularity

RB2. There is a faithfully flat extension of complete DVRs

\[ R\longrightarrow S,\qquad \pi S=\mathfrak m_S,\qquad S/\pi S=\bar k , \tag{RB3} \]

where \(\bar k\) is an algebraic closure of the perfect \(k\). A regular integral flat projective model of a smooth geometrically integral generic curve remains such a model after this extension.

Proof. For each finite subextension \(l\subset\bar k\), take RB1's lift. The uniqueness for residue-labelled embeddings supplies a compatible directed system: an embedding into the lift of a common finite compositum is unique, and composites have the prescribed residue embeddings. All maps are injective. Let

\[ R^{\mathrm{nr}}=\varinjlim_{l\subset\bar k}R_l,\qquad S=\varprojlim_n R^{\mathrm{nr}}/\pi^nR^{\mathrm{nr}}. \tag{RB4} \]

Perfectness makes all these finite residue extensions separable. Every nonzero element of the union is a power of \(\pi\) times a unit in some \(R_l\); its residue field is \(\bar k\). Every nonzero ideal has an element of least valuation, which then generates it. Thus the union is already a DVR. It is separated for powers of \(\pi\). The completion has the same description: a nonzero element has a first nonzero coefficient, its leading residue is in the field \(\bar k\), and the remaining unit is inverted by a convergent geometric series. Product orders add, and least valuations again make all ideals principal. Consequently \(S\) is a complete DVR with (RB3). It is torsion-free over \(R\), hence flat by the DVR module argument §0A. It is faithfully flat: a proper ideal of the local \(R\) remains proper since it is contained in \(\pi S\); the cyclic-submodule proof used in EA7 then detects every nonzero module.

Let \(X/R\) be the model in the statement. Projectivity and flatness survive base change, and \(X_S\) is Noetherian, since it is of finite type over the Noetherian DVR \(S\). Its generic fibre is smooth and geometrically integral. On an affine chart its coordinate ring is \(\pi\)-torsion-free and injects into its localization on that generic fibre, a domain. Hence the chart is a domain, and \(X_S\) is integral.

We check regularity also at points of the special fibre. For any field \(F/k\), the algebra \(F\otimes_k\bar k\) is a directed union of finite étale \(F\)-algebras. After localizing at a prime, each finite stage is a field, and the resulting local algebra is a directed union of fields, hence a field. Indeed a nonzero element and its inverse already occur in one of these field stages. Thus for a local map

\[ A=\mathcal O_{X,x}\longrightarrow B=\mathcal O_{X_S,z} \quad(z\text{ in the special fibre}), \tag{RB5} \]

flatness holds and the closed fibre is a field; consequently \(\mathfrak m_AB=\mathfrak m_B\). If \(d=\dim A\), regularity of \(A\) supplies \(d\) maximal-ideal generators. They generate that of \(B\). EC1 gives \(\dim B\le d\), while EA14's flat going-down proof lifts a length-\(d\) chain and gives the reverse inequality. Thus \(B\) is regular.
