On the generic fibre, smoothness gives regularity by SF1–SF3 and the regularity test after NM2. This proves the assertion at every point.

The identical local proof applies to a finite unramified lift \(R_l/R\). It applies as well when constructing \(S\) starting from any such finite lift. \(\square\)

2AA.3. Splitting the components over a finite residue extension

RB3. A reduced finite-type scheme over a perfect field stays reduced after algebraic closure. If it has finitely many irreducible components, a finite separable extension makes every component geometrically integral. For the reduced special fibre of a projective model, that extension has a finite unramified DVR lift by RB1.

Proof. On a reduced Noetherian affine chart \(A\), the map

\[ A\longrightarrow\prod_{\mathfrak p\ \mathrm{minimal}} \operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p) \tag{RB6} \]

is injective, since the intersection of the finitely many minimal primes is the nilradical, zero by EA2–EA4. After a finite separable extension \(l/k\), each field factor tensored with \(l\) is a finite étale algebra, a product of fields by EA10. Flat field tensor preserves the injection. Thus \(A\otimes_k l\) is reduced. Taking the injective directed union over \(l\subset\bar k\) proves reducedness over \(\bar k\).

The finitely many components over \(\bar k\) are closed reduced subschemes. On a finite affine cover, their prime ideals have finite generating lists. Each generator has finitely many coefficients in \(\bar k\). Choose a finite subextension \(l/k\) containing all those coefficients. The resulting ideals glue already over \(l\): agreement on principal overlaps, and any necessary ideal equality, is detected after the faithfully flat field extension to \(\bar k\). Their scalar extensions are the original prime ideals. Their quotients are therefore domains over \(l\), and remain the given integral components over \(\bar k\). The intersection of these ideals is zero, again detected after field extension, and none contains another. They are all the components of the scheme over \(l\).

Here is the field-extension criterion implicit in the word geometrically. If \(A\) is a finite-type domain over an algebraically closed field \(F\), then \(A\otimes_F L\) is a domain for every extension field \(L/F\). Otherwise take two nonzero elements with zero product and put their finitely many coefficients in a finite-type domain \(D\subset L\). Expand each in finitely many \(F\)-linearly independent elements of \(A\), and select a nonzero coefficient from each. Their product \(d\) is nonzero in \(D\). EA5's normalization and maximal-ideal argument gives an \(F\)-point of the nonzero finite-type algebra \(D[1/d]\). Specializing there keeps both elements nonzero while their product stays zero in \(A\), a contradiction. For an integral scalar extension to \(\bar k\), apply this argument after embedding \(\bar k\) into an algebraic closure of any proposed extension of \(k\); faithful field tensor then detects the domain property. This proves geometric integrality of the descended components. The same argument with (RB6) gives geometric reducedness.

All coefficient fields just used are finite separable extensions because \(k\) is perfect. Applying RB1 lifts the chosen \(l\) to a finite unramified extension of the original DVR. Reducedness commutes with this special-fibre field extension by the first part, so no nilpotent components are lost. \(\square\)

2AA.4. Genus-zero components and contractions over their field

RB4. Let \(D/k\) be a proper geometrically integral curve of arithmetic genus zero. A line of degree one gives an isomorphism \(D\simeq\mathbf P^1_k\). Consequently, on a regular model whose special components are geometrically integral, every component with \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\) admits the projective contraction of EC3–EC6 over its actual residue field \(k\).

Proof. Field extension commutes with coherent cohomology here by the finite affine Čech calculation SC12; flat tensor preserves its kernels and images. The degree \(\deg L=\chi(L)-\chi(\mathcal O_D)\) is therefore unchanged. Over \(\bar k\), RC1–RC2 give the normalization formula

\[ 0=g(D_{\bar k})= g(\widetilde D_{\bar k})+ \operatorname{length}(\nu_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde D_{\bar k}}/ \mathcal O_{D_{\bar k}}). \tag{RB7} \]

Both terms are nonnegative, so the curve is smooth of genus zero. The degree-one-function argument in MG7, using a point over \(\bar k\) and the proved curve Riemann–Roch formula, makes it \(\mathbf P^1_{\bar k}\). A degree-one line becomes \(\mathcal O(1)\). Thus its original global section space has dimension two; its evaluation map is surjective since its scalar extension is. The resulting morphism

\[ D\longrightarrow\mathbf P^1_k \tag{RB8} \]

becomes the degree-one projective-line isomorphism over \(\bar k\). Its geometric fibres are reduced points, so the proper closed-immersion criterion CIE1 makes (RB8) a closed immersion. The ideal of its image becomes zero over \(\bar k\), hence is already zero. This proves the isomorphism over \(k\).

For a component as in the statement, the line \(\mathcal O_X(-D)|_D\) has degree one, so the first part makes it \(\mathbf P^1_k\) and identifies its normal line with \(\mathcal O(-1)\). EC2 already allowed any residue field. EC3's projective-map construction uses \(H|_D=\mathcal O(a)\), the nonnegative projective-line cohomology and a section restricting to one, all valid over \(k\). The finite-algebra construction EC4 maps this connected \(D\) to one point \(y\). Its residue field embeds, over \(k\), in \(\Gamma(D,\mathcal O_D)=k\); it is therefore \(k\), without an algebraic-closure assumption. All subsequent completion, regularity, blowup, universal-property and numerical arguments EC4–EC6 now apply over \(k\) as written.

After a contraction the remaining components stay geometrically integral. The map from each old component to its image is proper and surjective and stays so after field extension: its nonempty field fibres remain nonempty after extension, as one sees on an affine chart by faithful field tensor. Its geometric source is irreducible, so the image is irreducible. The image curve is reduced over the perfect \(k\), hence geometrically reduced by RB3. This proves the assertion about all remaining components and permits repeated contractions. \(\square\)

2AA.5. Numerical data on the testing base

RB5. Suppose a regular integral flat projective model \(X/R\) has geometrically integral special components \(D_i\). Write

\[ \operatorname{div}(\pi)=\sum_i m_iD_i,\qquad p_i=h^1(D_i,\mathcal O_{D_i}),\qquad Q_{ij}=\deg_{D_i}\bigl(\mathcal O_X(D_j)|_{D_i}\bigr). \tag{RB9} \]

After the testing extension \(R\to S\) in RB2, these components, multiplicities, genera and intersection numbers are unchanged, with \(D_i\) replaced by \((D_i)_{\bar k}\). In particular numerical minimality is unchanged.

Proof. The base-changed components are integral by hypothesis and remain distinct and exhaustive; this follows on charts by tensoring their reduced ideals and by faithful flatness. Each is still an effective Cartier divisor, since a flat base change preserves its one-equation nonzero-divisor presentation. At its generic point, the local map in (RB5) has closed fibre a field. Both local rings are DVRs, and the old maximal ideal generates the new one. Thus an old local parameter is a new local parameter, giving

\[ \operatorname{ord}_{(D_i)_{\bar k}}(\pi)=m_i. \tag{RB10} \]

Flat field tensor in the special-fibre Čech complex preserves \(h^0,h^1\) dimensions and Euler characteristics. It therefore preserves \(p_i\), every line degree and the displayed \(Q_{ij}\). Numerical minimality means absence of an index with \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\); that condition is consequently the same on both bases. The generic genus is likewise unchanged by field extension. \(\square\)

We can now reach this minimality condition before passing to \(S\). First use RB3 and a finite unramified extension to make the special components geometrically integral. Whenever \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\), RB4 constructs its contraction over the finite base. The other components remain geometrically integral. Each contraction removes one component and preserves the generic curve; a one-component fibre has \(Q_{11}=0\), by restricting the principal divisor of \(\pi\). Thus the process terminates after at most one less than the current initial number of components. Only finite extensions and actual projective contractions have been used to construct this minimal model.

2AA.6. Prime choice, torsion splitting and the finite model

RB6. Choose a prime

\[ \ell>768(g-1),\qquad\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k. \tag{RB11} \]

There is a finite separable extension \(K_1/K\) with a rational point on \(C_{K_1}\) and full actual generic Picard \(\ell\)-torsion. Its integral closure \(R_1\) is a finite complete DVR over \(R\), with perfect residue field. If an initial regular integral flat projective model over \(R_1\) is supplied, further finite unramified extension and the contractions above produce a regular flat projective model \(Y/R_2\) whose base change to the complete unramified testing ring has reduced nodal special fibre.

Proof. The separable-point and torsion-splitting part of UB7 does not use algebraic closure of the residue field: a nonempty smooth curve chart has an étale map to an open of \(\mathbf A^1_K\); the powers of \(\pi\) make \(K\) infinite, so EA10 supplies a point over a finite separable extension. Construct its pointed Jacobian by JC, and split the finite étale \(\ell\)-torsion algebra by a finite separable normal extension, using CU–FF. Thus

\[ C(K_1)\ne\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{Pic}(C_{K_1})[\ell]\simeq (\mathbf Z/\ell)^{2g}. \tag{RB12} \]

The trace-lattice, Artin residue-algebra and idempotent-lifting argument in UB7 proves finiteness, localness and the complete DVR assertion for the integral closure without assuming a finite or algebraically closed residue field. Its residue field \(k_1\) is finite over \(k\), and therefore perfect. Only UB7's final identification of that residue field with \(k\) used algebraic closure, and no such identification is made here.

Start with the supplied regular model over \(R_1\). RB3 supplies a finite separable residue extension splitting all components, and RB1 lifts it to a finite unramified complete DVR \(R_2/R_1\). RB2 preserves regularity and integrality of the base-changed model. Apply the finite contraction process following RB5, obtaining \(Y/R_2\) with geometrically integral components and numerically minimal data. Its generic curve retains the point, genus and torsion in (RB12).

Construct \(S/R_2\) by RB2. The model \(Y_S\) is regular, integral, flat and projective, with algebraically closed residue field. RB5 preserves its precise numerical minimality. The point gives \(d=1\) by VP7; pointed JC and the unchanged full rational torsion give generic Picard rank \(2g\). UB6 bounds the torsion rank of this actual model's obstruction group, with the already chosen prime, and MG8 gives

\[ (Y_S)_{\bar k_2}\ \text{reduced and nodal, with smooth components and one transverse point for each meeting pair}. \tag{RB13} \]

This proves the assertion. In particular no equations or model over \(S\) have to be descended: \(Y\) was constructed over the finite base \(R_2\) before this test. \(\square\)

2AA.7. The actual split nodal fibre over the finite base

RB7. The finite model \(Y/R_2\) in RB6 already has reduced split nodal special fibre. Every component is smooth over \(k_2\); each node is \(k_2\)-rational with two distinct component branches. The algebraic charts of NE apply to this model, with thickness one since \(Y\) is regular.

Proof. A nilpotent section of the special fibre becomes zero in the reduced extension (RB13). Faithful field tensor makes it zero before extension, so the special fibre is reduced. Its components become smooth over \(\bar k_2\); the actual Jacobian-minor criterion SF1–SF3 descends this smoothness, since vanishing of the necessary cokernel is detected by faithful field extension.

For distinct components which meet, RB5 and (RB13) give \(Q_{ij}=1\). The local intersection formula, obtained exactly as in VP3 by restricting their Cartier equations, now includes residue degrees:

\[ 1=Q_{ij} =\sum_{x\in D_i\cap D_j} [\kappa(x):k_2]\, \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{Y,x}} \bigl(\mathcal O_{Y,x}/(f_i,f_j)\bigr). \tag{RB14} \]

Every summand is a positive integer. Thus there is exactly one meeting point, its residue field is \(k_2\), and its intersection length is one. No third component passes through it, by (RB13). At such a point \(x\), the regular surface ring \(B=\mathcal O_{Y,x}\) has

\[ \pi=u f_if_j,\qquad (f_i,f_j)=\mathfrak m_B,\qquad u\in B^*. \tag{RB15} \]

The factorization follows from NM2 and all fibre multiplicities being one; the ideal equality follows from the length-one quotient. The completed special local ring is a quotient of \(k_2[[s,t]]/(st)\), by sending \(s,t\) to \(f_i,f_j\). Surjectivity follows by successively expanding in these maximal-ideal generators, with coefficients lifted from its given \(k_2\)-algebra structure. Modulo \(s\), this map is the isomorphism onto the completed local ring of the smooth branch, \(k_2[[t]]\), because \(f_j\) is its parameter. Modulo \(t\), it is similarly an isomorphism onto \(k_2[[s]]\). Any kernel is therefore in

\[ (s)\cap(t)=0\quad\text{in }k_2[[s,t]]/(st). \tag{RB16} \]

This proves the full split node equation. A point on only one component is smooth, since that component is smooth and the fibre is reduced.

NE explicitly assumes a complete DVR and split rational nodes, rather than an algebraically closed residue field. Its actual construction therefore gives étale charts \(ab=\varepsilon\pi^h\) here. NS's local regularity calculation forces \(h=1\): for \(h>1\), the closed local ring has three independent cotangent generators but dimension two. Thus the finite model has the asserted actual algebraic charts. \(\square\)

2AA.8. Scope of the residue-field passage and supplied actions

RB8. In the genus-\(\ge2\) curve argument over a complete DVR with perfect residue field, initial regular-model existence after the torsion-splitting extension is now the remaining model-existence input. No separate weighted numerical classification is required for this perfect-field passage. This includes finite residue fields. Supplied finite actions descend through the contractions when their action on the chosen finite model is actually given.

Proof. RB1–RB7 use finite separable generic extension, finite unramified component splitting, and projective contractions over the finite base. They test their numerical data on \(S\) and produce the finite split nodal model itself. These are exactly the residue-field and minimalization steps needed to apply UB and MG.

For supplied actions, the set of components with \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\) is stable. Such components are disjoint when \(g\ge2\): after the testing base change their data are unchanged, and EC7's negative-energy and genus-budget proof applies. Each is already \(\mathbf P^1_{k_2}\) by RB4. Contract a whole orbit. The universal property proved in EC5 and valid over \(k_2\) gives the descended action, with its group law and semilinear base twists proved by uniqueness. This does not assert that an unspecified generic action extends to a chosen model or lifts to an unspecified finite extension.

Perfectness has a concrete role. For example, if \(k=\mathbf F_p(a)\) with \(a\) transcendental and \(l=k(a^{1/p})\), then \(l\) is a field but

\[ l\otimes_k\bar k\simeq \bar k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^p). \tag{RB17} \]

Thus the regular proper integral \(k\)-curve \(\mathbf P^1_l\) is not geometrically reduced over \(k\). Finite separable residue extensions do not remove this purely inseparable constant extension. RB3's perfect-field assertion cannot be used for this example. The example is a statement about a special-field curve; it is not a counterexample satisfying the smooth geometrically integral generic-curve hypotheses.

Initial regular-model construction is still required. The whole integral/formal semiabelian lift, genuine initial analytic Jacobian period cover, finite-extension point lifting and geometric pairing identification remain further parts of the abelian-variety theorem. The present argument establishes the required perfect-residue-field passage from an initial regular model and preserves all those remaining obligations. \(\square\)

2AA.9. Graded exercise: residue lifts, components and finite nodal models

Exercise 2AA (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. Lift \(l=\mathbf F_4=\mathbf F_2[\alpha]/(\alpha^2+\alpha+1)\) to an unramified complete DVR over \(\mathbf Z_2\). Exhibit its basis, residue field, uniformizer and degree. Explain why its derivative is a unit and why a prescribed residue embedding has a unique lift.
  2. In \(A=(\mathbf Z/8)[T]/(T^2+T+1)\), compute \((1+2T)^{-1}\), the number of elements of each valuation \(0,1,2\), and the zero element. Explain why this ring is not a field, despite having a field as its residue algebra.
  3. Construct the testing ring in RB2 and prove it is a DVR. For a field \(F/k\), explain why every local ring of \(F\otimes_k\bar k\) is a field when \(k\) is perfect. Use this fact to prove regularity of the base-changed model at every special-fibre point.
  4. Over \(\mathbf F_3\), consider the reduced plane curve\[ Z=V(x^2+y^2)\subset\mathbf P^2. \tag{RBX1} \] Describe its two components over \(\mathbf F_9\), their intersection point, and the Galois permutation. Explain how the finite-coefficient argument in RB3 generalizes this splitting and why it must be applied to geometric components rather than just the original components.
  5. Prove the genus-zero degree-one-line argument in RB4, including the actual morphism to \(\mathbf P^1\). Apply it to \(\mathcal O_X(-D)|_D\) when \(p_D=0,D^2=-1\). Identify the precise step that replaces the use of an algebraically closed residue field in EC4.
  6. Assume a model has geometrically integral components and has reached numerical minimality over its perfect residue field. Prove that its multiplicities, arithmetic genera, every intersection number and its minimality are preserved by the testing extension. Explain the local parameter calculation and the global Euler-degree calculation separately.
  7. A meeting pair of components has total intersection one over \(k\). Prove that its meeting point is rational, unique and transverse, retaining residue-degree factors. Compare with one closed point of degree two and local intersection length one.
  8. Let \(B\) be the regular local surface ring at that rational meeting point, with \(\pi=u f g\) and \((f,g)=\mathfrak m_B\). Construct the isomorphism of the completed special local ring with \(k[[s,t]]/(st)\), checking both the surjection and its kernel. Deduce the thickness in an NE chart.
  9. Set \(k=\mathbf F_p(a)\) and \(l=k(a^{1/p})\). Prove that \(l/k\) has degree \(p\), calculate its scalar extension to \(\bar k\), and explain what happens to \(\mathbf P^1_l\). Explain why adjoining only separable residue extensions does not correct this example.
  10. State the complete order of choices in RB6–RB7 and the resulting finite-extension conclusion. Identify the actual remaining initial-model hypothesis. State what may be concluded about a supplied finite action and what extension of an action has not been constructed.

Complete solution.

  1. Take

    \[ R_l=\mathbf Z_2[T]/(T^2+T+1). \tag{RBX2} \]

    Its basis is \(1,T\). It is free of rank two and complete; reduction gives the irreducible quadratic extension \(\mathbf F_4\). Its maximal ideal is \(2R_l\), its uniformizer is \(2\), and the fraction field has degree two over \(\mathbf Q_2\). Every nonzero element is a power of two times a unit by its first nonzero residue coefficient, so the ring is a DVR and a domain. The derivative \(2T+1\) reduces to one, hence is a unit. A specified image of \(\alpha\) is a simple residue root of the lifted polynomial; complete-local Newton iteration gives one and only one lifted root, which supplies the unique algebra embedding. The other residue embedding sends \(\alpha\) to \(\alpha^2\) and lifts to the corresponding conjugation, not to a second lift of the same prescribed embedding.

  2. Since \(T^2=-T-1\), direct multiplication gives

    \[ (1+2T)(5+2T)=5+12T+4T^2=1+8T=1 \quad\hbox{in }A. \tag{RBX3} \]

    One way to find the inverse is the finite geometric-series calculation

    \[ (1+2T)(1-2T+4T^2)=1+8T^3=1,\qquad 1-2T+4T^2=5+2T\quad\hbox{in }A. \tag{RBX4} \]

    Therefore the inverse is \(5+2T\); multiplying with \(T^2=-T-1\) gives one directly. The ring has \(8^2=64\) elements. Its ideals \(2A\) and \(4A\) have \(16\) and \(4\) elements. Hence the valuation counts are \(48\) units, \(12\) elements of valuation one, \(3\) elements of valuation two, and one zero element. Its nonzero element \(2\) is nilpotent modulo eight and not invertible. Having residue field \(\mathbf F_4\) makes the ring local, not a field.

  3. Lift every finite subfield extension of \(\bar k/k\) by RB1, using the unique maps for residue inclusions. Their directed union has residue \(\bar k\) and uniformizer \(\pi\). Every nonzero element has an integer valuation and is a power of \(\pi\) times a unit. An element of least valuation generates any nonzero ideal. The same description holds in its separated \(\pi\)-adic completion, by taking the first nonzero coefficient and inverting the remaining unit. Thus the completion is the required complete DVR \(S\). It is faithfully flat over \(R\) by torsion-free DVR flatness and its nonzero residue fibre.

    For finite separable \(l/k\), the algebra \(F\otimes_k l\) is a finite product of fields. At a chosen prime of the directed union, localizing each stage selects a field. Its transition maps are injective field maps; every nonzero element has an inverse in a finite stage. Thus the limit local ring is a field. At a special point of \(X_S\), the flat local map from the original regular local ring consequently has maximal ideal generated by the old maximal ideal. If the old dimension is \(d\), its \(d\) parameters generate the new maximal ideal. EC1 bounds the new dimension above by \(d\), and flat going down bounds it below by \(d\). This proves regularity, including at generic points of components rather than only at closed points.

  4. The polynomial \(T^2+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbf F_3\). Let \(\alpha^2=-1\) in \(\mathbf F_9\). Then

    \[ x^2+y^2=(x-\alpha y)(x+\alpha y), \qquad \alpha^3=-\alpha. \tag{RBX5} \]

    The two distinct geometric components are lines. They meet only at \([0:0:1]\), with local equations having independent linear parts, so intersection length one. Frobenius exchanges them. Over \(\mathbf F_3\) the homogeneous polynomial is irreducible, so the original curve is integral; over \(\mathbf F_9\) it has these two geometrically integral components. In general, choose generators for each geometric component ideal on a finite affine cover. Only finitely many algebraic coefficients occur, so one finite separable extension contains them; faithful field tensor detects the overlap equalities, exhaustiveness and reduced ideal intersection. Splitting the original list alone would miss components such as this conjugate pair.

  5. Over \(\bar k\), the normalization genus and singularity-length formula gives a sum of two nonnegative terms equal to zero. Thus the curve is smooth of genus zero, and the proved degree-one-function argument makes it \(\mathbf P^1_{\bar k}\). A degree-one line becomes \(\mathcal O(1)\). Its section space over \(k\) has dimension two by field Čech base change, and evaluation is surjective because its cokernel becomes zero over \(\bar k\). The resulting \(D\to\mathbf P^1_k\) becomes an isomorphism; CIE1 makes it a closed immersion, and faithful field tensor makes its image ideal zero. It is an isomorphism over \(k\). For the component, \(\mathcal O_X(-D)|_D\) has degree \(-D^2=1\), so it supplies exactly this construction, including its normal line \(\mathcal O(-1)\). In EC4 the contracted point's residue field embeds over \(k\) into \(\Gamma(D,\mathcal O_D)=k\); hence it is \(k\). Algebraic closure is unnecessary for that step.

  6. At a component's generic point, the flat local base-change map has a field as closed fibre. The old maximal ideal therefore generates the new one. Both local rings are DVRs, so an old parameter remains a parameter, and the order of \(\pi\) is unchanged. For each proper component and each restricted line, its finite affine Čech complex tensors with the residue-field extension. Flatness preserves the cohomology; its dimensions over the new field equal the original dimensions. Thus \(p_i\) and \(\chi(L)-\chi(\mathcal O)\) are unchanged, giving every \(Q_{ij}\), including diagonal terms. There is exactly one new component for each old one because they are geometrically integral. Hence the test \(p_i=0,Q_{ii}=-1\) is identical on both bases, as are all multiplicities and their gcd. A change in the number of geometric components would invalidate this argument; that is why splitting them preceded minimalization.

  7. The local formula is

    \[ Q_{ij}=\sum_x[\kappa(x):k]\, \operatorname{length}(B_x/(f_i,f_j)). \tag{RBX6} \]

    Every term is a positive integer. A sum equal to one has exactly one term, and both its degree and its length are one. Thus the point is rational and unique, and the two equations generate its maximal ideal. On a regular surface they are independent parameters, which is the asserted transversality. A single degree-two point of length one contributes two, so cannot satisfy \(Q_{ij}=1\), even though its local length alone is one.

  8. The completed special local ring is a complete \(k\)-algebra generated topologically by the images of \(f,g\), because those generate its maximal ideal. Successive homogeneous correction gives a surjection \(k[[s,t]]\to\widehat{B/(\pi)}\). Since \(\pi=u f g\), it factors through \(D=k[[s,t]]/(st)\). Modulo \(s\), the resulting map identifies \(k[[t]]\) with the completed local ring of the smooth first component; \(g\) is its parameter. Modulo \(t\), the other component gives \(k[[s]]\). A kernel element must therefore be in both \((s)\) and \((t)\) in \(D\). Every element of \(D\) has unique form \(c+s a(s)+t b(t)\); these two ideals have zero intersection. Thus the kernel is zero and the completed ring is exactly the split node. NE gives actual étale charts \(uv=\varepsilon\pi^h\). If \(h>1\), the relation lies in the square of the maximal ideal on the three generators \(\pi,u,v\), giving embedding dimension three in dimension two, contrary to regularity. Hence \(h=1\).

  9. The element \(a\) is not a \(p\)-th power in \(\mathbf F_p(a)\): the order at the irreducible polynomial \(a\) in a rational \(p\)-th power is divisible by \(p\), whereas the order of \(a\) is one. Thus \(T^p-a\) has no root in \(k\), and its purely inseparable root has degree \(p\). Over \(\bar k\), write \(b=a^{1/p}\). Then

    \[ T^p-a=(T-b)^p,\qquad l\otimes_k\bar k=\bar k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^p). \tag{RBX7} \]

    The integral regular curve \(\mathbf P^1_l\) consequently becomes a nonreduced thickening of \(\mathbf P^1_{\bar k}\). If \(a^{1/p}\) belonged to a separable extension of \(k\), it would be both purely inseparable and separable over \(k\), forcing it to lie in \(k\), a contradiction. Hence finite separable residue splitting does not remove this obstruction. This example has no smooth geometrically integral generic-curve claim attached to it.

  10. First fix the genus and choose \(\ell>768(g-1)\) away from the residue characteristic. Next take a finite separable generic extension making a point and all geometric Jacobian \(\ell\)-torsion rational, with its finite complete DVR integral closure \(R_1\). Supply an initial regular integral flat projective model over \(R_1\). Split its geometric special components over a finite separable residue extension, lift that extension unramified to \(R_2\), and perform the actual projective contractions there until numerical minimality is reached. These operations keep the components geometrically integral and retain the generic curve, point and torsion. Only now form the complete unramified testing ring \(S/R_2\). Its regular model has exactly the same numerical data. UB and MG force the reduced nodal fibre over \(\bar k_2\), and RB7 proves that the already constructed finite model itself is reduced and split nodal, with actual thickness-one charts.

    The remaining model-existence input is the initial regular projective model after the torsion-splitting extension. The perfect-residue passage and terminating contractions have now been constructed; finite residue fields are included. A finite action actually supplied on the chosen finite model descends through its stable exceptional orbits, by the contraction universal property and uniqueness. No extension of an unspecified generic action to that model or to an unspecified finite field extension is asserted. The semiabelian lift, initial analytic covering and geometric pairing remain further abelian-variety requirements.

2AB. Finite normal curve models and the resolution problem

A regular projective model is still needed in RB6. We first construct a normal projective model directly. Normality settles every local ring of dimension one, but permits singular local rings of dimension two. The construction also extends a finite group of automorphisms of the generic curve to a normal model. Resolving that model, with any required action, remains a separate geometric step.

Let \(R\) be a DVR, with fraction field \(K\), uniformizer \(\pi\) and residue field \(k\). For the curve construction assume \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), as in Theorem 2.4. Completeness is unnecessary in this section. The free comparison for the algebra is the Stacks project's finite separable normalization lemma. We supply the trace argument and all the constructions needed here. We do not invoke surface resolution as a proof of regular-model existence.

2AB.1. A finite trace enclosure

TN1. Let \(A\) be a Noetherian integrally closed domain, \(F=\operatorname{Frac}A\), and \(L/F\) a finite separable extension of degree \(n\). Its integral closure \(B\) is finite over \(A\). There is an integral \(F\)-basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) such that, with the trace-dual basis \(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*\),

\[ \begin{gathered} A[b_1,\ldots,b_n]\subset B \subset M:=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A b_i^* \subset \Delta^{-1}\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A b_i,\\ \Delta=\det\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/F}(b_i b_j)\bigr)\ne0. \end{gathered} \tag{TN1} \]

Here \(M\) is a containing module, generally not an algebra or the integral closure.

Proof. The primitive-element proof in Lesson 1, EA5, gives \(L=F(\theta)\). Multiply \(\theta\) by one nonzero denominator \(a\in A\). If its monic equation has coefficients \(c_i\in F\), indexed by the drop \(i\) in degree, choose \(a\) with \(ac_i\in A\) for all \(i\). The new coefficients \(a^ic_i\) belong to \(A\). Thus \(a\theta\) is integral. Its powers of exponents \(0,\ldots,n-1\) give the required integral basis.

Integral elements form a ring. Indeed finitely many integral generators produce a finite module, by bounding the power of each generator with its monic equation. Multiplication by any element of this algebra on a finite generating tuple gives a matrix over \(A\). The adjugate identity makes its characteristic polynomial annihilate the tuple, and hence \(1\). This proves integrality of every element of the algebra and also proves transitivity of integrality by using a finite list of coefficients. In particular each product \(zb_i\), for integral \(z\), is integral.

Take a splitting field of the separable minimal polynomial. Distinct roots give, by polynomial Chinese remainders, a product of \(n\) copies of that field after scalar extension. Multiplication is diagonal there, so its trace is the sum of the \(n\) conjugates. The trace Gram matrix for the power basis is \(V^{\mathsf T}V\), where \(V\) is the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct roots. Its determinant is nonzero. A change of basis preserves nondegeneracy. This argument works when the characteristic divides \(n\); it does not divide by \(n\).

The conjugates of an integral element are integral over \(A\); their sum is integral by the finite-module argument. Its trace belongs to \(F\), and therefore to \(A\), since \(A\) is integrally closed. Thus \(\operatorname{Tr}(zb_i)\in A\) for every \(z\in B\). The nondegenerate pairing gives a unique dual basis, and explicitly

\[ z=\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}(zb_i)b_i^*, \qquad (b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)G^{-1}, \quad G_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}(b_ib_j). \tag{TN2} \]

The adjugate formula \(G^{-1}=\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(G)\) proves (TN1). The module \(M\) is free of rank \(n\). Its submodule \(B\) is finite because \(A\) is Noetherian. The first inclusion in (TN1) follows from integrality of the chosen basis. The closure \(B\) is integrally closed: an element of \(L\) integral over \(B\) is integral over \(A\), by transitivity. Its fraction field is \(L\), since it contains an \(F\)-basis and \(F\subset\operatorname{Frac}B\). \(\square\)

No assertion of freeness of \(B\) over a higher-dimensional base is part of TN1.

2AB.2. Localization and the two affine base charts

TN2. Integral closure in a fixed field commutes with localization. Moreover \(R[t]\), \(R[t^{-1}]\) and their overlap \(R[t,t^{-1}]\) are Noetherian integrally closed domains.

Proof. Let \(S\subset A\setminus\{0\}\) be multiplicative and let \(B\) be the integral closure of \(A\) in \(L\). The inclusion \(S^{-1}B\) in the closure of \(S^{-1}A\) follows by localizing a monic equation. Conversely, suppose \(z\) satisfies a monic equation over \(S^{-1}A\). Choose one \(s\in S\) clearing the finitely many coefficient denominators. For a sufficiently large \(N\), multiplication of the equation by \(s^{Nn}\) makes it a monic equation over \(A\) for \(s^Nz\): its coefficient at the drop \(i\) is \(s^{Ni}c_i\in A\). Hence \(s^Nz\in B\), so \(z\in S^{-1}B\). This proves

\[ \overline{S^{-1}A}^{\,L}=S^{-1}\overline A^{\,L}. \tag{TN3} \]

For the polynomial rings, the Noetherian assertion is the polynomial-ring proof in Lesson 3, N1–N2. Here is the needed normality argument. Every nonzero polynomial over \(R\) is \(\pi^a\) times a primitive polynomial, where primitive means that some coefficient is a unit. A product of primitive polynomials is primitive: its reduction is the product of two nonzero polynomials in the domain \(k[t]\). Factor a primitive polynomial over the Euclidean ring \(K[t]\), and scale each factor to be primitive over \(R\). The product of those scaled factors is primitive. The remaining scalar has valuation zero and is a unit of \(R\). Uniqueness follows from uniqueness over \(K[t]\), together with the unique content exponent. A primitive irreducible over \(K[t]\) is prime in \(R[t]\). Indeed divisibility over \(K[t]\) gives a quotient \(q\); the minimum coefficient valuation of a product is the sum of those of its factors, by scaling both to primitive polynomials and reducing modulo \(\pi\). If the dividend is over \(R\) and the divisor is primitive, the minimum valuation of \(q\) is therefore nonnegative, so \(q\in R[t]\). Primality over \(K[t]\) consequently implies primality over \(R[t]\). Also \(\pi\) is prime, since the quotient is \(k[t]\). Thus \(R[t]\) is a UFD.

In a UFD, inserting a coprime fraction \(a/b\) into a monic equation forces \(b\mid a^n\), so every prime factor of \(b\) divides \(a\); hence \(b\) is a unit. This proves integral closedness. The same proof applies with the variable named \(t^{-1}\). Localization preserves integral closedness by (TN3) applied to the fraction field itself, and preserves the Noetherian property by clearing denominators from ideal generators. It gives the overlap assertion. \(\square\)

2AB.3. Dimension of a finite model

TN3. Every finite domain extension of \(R[t]\) has dimension two. Its primes of height one have DVR local rings if the extension ring is normal.

Proof. First classify chains in \(R[t]\). A prime disjoint from \(R\setminus\{0\}\) corresponds to a prime of \(K[t]\), so a chain of such primes has length at most one. Primes containing \(\pi\) correspond to primes of \(k[t]\), so they are \((\pi)\) or maximal ideals lying above an irreducible polynomial in \(k[t]\). No nonzero prime disjoint from \(\pi\) can be contained in \((\pi)\). Indeed take a nonzero polynomial in such a prime, remove its largest common \(\pi\)-power, and use primality to keep its primitive part in the prime. That part does not belong to \((\pi)\). Thus every chain has length at most two, and

\[ (0)\subsetneq(\pi)\subsetneq(\pi,t) \tag{TN4} \]

has length two.

We record the finite-extension chain arguments. For an injective finite extension \(A\subset D\), localization at a prime \(\mathfrak p\) leaves a nonzero finite module. Nakayama shows that its quotient by \(\mathfrak p\) is nonzero. A maximal ideal of that quotient gives a prime lying over \(\mathfrak p\). Applying this to \(A/\mathfrak p\subset D/\mathfrak q\) proves going up from any chosen \(\mathfrak q\) over \(\mathfrak p\).

There are no two strictly nested primes of \(D\) contracting to the same \(\mathfrak p\). Localize at \(\mathfrak p\) and quotient by the smaller prime. The resulting domain is integral over the field \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\). Such a domain is a field: a nonzero integral element has an equation with nonzero constant term of least degree, which expresses its inverse as a polynomial in it. Consequently the larger prime cannot remain strictly larger. Localization cannot have identified the two primes, since both are disjoint from \(A\setminus\mathfrak p\). This is incomparability.

Contraction therefore sends every strict chain in \(D\) to a strict chain in \(A\), and going up lifts (TN4). This proves the dimension assertion. A height-one localization of a Noetherian normal domain is a normal one-dimensional local domain. The determinant and minimal-power argument in RC1 proves directly that every such ring is a DVR; that part of RC1 has no field hypothesis. This proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

2AB.4. A finite map of the smooth generic curve

TN4. Every smooth geometrically integral projective curve \(C/K\) in characteristic zero has a finite surjective map \(f:C\to\mathbf P^1_K\) inducing a finite separable extension of function fields. The curve is the normalization of \(\mathbf P^1_K\) in \(K(C)\) for this map.

Proof. A nonempty affine chart has fraction field \(L=K(C)\), of transcendence degree one by EA5 and the dimension calculation for a curve. Choose an element \(t\in L\) transcendental over \(K\). The field \(L\) is finitely generated and algebraic over \(K(t)\), hence finite: adjoining its finite list of generators gives a finite tower of finite algebraic extensions. Characteristic zero makes that extension separable.

At a closed point of the smooth curve its local ring is a DVR, by the regularity proof SF1–SF3 and the one-dimensional argument in RC1. Either \(t\) or \(t^{-1}\) lies in that ring. Such a rational function is regular on some neighborhood, by the definition of the local ring; when both lie in the ring they are reciprocal units. The two affine descriptions consequently glue to \(f\). The function-field inclusion makes \(f\) dominant. The graph is closed because \(\mathbf P^1_K\) is separated; its projection from \(C\times_K\mathbf P^1_K\) is proper. Thus \(f\) is proper and its closed image is all of \(\mathbf P^1_K\).

A fibre has finitely many points. Over a closed base point it is a proper closed subset of the integral Noetherian curve, hence zero dimensional and finite. Over the generic point it has only the curve's generic point: no closed point of \(C\), whose residue field is finite over \(K\) by EA5, can map to the transcendental generic point. Its finite-type zero-dimensional algebra over \(K(t)\) is finite by EA5 and finite generation, and its field is \(L\). These fibres are finite schemes over their residue fields and stay finite under field extension. The proper finite-fibre theorem proved in Lesson 3, §0F, now makes \(f\) finite.

On an affine base chart its inverse image has a finite coordinate algebra \(D\), a normal domain because the smooth curve is regular and normal. Its fraction field is \(L\). Every element of \(D\) is integral over the base polynomial ring. Conversely an element of \(L\) integral over that ring is integral over \(D\), by the same equation, and belongs to \(D\) by normality. Thus \(D\) is exactly the integral closure. This proves the normalization assertion on both charts. \(\square\)

2AB.5. Constructing the normal projective model

TN5. There is a normal integral flat projective \(R\)-scheme \(X\) with generic fibre \(C\). It is finite over \(\mathbf P^1_R\), has dimension two, and every height-one local ring is a DVR.

Proof. Use TN4 to fix \(L/K(t)\). In the two affine base charts put

\[ A_0=R[t],\qquad A_\infty=R[t^{-1}],\qquad B_0=\overline{A_0}^{\,L},\qquad B_\infty=\overline{A_\infty}^{\,L}. \tag{TN5} \]

TN1–TN2 make the \(B\)'s finite normal domains. Their localizations on the overlap are the same integral closure of \(R[t,t^{-1}]\) in \(L\). Glue their spectra by that identity. This gives an \(R\)-scheme and a finite morphism

\[ X\longrightarrow\mathbf P^1_R. \tag{TN6} \]

Both charts contain the same generic point with field \(L\); their overlap is nonempty, so their union is integral. The finite-over-projective construction in Lesson 3, Theorem 0F7, makes \(X\) projective over \(R\), in particular proper and finitely presented. Every affine coordinate module is torsion-free over \(R\), hence flat by NS1.

Localizing at \(\pi\) in (TN5) gives the integral closures of \(K[t]\) and \(K[t^{-1}]\), by TN2. TN4 identifies their gluing with the original curve, not just a birational curve. Thus \(X_K=C\). Finite lying over shows that (TN6) is surjective, including on the special fibre. TN3 proves dimension two and the height-one DVR assertion on each chart. This constructs the claimed model. It proves no regularity at the local rings of dimension two. \(\square\)

2AB.6. Extending a supplied finite group to a normal model

TN6. Suppose a finite group \(H\) acts on \(C\) by \(K\)-automorphisms. The finite map in TN4 may be chosen \(H\)-invariant. For that choice TN5 gives a normal projective model with an actual \(H\)-action extending the supplied action. No inversion of \(|H|\) is used.

Proof. Regard the left action on the function field as \(h(u)=(h^{-1})^*u\), so its multiplication order agrees with that in \(H\). Choose a transcendental \(u\in L\). Form the orbit polynomial, allowing repeated factors if a stabilizer is nontrivial:

\[ P(T)=\prod_{h\in H}(T-h(u))\in L^H[T]. \tag{TN7} \]

At least one coefficient is transcendental over \(K\). Otherwise its finitely many coefficients generate an algebraic extension of \(K\); the equation \(P(u)=0\) would make \(u\) algebraic over that extension, and hence over \(K\), a contradiction. Choose such a coefficient as \(t\). Then \(L/K(t)\) is finite separable as in TN4, and every \(h\) fixes \(K(t)\).

An automorphism fixing \(A_0\) preserves the elements integral over \(A_0\), since it preserves their monic equations. Thus it acts on \(B_0\); the same holds for \(B_\infty\). Define the scheme automorphism indexed by \(h\) using the inverse field automorphism as its pullback. These maps agree on the common localization and glue to automorphisms of \(X\). The group identities hold because pullback reverses the order and the field inverses reverse it back. The generic identification in TN4 is the normalization identification in that same field, so it recovers the given action on \(C\). This proves the assertion with its actual group law. It does not extend a semilinear action changing \(K\), nor does it resolve the singularities of this normal model. \(\square\)

2AB.7. A normal surface local ring can still be singular

TN7. When \(2\in R^\times\), the domain

\[ A=R[x,y]/(xy-\pi^2) \tag{TN8} \]

is normal, but its local ring at \(\mathfrak m=(\pi,x,y)\) is not regular. Its generic fibre is smooth. Consequently the normalization construction does not, by itself, furnish the initial regular model needed in RB6.

Proof. Let \(D=R[u,v]/(uv-\pi)\). The thickness-one calculation in NS3 proves that this is a regular domain; NM2 then gives normality. The involution \(\sigma(u)=-u\), \(\sigma(v)=-v\) fixes \(R\). The Laurent normal form in NS3 is a unique finite sum of a constant, positive powers of \(u\) and positive powers of \(v\), with coefficients in \(R\). Its invariant elements have no odd powers, since \(2\) is a unit. Hence

\[ \begin{aligned} D^\sigma&=R[u^2,v^2]\\ &\simeq R[x,y]/(xy-\pi^2)=A. \end{aligned} \tag{TN9} \]

The same normal form proves injectivity of the displayed map. If \(z\in\operatorname{Frac}A\) is integral over \(A\), its equation also makes it integral over \(D\). It lies in \(D\) by normality, and is fixed by \(\sigma\) because \(\operatorname{Frac}A\) is fixed. Thus \(z\in D^\sigma=A\). This proves normality of \(A\), including its localizations by TN2.

Put \(t=x+y\). Eliminating \(y\) identifies \(A\) with

\[ R[t,x]/(x^2-tx+\pi^2). \tag{TN10} \]

This is a free rank-two extension of \(R[t]\), with basis \(1,x\). TN3 bounds every local dimension by two. The prime chain

\[ (0)\subsetneq(\pi,x)\subsetneq(\pi,x,y) \tag{TN11} \]

has length two, since the middle quotient is \(k[y]\). Thus \(\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=2\). In the polynomial local ring before quotienting, \(\pi,x,y\) have three independent linear classes. Its defining equation \(xy-\pi^2\) belongs to the square of its maximal ideal, so imposes no linear relation. Hence

\[ \dim_k\mathfrak m A_{\mathfrak m}/(\mathfrak m A_{\mathfrak m})^2=3. \tag{TN12} \]

The local ring is not regular. On the generic fibre \(x\) and \(y\) are units because their product is \(\pi^2\in K^\times\); either variable eliminates the other, giving the smooth algebra \(K[x,x^{-1}]\). \(\square\)

2AB.8. What is required for the regular model

TN8. To complete the model-existence input of RB6, it suffices to construct a projective modification \(X'\to X\) of the normal model TN5, supported in its special fibre, with \(X'\) regular and integral. For an action supplied by TN6, an equivariant such modification supplies the corresponding regular-model action. Normality and the trace enclosure alone do not prove the existence of this modification.

Proof. A modification as stated is an isomorphism on the generic fibre. Its composite with the projective map \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) is projective: compose the two closed projective embeddings and use the Segre embedding, as in NS2. An affine coordinate domain on \(X'\) injects into its generic localization, so is torsion-free over \(R\); NS1 proves flatness. Thus \(X'\) has exactly the regular integral flat projective model properties needed in RB6. An equivariant map has, by definition, an action with its group law, and this gives the supplied action required for the contraction arguments. The nonregular normal local ring TN7 shows why regularity cannot be inferred merely from TN5. No termination of arbitrary singular-point blowups,normality of completed surface local rings,or resolution theorem has been assumed in this argument. Those are remaining parts of the initial regular-model construction. \(\square\)

2AB.9. Graded exercise: trace enclosures and normal models

Exercise 2AB (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. Prove TN1's trace-dual enclosure, including the explicit denominator \(\Delta\). Explain exactly where Noetherianity, normality and separability enter. Does the argument prove that the integral closure is free?
  2. In \(\mathbf F_4=\mathbf F_2[\alpha]/(\alpha^2+\alpha+1)\), compute the trace Gram matrix for \(1,\alpha\) and its dual basis. Explain how the pairing can be nondegenerate when the trace of \(1\) is zero.
  3. Put \(A=\mathbf Q[s^2,s^3]\subset\mathbf Q(s)=L\). Identify its integral closure and show precisely why the trace-enclosure argument fails when normality of the base is omitted. Do not claim that normalization is infinite in this example.
  4. Let \(F=\mathbf F_p(s)\) and \(L=F(u)\), where \(u^p=s\). Prove that \([L:F]=p\) and that the trace pairing is identically zero. State the limit this imposes on TN1.
  5. For \(A=\mathbf Z_3[t]\) and \(L=\mathbf Q_3(\theta)\), with \(t=\theta^2\), compute the integral closure \(B\), the trace-dual module \(M\), the determinant \(\Delta\), and \(M/B\). Check whether \(M\) is an algebra.
  6. Prove the localization identity TN3, specifying how a denominator multiple of an integral element is chosen. Explain why localization at \(\pi\) identifies TN5's generic fibre with the original \(C\), rather than just a birational curve.
  7. For the map \(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf Q_3}\to\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf Q_3}\) given by \(t=\theta^2\), carry out both normalizations over \(\mathbf Z_3\) and identify their overlap. What model is produced? Compute the two trace discriminants.
  8. Prove normality and nonregularity of \(\mathbf Z_3[x,y]/(xy-9)\) at \((3,x,y)\), using the involution construction. Determine its dimension, embedding dimension and generic coordinate algebra.
  9. Prove TN6's invariant-coefficient argument and verify the pullback convention for the group law. Work it out for \(u\mapsto-u\) on \(\mathbf P^1_K\). As a separate positive-characteristic calculation, compute the orbit polynomial for translations \(u\mapsto u+a\), \(a\in\mathbf F_p\), and decide whether its function-field extension is separable.
  10. State the precise modification still required after TN5 to supply RB6's initial model. Prove that such a modification would preserve the generic fibre,projectivity and flatness. Explain which finite-action case TN6 handles and which action and resolution assertions it leaves unproved.

Complete solution.

  1. Scale a primitive generator to be integral and use its powers as an \(F\)-basis \(b_i\). Over a splitting field, the trace Gram matrix is a Vandermonde matrix times its transpose, so separability gives an invertible matrix \(G\). The trace of every integral \(zb_i\) is integral: it is a sum of integral conjugates, and the finite-module determinant argument proves closure under such sums. It belongs to \(F\), hence lies in \(A\) by normality. Consequently
\[ z=\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}(zb_i)b_i^* \in\bigoplus_i A b_i^* \subset\Delta^{-1}\sum_i A b_i. \tag{TNX1} \]

The last inclusion is the adjugate formula, with \(\Delta=\det G\). The containing module is free of rank \(n\); Noetherianity makes its integral-closure submodule finite. A submodule of a free module over an arbitrary Noetherian domain need not be free, so the argument makes no freeness assertion for \(B\).

  1. Frobenius sends \(\alpha\) to \(\alpha^2=\alpha+1\). Thus \(\operatorname{Tr}(1)=0\), \(\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^2)=1\). It follows that
\[ G=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b_1^*=1+\alpha,\quad b_2^*=1. \tag{TNX2} \]

Both matrices have determinant one in \(\mathbf F_2\). Nondegeneracy means that no nonzero element pairs to zero with every element, not that every element has nonzero self-pairing. In particular \(1\) pairs nontrivially with \(\alpha\). No division by the degree two is possible or necessary.

  1. The element \(s\) is integral over \(A\), because it satisfies \(T^2-s^2=0\). The ring \(\mathbf Q[s]\) is finite over \(A\), generated by \(1,s\), and is integrally closed by the Euclidean polynomial argument. An element integral over \(A\) is integral over \(\mathbf Q[s]\) by the same equation, so it belongs to \(\mathbf Q[s]\). Thus this is exactly the integral closure. Here \(L=\operatorname{Frac}A\), the extension has degree one, and its trace is the identity. The integral element \(s\) has trace \(s\notin A\). Normality is exactly the failed inference from an integral element of \(\operatorname{Frac}A\) to an element of \(A\). The normalization is finite in this example; it demonstrates the failure of that inference, not a failure of finiteness.

  2. The order at the irreducible polynomial \(s\) of a \(p\)-th power in \(\mathbf F_p(s)\) is divisible by \(p\), while the order of \(s\) is one. Hence \(s\) is not a \(p\)-th power. The irreducible polynomial of \(u\) divides \(T^p-s\); over an algebraic closure the latter is \((T-u)^p\). A monic proper factor would be \((T-u)^d\), with \(0<d<p\). Its coefficient \(-du\) would belong to \(F\), forcing \(u\in F\), a contradiction. Thus the degree is \(p\).

Multiplication by \(1\) has trace \(p=0\). For \(1\le j<p\), multiplication by \(u^j\) on the basis \(1,u,\ldots,u^{p-1}\) shifts every exponent by \(j\) modulo \(p\), multiplying the wraparound terms by \(s\). No basis element contributes to its own diagonal entry, so its trace is zero. Linearity proves that the trace of every element of \(L\) is zero, and hence that every value \(\operatorname{Tr}(ab)\) is zero. The trace-dual enclosure is unavailable without separability; this calculation does not assert that all inseparable normalizations are infinite.

  1. We have \(A[\theta]=\mathbf Z_3[\theta]\), a polynomial ring in the transcendental element \(\theta\), and it is normal by TN2. It is integral over \(A\), with basis \(1,\theta\). Any element of \(L\) integral over \(A\) is integral over this normal ring and therefore lies in it. Thus
\[ \begin{gathered} B=A\oplus A\theta,\qquad G=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2t\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Delta=4t,\\ M=A\frac12\oplus A\frac{\theta}{2t}. \end{gathered} \tag{TNX3} \]

Since \(2\) is a unit, the constant summand is already \(A\). The quotient is generated by the class of \(\theta/(2t)\), with annihilator exactly \((t)\), so \(M/B\simeq A/(t)\). Squaring this generator inside \(L\) gives \(1/(4t)\), which does not lie in the constant summand of \(M\); uniqueness in the basis \(1,\theta\) rules out a different expression. Thus \(M\) is not an algebra. After inverting \(t\), the enclosure becomes equality \(B_t=M_t\).

  1. If \(z\) is integral after localization, write its monic equation with coefficients \(c_i\), where \(i\) is the drop in degree. One element \(s\) of the multiplicative set contains all denominator factors. Choose \(N\) large enough that \(s^{Ni}c_i\in A\) for each \(i\). Then \(s^Nz\) satisfies a monic equation over \(A\), so belongs to \(B\), and \(z\in S^{-1}B\). The reverse inclusion follows by localizing monic equations. For \(S=\{1,\pi,\pi^2,\ldots\}\), this says that the two generic chart algebras in TN5 are the normalizations of \(K[t]\) and \(K[t^{-1}]\). The finite map in TN4 identifies the actual inverse-image coordinate rings of \(C\) with those integral closures. Their overlap maps are the identities in \(K(C)\). Thus gluing recovers \(C\) itself with its map, not an unspecified curve with the same function field.

  2. On the \(t\)-chart the normalization is \(\mathbf Z_3[\theta]\), with \(t=\theta^2\). On the chart \(z=t^{-1}\), put \(\eta=\theta^{-1}\). The same polynomial-ring argument gives the normalization \(\mathbf Z_3[\eta]\), with \(z=\eta^2\). Localizing either chart on the base overlap forces its generator to be invertible, so the common ring is \(\mathbf Z_3[\theta,\theta^{-1}]\), with \(\eta=\theta^{-1}\). The glued scheme is \(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf Z_3}\); its finite map has degree two. The respective trace determinants are \(4t\) and \(4z\). These depend on the two chart power bases; there is no assertion that one is a global function on the projective base.

  3. Start with \(D=\mathbf Z_3[u,v]/(uv-3)\), a regular domain by NS3. The involution negating both variables has fixed ring \(\mathbf Z_3[u^2,v^2]\), because its unique normal form has no invariant odd powers. Mapping \(x\) to \(u^2\) and \(y\) to \(v^2\) identifies this ring with \(A=\mathbf Z_3[x,y]/(xy-9)\). If an element of \(\operatorname{Frac}A\) is integral over \(A\), it is integral over the normal ring \(D\), belongs to \(D\), and is fixed by the involution. It therefore belongs to \(A\), proving normality.

Writing \(t=x+y\) gives a finite free quadratic extension of \(\mathbf Z_3[t]\); TN3 bounds dimension by two. The chain \((0)\subset(3,x)\subset(3,x,y)\) gives local dimension two. The equation \(xy-9\) has no linear term in the maximal ideal of the ambient polynomial local ring, so the cotangent space has independent classes \(3,x,y\), of dimension three. Hence the local ring is singular. Its generic algebra is \(\mathbf Q_3[x,x^{-1}]\), which is smooth.

  1. If all coefficients of \(\prod_h(T-h(u))\) were algebraic over \(K\), their finite generated field would be algebraic over \(K\), and its monic equation for \(u\) would make \(u\) algebraic over \(K\). Therefore a coefficient is transcendental and fixed by \(H\). It supplies the invariant \(t\) used in TN6. For a left scheme action define \(h\) on functions by \((h^{-1})^*\); on the normalized charts use the inverse as the scheme pullback. Pullback reverses composition, so these two reversals give exactly the original left group law. The restrictions are actual automorphisms of the integral closures, since monic equations are preserved, and they agree on the overlap.

For \(u\mapsto-u\), the orbit polynomial is \(T^2-u^2\), and we may take \(t=u^2\). In characteristic zero this is a separable quadratic function-field extension. The two-chart model for \(C=\mathbf P^1_K\) is \(\mathbf P^1_R\), with the evident involution on its affine coordinate and its reciprocal.

Separately, over a field of characteristic \(p\), the translation orbit polynomial is

\[ \prod_{a\in\mathbf F_p}(T-(u+a)) =(T-u)^p-(T-u) =T^p-T-(u^p-u). \tag{TNX4} \]

The identity \(\prod_a(Z-a)=Z^p-Z\) follows because both monic degree-\(p\) polynomials have exactly those distinct roots. Set \(t=u^p-u\). The polynomial has derivative \(-1\), so the extension is separable. Its degree is \(p\): \(u\) has at least the \(p\) distinct images \(u+a\) under automorphisms fixing \(t\), and at most degree \(p\) from this equation. This illustrates an invariant finite separable map without dividing by a group order that is zero in the field. It does not enlarge the standing characteristic-zero assertion TN4 without checking its separating-parameter step.

  1. One must construct a projective modification \(X'\to X\), an isomorphism on the generic fibre, with \(X'\) regular and integral. Projective composition uses the Segre embedding. The generic fibre remains exactly \(C\). The affine coordinate domains are torsion-free over \(R\), and the directed-union proof of NS1 gives flatness. These facts supply the regular integral flat projective model required by RB6 if such a modification has actually been constructed. TN5 alone supplies its normal starting model, and TN7 shows why that is insufficient.

TN6 extends finite groups of \(K\)-automorphisms to an actual normal model. It proves neither equivariant resolution of that model nor extension of a semilinear action moving the base field. Normality of all completed surface local rings and termination of a sequence of normalized blowups also require their own proofs if that resolution route is used. After initial regular-model existence, the remaining arbitrary-abelian-variety work still includes the whole semiabelian lift,the genuine analytic covering and its finite point-lifting and kernel properties,and the geometric pairing identification. None follows from the trace enclosure.

2AC. Principalization and domination on a regular surface

Surface resolution needs control of modifications, not just their individual blowup charts. We prove that ideals on a regular surface can be made invertible by a terminating sequence of point blowups. We then dominate every proper birational modification of a regular local surface, including one not initially assumed projective. This proves the vanishing of its first structure-sheaf cohomology. These results concern a regular base. Applying them to the singular normal model TN5 without a further argument would be circular.

Throughout, \((A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)\) is a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension two, and \(F=\operatorname{Frac}A\). No coefficient field, perfectness, completeness or characteristic assumption is made. Write \(\lambda_A\) for module length. A modification is a proper birational morphism of integral schemes. The free comparisons are the Stacks project's point-blowup calculations, domination results, and regular-base vanishing, Lemma 54.8.7. All assertions used here are proved below from the earlier local algebra and cohomology proofs.

2AC.1. The exceptional line over its actual residue field

BP1. The blowup \(b:X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) at \(\mathfrak m=(x,y)\) is regular and integral. Its exceptional divisor \(E\) is \(\mathbf P^1_\kappa\), with conormal line \(\mathcal O_E(-E)=\mathcal O(1)\). It is projective and is an isomorphism outside the closed point.

Proof. The affine graph construction of NS2 applies to the generators \(x,y\) over any Noetherian affine base. It gives the two subrings of \(F\)

\[ X_x=\operatorname{Spec}A[y/x],\qquad X_y=\operatorname{Spec}A[x/y]. \tag{BP1} \]

They glue on their common fraction chart and form the closed graph in \(\mathbf P^1_A\). The universal property is exactly NS2's cancellation of a locally principal nonzerodivisor; no DVR assumption occurs in that ring argument.

NM1–NM2 give \(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m}A=\kappa[\bar x,\bar y]\), a domain, and the regular sequence \(x,y\). On the first chart its presentation is \(A[t]/(xt-y)\). To check that no extra component is hidden in this equation, reduce an identity \(xP=(xt-y)Q\) modulo \(x\). The nonzerodivisor \(y\) in \(A/(x)\) forces \(Q\) to be divisible by \(x\); cancel \(x\). Thus \(x\) stays a nonzerodivisor, and localization embeds the presentation in \(F\). Modulo \(x\) this chart is \(\kappa[t]\). The other chart is the same calculation with \(x,y\) reversed.

At a closed point of this affine exceptional line, the maximal ideal is generated by \(x\) and a lift of the irreducible residue polynomial in \(\kappa[t]\). There is a strict prime chain of length two, passing through \((x)\); EC1 bounds dimension by the two displayed generators. The local ring is regular of dimension two. At the generic point of the exceptional line the same argument gives a one-dimensional regular local ring. Outside the exceptional divisor the blowup is an open part of the regular base. This proves regularity at every point, even when a closed exceptional point has inseparable residue field over \(\kappa\).

The homogeneous initial forms identify the fibre and its tautological line as

\[ E=\operatorname{Proj}\kappa[\bar x,\bar y] =\mathbf P^1_\kappa,\qquad \mathfrak m\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_X(-E),\qquad \mathcal O_E(-E)=\mathcal O(1). \tag{BP2} \]

Equivalently the two local equations for \(E\) are \(x,y\), whose transition is the ratio of the two projective coordinates. These calculations also verify the scheme structure of the fibre and the conormal sign. \(\square\)

2AC.2. Cohomology of every exceptional twist

BP2. For this blowup, with \(\mathfrak m^0=A\),

\[ \begin{gathered} \Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X(-nE))=\mathfrak m^n, \quad H^1(X,\mathcal O_X(-nE))=0\quad(n\ge0),\\ \Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X(dE))=A, \quad\lambda_A H^1(X,\mathcal O_X(dE))=\frac{d(d-1)}2 \quad(d\ge0). \end{gathered} \tag{BP3} \]

Every quasi-coherent sheaf on \(X\) has zero cohomology in degrees at least two. Every coherent globally generated sheaf \(\mathcal G\) on \(X\) has \(H^1(X,\mathcal G)=0\).

Proof. The two affine charts in BP1 and their affine intersection give a Čech complex with only degrees zero and one, by the affine comparison proved in Lesson 3, SC11–SC12. This proves the cohomological dimension assertion.

First \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)=A\). Proper coherent cohomology, Lesson 3, Theorem 0.C.10, makes this a finite \(A\)-algebra. Integrality and birationality embed it in \(F\); the determinant argument makes all its elements integral over \(A\). NM2's normality then gives equality. More generally, a section of \(\mathcal O_X(dE)\), for \(d\ge0\), is a rational function regular off the closed point of the base. It belongs to every height-one localization of \(A\), so belongs to \(A\) by the height-one intersection proof in NM2. Every element of \(A\) is such a section. This gives the second degree-zero assertion.

The first degree-zero assertion follows from the exceptional order. If \(f\in A\setminus\{0\}\) has \(\mathfrak m\)-adic order \(r\), its first homogeneous form in \(\kappa[\bar x,\bar y]\) is nonzero. On the generic point of \(E\) it gives a nonzero rational homogeneous form, so the order of the pullback along \(E\) is exactly \(r\). Thus vanishing along \(nE\) is equivalent to membership in \(\mathfrak m^n\). Krull separation, already proved in DFR, ensures that a nonzero \(f\) has finite order.

The line \(\mathcal O_X(-E)\) is the restriction of \(\mathcal O(1)\) in the closed projective graph. High-twist vanishing PF8 gives \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X(-nE))=0\) for sufficiently large \(n\). Use the exact sequences

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(-(j+1)E) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(-jE) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_E(j)\longrightarrow0. \tag{BP4} \]

The actual projective-line Čech calculation PF5 gives \(H^1(E,\mathcal O_E(j))=0\) for \(j\ge-1\). Descending induction proves vanishing through \(\mathcal O_X(E)\). For \(d\ge2\), the same sequence with quotient \(\mathcal O_E(-d)\), together with the already identified identical spaces of global sections \(A\), gives a short exact sequence from \(H^1(\mathcal O_X((d-1)E))\) to \(H^1(\mathcal O_X(dE))\) with quotient \(H^1(\mathcal O_E(-d))\). Its length is \(d-1\). Summing from \(d=2\) gives \(d(d-1)/2\). These are finite-length modules, since the successive quotients are finite-dimensional \(\kappa\)-spaces.

Finally a finite generating list for a coherent globally generated \(\mathcal G\) gives a surjection from a finite sum of copies of \(\mathcal O_X\). Its kernel is coherent. The long exact sequence, \(H^1(\mathcal O_X)=0\) and the two-chart \(H^2\)-vanishing imply \(H^1(\mathcal G)=0\). In particular this applies to \(I\mathcal O_X\) for every ideal \(I\subset A\); no flatness of that ideal sheaf is required. \(\square\)

2AC.3. A decreasing weighted colength

BP3. Let \(I\subsetneq A\) be \(\mathfrak m\)-primary, and let \(r\ge1\) be its order, namely the largest integer for which \(I\subset\mathfrak m^r\). Its weak transform is the coherent ideal

\[ I^{\mathrm w}=I\mathcal O_X(rE)\subset\mathcal O_X. \tag{BP5} \]

Its quotient is supported at finitely many closed points \(q\in E\), and

\[ \sum_q[\kappa(q):\kappa]\, \lambda_{\mathcal O_{X,q}}(\mathcal O_{X,q}/I^{\mathrm w}_q) \le \lambda_A(A/I)-\frac{r(r+1)}2. \tag{BP6} \]

For a two-generated \(\mathfrak m\)-primary ideal \(I=(a,b)\), the left side is exactly \(\lambda_A(A/I)-r^2\).

Proof. Every element of \(I\) vanishes along \(rE\), so (BP5) is an ideal. An element of order exactly \(r\) has a nonzero initial homogeneous form, and therefore its weak transform does not vanish at the generic point of \(E\). Outside \(E\), the original primary ideal is the unit ideal. Hence the support of the quotient is a proper closed subset of the projective line, a finite set of closed points.

For any coherent sheaf supported at finitely many closed points, its stalk modules have finite length and its global sections are their direct sum, with no higher cohomology. One can check this on disjoint neighborhoods in its zero-dimensional support scheme: each local Artinian ring is affine, and the sheaf is extended by zero. A simple module at \(q\) is \(\kappa(q)\). Thus its length as an \(A\)-module is its local length times \([\kappa(q):\kappa]\). Tensoring such a sheaf with an invertible line changes none of these lengths, because a line is free on every Artinian local support.

Put \(\mathcal S=\mathcal O_X(-rE)/I\mathcal O_X\). This is such a finite-support sheaf, and twisting it by \(rE\) gives \(\mathcal O_X/I^{\mathrm w}\). There is an exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal S \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X/I\mathcal O_X \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X/\mathcal O_X(-rE) \longrightarrow0. \tag{BP7} \]

It stays exact on global sections. BP2 also gives a surjection \(A/I\twoheadrightarrow\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X/I\mathcal O_X)\), since \(I\mathcal O_X\) is globally generated. The last term of (BP7) has global sections \(A/\mathfrak m^r\), by BP2. Its length is \(r(r+1)/2\): NM1 gives graded pieces of dimensions \(1,2,\ldots,r\). Taking lengths proves (BP6), including all residue-degree factors.

For the exact two-generator formula, divide the common exceptional factor of order \(r\). The resulting two sections of \(\mathcal O_X(-rE)\) have no common curve: none exists off \(E\), because \((a,b)\) is primary, and at least one section is nonzero at the generic point of \(E\). Their zero scheme \(Z\) is therefore zero dimensional. In each regular local surface ring the two nonunit equations form a regular sequence. Explicitly, factoriality shows that they share no prime factor; if the first divides the second times an element, it already divides that element. Their Koszul sequence is consequently exact:

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(2rE) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X(rE)^{\oplus2} \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X \longrightarrow\mathcal O_Z\longrightarrow0. \tag{BP8} \]

Here \(Z\) is exactly the weak-transform quotient for this pair. To compute its length, use the two-chart Čech complexes for the first three sheaves. The row of degree-zero sheaf cohomology is the ordinary Koszul complex \(A\to A^2\to A\) on \(a,b\), with only the final cohomology \(A/(a,b)\). The other row consists of finite-length first cohomology modules from BP2. Filter this bounded double complex in the two orders. Additivity of length on its cycle and boundary exact sequences gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \lambda_A\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z) &=\lambda_A(A/(a,b)) -\frac{(2r)(2r-1)}2 +2\frac{r(r-1)}2\\ &=\lambda_A(A/(a,b))-r^2. \end{aligned} \tag{BP9} \]

Only finite-length cohomology contributes to this identity; no length is assigned to the free \(A\)-terms of the Koszul row. This proves the exact formula. \(\square\)

2AC.4. An intrinsic terminating principalization

BP4. Every nonzero ideal \(I\subset A\) becomes an invertible ideal after finitely many blowups at closed points over \(\mathfrak m\). At each stage one may blow up the entire reduced finite locus where the current pullback ideal is not invertible. All intermediate schemes are regular, integral and projective over \(A\).

Proof. Factor the greatest common divisor of a finite generating tuple in the UFD \(A\): write \(I=dJ\), where \(J\) is either the unit ideal or an \(\mathfrak m\)-primary ideal. Indeed any nonzero nonunit prime containing \(J\) must have height two, since a common height-one prime factor has been removed, and the only such prime is \(\mathfrak m\). The factor \(d\) already generates an invertible ideal, so start with \(J\). If it is the unit ideal there is nothing to do.

After any stage, write the pullback of the original ideal as an invertible ideal times a residual coherent ideal \(J_i\) with no divisorial factor. Locally this just removes the minimum exponent of every common prime factor. Factoriality of all regular local rings, NM2, makes these local divisorial factors a Cartier divisor. On an overlap their equations have the same order at every height-one prime; the height-one intersection statement applied to their quotient and its inverse makes that quotient a unit. Thus the invertible ideals and the residual ideals agree on overlaps. There are only finitely many components, by finite generation and a finite affine cover. The quotient by \(J_i\) has zero-dimensional closed support, a finite set of closed points. All these points lie over the original closed point; their residue fields are finite over \(\kappa\), by EA5 on the finite-type closed fibre.

Measure this residual ideal by

\[ N_i=\sum_{q\in\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal O/J_i)} [\kappa(q):\kappa]\, \lambda_{\mathcal O_{X_i,q}}(\mathcal O_{X_i,q}/(J_i)_q). \tag{BP10} \]

Initially \(N_0=\lambda_A(A/J)\). At a selected point \(q\), its local ring is regular of dimension two by BP1. Apply BP3 there. Dividing the new exceptional factor of order \(r_q\) gives the new residual ideal. It has no new divisorial factor: it is generically the unit ideal on the new exceptional line, and elsewhere the old ideal had no such factor. Residue degrees multiply in the finite field tower. Thus blowing up all current support points gives

\[ N_{i+1}\le N_i- \sum_q[\kappa(q):\kappa]\frac{r_q(r_q+1)}2 <N_i\qquad(N_i>0). \tag{BP11} \]

Outside these points the residual ideal is already the unit ideal and is unchanged. Every term being subtracted is a positive integer. The process therefore stops, after at most \(N_0\) individual point blowups, with unit residual ideal. The original pullback is then invertible.

Blowing up a finite reduced union of disjoint points is locally the point blowup and the identity off those points. It is also the composition of the individual point blowups in any order: those local descriptions agree on a cover, or equivalently give the same blowup universal property. BP1 proves regularity at every stage. The graph and twisted-generator construction of NS2, with base \(A\), proves projectivity; successive compositions are projective by the Segre embedding. The charts remain subrings of the same function field, so the schemes are integral. The chosen centre is exactly the noninvertibility locus, since after divisorial factors are removed a proper ideal supported at a regular two-dimensional closed point cannot be invertible: a nonunit principal ideal has a height-one prime factor. This also proves that the algorithm is intrinsic. \(\square\)

2AC.5. Finite actions and projective modifications

BP5. If a finite group acts on the local ring \(A\) and preserves \(I\), the algorithm BP4 is equivariant, including when the action on \(\kappa\) is nontrivial or its order is not invertible. Every projective modification \(Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is dominated by a sequence of these regular point blowups.

Proof. Use the inverse ring automorphism as the pullback of the corresponding scheme action, as in TN6. The divisorial exponents, noninvertibility locus and local orders are preserved under isomorphism of the pair consisting of a scheme and its ideal. Thus the entire reduced centre at each stage is stable. NS2's universal property lifts every automorphism uniquely to the blowup. The identity and composition relations lift by that same uniqueness, and the pulled-back ideal is again stable. The integer proof of termination in BP4 applies to this sequence. Nothing averages over the group or divides its order. No assertion of equivariance for a modification lacking supplied actions is inferred from this statement.

Now take a closed projective embedding \(Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^s_A\). Its generic fibre is a single \(F\)-point. Choose homogeneous coordinates for that point and clear denominators, obtaining \(a_0,\ldots,a_s\in A\), not all zero. The integral scheme \(Y\) is exactly the scheme-theoretic closure of this generic point in \(\mathbf P^s_A\): a local function on an integral scheme which vanishes at its generic point is zero. The affine graph description NS2 therefore identifies

\[ Y=\operatorname{Bl}_{(a_0,\ldots,a_s)}\operatorname{Spec}A. \tag{BP12} \]

A common nonzero factor can be cancelled from the tuple without changing its graph or blowup; on the Rees algebra this is the graded isomorphism multiplying degree \(n\) by the factor's \(n\)-th power. BP4 makes this ideal invertible on a regular point-blowup sequence \(W\). The actual universal property then gives a map \(W\to Y\) over \(A\), which is the required domination. In particular the centre of the sequence lies over \(\mathfrak m\), not over a point where that ideal was already invertible. \(\square\)

2AC.6. Projectivizing an arbitrary proper modification

BP6. Every modification \(Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A\), without an assumed projective embedding, is dominated by an integral projective modification. It is consequently dominated by a regular point-blowup sequence as in BP5.

Proof. Cover \(Y\) by finitely many nonempty affine opens \(U_i\). Their coordinate algebras are finite type over \(A\); choose finite generating lists and closed immersions \(U_i\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^{n_i}_A\subset\mathbf P^{n_i}_A\). The intersection \(V=\bigcap_iU_i\) is a dense open, because \(Y\) is integral. Each embedding gives a rational map from \(Y\) to its projective space. Take the scheme-theoretic closure \(Z\) of their joint graph on \(V\) in

\[ Y\times_A P,\qquad P=\prod_i\mathbf P^{n_i}_A. \tag{BP13} \]

The graph is integral, so its closure is integral; on an affine chart its defining ideal is the kernel of restriction into the function field. The projection \(Z\to Y\) is proper and birational, and is an isomorphism over \(V\). The projection \(Z\to P\) is proper because \(Y\) is proper over \(A\).

This latter map has finite geometric fibres. On the inverse image of \(U_i\), its \(i\)-th projective coordinate equals the specified embedding of \(U_i\). Indeed the graph of that everywhere defined map is closed there and contains the dense original graph. Hence \(Z|_{U_i}\to P\) is a locally closed immersion: the \(i\)-th coordinate recovers the point and full scheme structure on \(U_i\), and the remaining graph equations give a closed subscheme of its product with the other factors. In particular any geometric fibre in this open has at most one point. The finitely many such opens cover \(Z\), so every geometric fibre is finite. The proper finite-fibre theorem proved in Lesson 3, §0F, makes \(Z\to P\) finite. The explicit finite-over-projective construction, Theorem 0F7, then makes \(Z\) projective over \(A\). Its composite to \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) is birational, and BP5 supplies a regular point-blowup sequence dominating it and hence \(Y\).

For completeness this also shows that every such \(Y\) is an isomorphism off \(\mathfrak m\). The projective \(Z\) is the blowup of an ideal of \(A\). Cancel its gcd; the residual ideal is primary or a unit, so \(Z\) is an isomorphism on the punctured spectrum \(U\). The proper map \(Z\to Y\) is surjective, since its closed image contains the generic point of the integral \(Y\). Its restriction there is a surjective section \(U\to Y_U\) of \(Y_U\to U\). A section of a separated morphism is a closed immersion, by the diagonal. A surjective closed immersion into a reduced scheme has zero defining ideal, since that ideal is contained in its nilradical. Thus it is an isomorphism. \(\square\)

2AC.7. The regular-base cohomological vanishing

BP7. If \(Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is a normal modification, then

\[ \Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=A, \qquad H^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=0. \tag{BP14} \]

In particular the regular base has the structure-sheaf vanishing used in reduction to rational singularities.

Proof. First, for any proper birational map \(g:T\to S\) of integral Noetherian schemes with \(S\) normal, one has \(g_*\mathcal O_T=\mathcal O_S\).
