Over an affine \(\operatorname{Spec}B\subset S\), proper coherent cohomology makes \(\Gamma(g^{-1}\operatorname{Spec}B,\mathcal O_T)\) a finite \(B\)-module inside \(\operatorname{Frac}B\). It is a ring, so the determinant argument makes its elements integral over \(B\); normality forces equality with \(B\). This proves the sheaf identity, and gives the degree-zero assertion of (BP14).

For a point blowup on a regular surface, BP2 gives all positive direct images of the structure sheaf equal to zero. At the centre this is checked after localization, using the two affine charts and their Čech complex; cohomology commutes with that localization, by SC14. Off the centre the map is an isomorphism. The degree-zero direct image is the original structure sheaf by the preceding paragraph. Apply the actual vanishing-higher-image collapse SC15 successively to a point-blowup sequence \(W\to\operatorname{Spec}A\). Since the base is affine, \(H^j(W,\mathcal O_W)=0\) for every \(j>0\).

BP6 gives such a regular \(W\) with a map \(g:W\to Y\). This map is proper: its graph is closed in \(W\times_A Y\), and the projection to \(Y\) is proper. It is birational and \(Y\) is normal, so \(g_*\mathcal O_W=\mathcal O_Y\). The low-degree cohomology map is injective. Here is an explicit argument which does not assume the higher direct images vanish. Push a flasque resolution of \(\mathcal O_W\) to \(Y\), calling the resulting complex \(C^\bullet\). Its terms remain flasque, and its degree-zero cohomology sheaf is \(\mathcal O_Y\). Put \(B^1=\operatorname{im}(C^0\to C^1)\) and \(Z^1=\ker(C^1\to C^2)\). The exact sequence \(0\to\mathcal O_Y\to C^0\to B^1\to0\) identifies \(H^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) with \(\Gamma(B^1)/\operatorname{im}\Gamma(C^0)\). The inclusion \(B^1\subset Z^1\) embeds this quotient into \(\Gamma(Z^1)/\operatorname{im}\Gamma(C^0)=H^1(W,\mathcal O_W)\). The latter is zero, proving (BP14). This proves the claimed vanishing without assuming an unproved resolution of the normal target. \(\square\)

2AC.8. Resolving rational maps, and the remaining surface theorem

BP8. A rational \(A\)-map from \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) to a proper \(A\)-scheme extends to a morphism after finitely many regular point blowups. These results do not yet resolve a singular normal local surface or prove the initial regular-model input of RB6.

Proof. Take the closure of the graph of the given rational map in its proper target. Its generic fibre is the specified \(F\)-rational point, a closed point of that fibre, so the closure is an integral proper birational modification of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). BP6 dominates it by regular point blowups. The map to the target then extends the original rational map. It agrees on the given domain because the target is separated and that domain is reduced and integral. Every centre lies above \(\mathfrak m\). If the given domain contains that point, it is the entire local spectrum and no blowup is needed; otherwise all the centres avoid the given domain.

The regularity of the base was used in its factoriality, its polynomial associated graded ring, the exceptional-line calculation and the decreasing colength. TN5 supplies a normal surface, whose closed local rings can be singular by TN7. None of these regular-base arguments permits substituting such a local ring for \(A\). A proof of resolution for those normal surface singularities,including the needed finite-cover boundedness and termination arguments or another complete route,remains required. Equivariant ideal principalization on a regular base is proved;equivariant resolution of the singular normal model is not inferred from it. The whole semiabelian lift,the genuine analytic covering and the geometric pairing identification remain separate abelian-variety constructions. \(\square\)

2AC.9. Graded exercise: lengths, infinitely near points and domination

Exercise 2AC (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).

  1. Construct the blowup charts of a regular two-dimensional local ring at its maximal ideal. Prove regularity at a closed exceptional point with arbitrary finite residue extension. Identify the conormal line, including its sign.
  2. Calculate \(\Gamma(\mathcal O_X(-nE))\), \(H^1(\mathcal O_X(-nE))\) for \(n\ge0\), and the length of \(H^1(\mathcal O_X(dE))\) for \(d\ge0\). Give the lengths at \(d=0,1,2,3,4,5\). Explain why \(I\mathcal O_X\) has vanishing first cohomology without assuming that it is flat.
  3. Prove the weighted inequality BP6 for an arbitrary primary ideal. Identify the source of the term \(r(r+1)/2\), and distinguish the original ideal from the kernel of \(A\to\Gamma(\mathcal O_X/I\mathcal O_X)\).
  4. For \(I=(x^a,y^b)\subset k[[x,y]]\), calculate the original colength and the weak transforms on both charts. Prove that their total colength drops by \(\min(a,b)^2\). Derive the same length identity from the Koszul sequence BP8. Which parts also apply to \((\pi^a,z^b)\subset\mathbf Z_p[[z]]\)?
  5. Principalize \(I=(x^4,x^2y^2,y^5)\subset k[[x,y]]\). Give every nonunit residual ideal in suitable successive local coordinates, its colength and its order. Check the general bound at every step and compare with the two-generated ideal \((x^4,y^5)\).
  6. In \(A=\mathbf F_3[[x,y]]\), use \(I=(x^2+y^2,x^3)\). Compute its colength and first weak transform. Identify the degree-two closed point on the exceptional line, its local colength and its contribution to BP6. Complete principalization. Explain what changes in characteristics five and two.
  7. Give the terminating algorithm for arbitrary nonzero \(I\subset A\), including its divisorial factor. Prove finite-group equivariance without choosing one point from a nontrivial orbit or dividing by the group order. Apply it to \((x^a,y^a)\) with the action interchanging \(x\) and \(y\), including in characteristic two.
  8. Show directly that every integral projective modification of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) is a blowup of an ideal, using the homogeneous coordinates of its generic point. Explain why common factors may be cancelled, and why principalizing the resulting ideal gives an actual factorization through the modification.
  9. For an arbitrary proper modification, prove the projectivization construction BP6. Explain why the graph closure has finite geometric fibres over the product of projective spaces, and why finiteness over that product gives projectivity. Deduce domination and the isomorphism on the punctured spectrum.
  10. Prove \(H^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=0\) for every normal modification of the regular base. In particular justify the low-degree injection without assuming all higher direct images vanish. State precisely why this does not resolve the singular normal model TN5.

Complete solution.

  1. With \(\mathfrak m=(x,y)\), the charts are \(A[t]/(xt-y)\) and \(A[s]/(ys-x)\). Reduction modulo the exceptional equation gives \(\kappa[t]\) and \(\kappa[s]\), with \(s=t^{-1}\) on the overlap. The regular sequence \(x,y\) shows, by reducing a possible \(x\)-torsion relation modulo \(x\) and cancelling, that the first chart embeds in \(F\) as \(A[y/x]\); the second is identical with the variables exchanged. Thus no unsaturated extra component is retained.

A closed point in the first exceptional chart is given by an irreducible polynomial \(h(t)\in\kappa[t]\). Its local maximal ideal has the two generators \(x,\widetilde h(t)\), and there is a strict chain through the prime \((x)\), of length two. EC1 and that chain give dimension two and embedding dimension two. No separability of \(h\) was used. At the generic exceptional point the maximal ideal is generated by \(x\), giving dimension one. Off the exceptional line the base is unchanged. The exceptional scheme is \(\mathbf P^1_\kappa\); its local equations satisfy \(y=tx\). Hence its ideal restricts as \(\mathcal O(1)\), so the conormal line is \(\mathcal O_E(-E)=\mathcal O(1)\) and the normal line is \(\mathcal O(-1)\).

  1. The two-chart Čech complex has no terms in degrees above one. High-twist vanishing for \(\mathcal O_X(-E)\), followed by the successive projective-line quotients in BP4, gives \(H^1(\mathcal O_X(-nE))=0\) for \(n\ge0\), and also \(H^1(\mathcal O_X(E))=0\). The exceptional order of a base function equals its \(\mathfrak m\)-adic order, so \(\Gamma(\mathcal O_X(-nE))=\mathfrak m^n\). Normality and height-one intersection give \(\Gamma(\mathcal O_X(dE))=A\) for \(d\ge0\).

The quotient from \(d-1\) to \(d\) is \(\mathcal O_E(-d)\). For \(d\ge2\) its first cohomology has dimension \(d-1\), and its global sections are zero. Thus

\[ \begin{gathered} \lambda_A H^1(\mathcal O_X(dE))=\sum_{j=2}^d(j-1) =\frac{d(d-1)}2,\\ d=0,1,2,3,4,5:\qquad 0,0,1,3,6,10. \end{gathered} \tag{BPX1} \]

A finite generating tuple of \(I\) gives a surjection \(\mathcal O_X^{\oplus m}\to I\mathcal O_X\). The kernel has zero \(H^2\), while \(H^1(\mathcal O_X)=0\). The long exact sequence therefore gives the required \(H^1\)-vanishing. There is no use of flatness of \(I\mathcal O_X\).

  1. Put \(r=\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m}I\) and \(\mathcal S=\mathcal O_X(-rE)/I\mathcal O_X\). An element with nonzero degree-\(r\) initial form shows that \(\mathcal S\) has finite support on \(E\). Twisting it by \(rE\) gives the weak quotient and changes none of its local lengths. Global generation gives the surjection \(A/I\to\Gamma(\mathcal O_X/I\mathcal O_X)\); its kernel can be larger than zero, so equality of these two modules must not be assumed. Sequence BP7 and vanishing of the higher cohomology of \(\mathcal S\) give
\[ \begin{aligned} \lambda_A(A/I) &\ge\lambda_A\Gamma(\mathcal S) +\lambda_A(A/\mathfrak m^r),\\ \lambda_A\Gamma(\mathcal S) &=\sum_q[\kappa(q):\kappa]\, \lambda_{\mathcal O_{X,q}}(\mathcal O_{X,q}/I^{\mathrm w}_q). \end{aligned} \tag{BPX2} \]

The graded pieces of \(A/\mathfrak m^r\) have dimensions \(1,2,\ldots,r\), so its length is \(r(r+1)/2\). This proves BP6. The degree factor counts the \(\kappa\)-dimension of a local simple module \(\kappa(q)\); omitting it would change the actual length.

  1. The monomials \(x^iy^j\), with \(0\le i<a\) and \(0\le j<b\), give a basis of the quotient, so its length is \(ab\). Assume \(a\le b\), so \(r=a\). On the \(x\)-chart, division by \(x^a\) gives \((1,x^{b-a}t^b)\), the unit ideal. On the \(y\)-chart, division by \(y^a\) gives \((s^a,y^{b-a})\). If \(a=b\), this is also the unit ideal. Otherwise it is supported at the origin and has colength \(a(b-a)\). Thus the drop is \(ab-a(b-a)=a^2=r^2\). The case \(b<a\) exchanges the variables.

For the cohomological derivation, the two divided generators are sections of \(\mathcal O_X(-rE)\), with the exact Koszul complex BP8. Its degree-zero cohomology row is the base Koszul complex with final quotient of length \(ab\). The first-cohomology row contributes \(-c(2r)+2c(r)\), where \(c(d)=d(d-1)/2\), giving \(ab-r^2\). This also explains why the exact drop for a pair is generally larger than the triangular lower bound for an arbitrary ideal.

For \((\pi^a,z^b)\subset\mathbf Z_p[[z]]\), the quotient is \((\mathbf Z_p/\pi^a)[[z]]/(z^b)\), of length \(ab\). The two regular parameters have the same blowup exponent substitutions, and the cohomology calculation applies to this regular local ring as well. It does not require an embedded residue coefficient field in the mixed-characteristic ring.

  1. For \(I=(x^4,x^2y^2,y^5)\), the allowed powers of \(y\) are five each in columns \(x^0,x^1\), and two each in columns \(x^2,x^3\). Thus the colength is \(14\), and the order is four. On the \(x\)-chart the weak ideal is the unit ideal. On the \(y\)-chart, with \(x=ys\), it is \((s^4,s^2,y)=(s^2,y)\), of colength two and order one. Blowing up its origin gives the only nonunit residual ideal \((s,t)\) on the chart \(y=st\); its colength and order are one. Blowing up that maximal ideal gives unit residual ideal. Hence
\[ \begin{gathered} 14\longrightarrow2\longrightarrow1\longrightarrow0,\\ \text{orders }4,1,1;\qquad \text{drops }12,1,1\ \ge\ 10,1,1. \end{gathered} \tag{BPX3} \]

For the pair \((x^4,y^5)\), the first residual ideal is \((s^4,y)\), of colength four. Its initial colength is twenty and its first drop is sixteen. The extra middle generator in the three-generated ideal changes both colengths; it is not legitimate to apply the exact pair formula directly to the three-generated ideal.

  1. In the original quotient, \(x^3=0\) and \(y^2=-x^2\). It is free with basis \(1,y\) over \(\mathbf F_3[x]/(x^3)\), so its length is six. The order of the ideal is two. On the \(x\)-chart, with \(y=xt\), the weak ideal is \((1+t^2,x)\). Its support on the exceptional line is the single closed point defined by the irreducible polynomial \(t^2+1\) over \(\mathbf F_3\). Its residue field is \(\mathbf F_9\), its local colength is one, and its contribution to the length over the original residue field is two. The other chart gives the same closed point on the overlap, so it must not be counted a second time. The weak quotient is exactly \(\mathbf F_3[t]/(t^2+1)\). The exact pair formula gives the same value \(6-2^2=2\).

At that degree-two point the ideal \((x,t^2+1)\) is the maximal ideal of a regular local surface ring. One further point blowup makes it invertible. Thus two point blowups suffice; the second is a single degree-two closed point, not two rational closed points over \(\mathbf F_3\). Its weighted drop is two, while its local colength drop is one.

Over \(\mathbf F_5\), the polynomial has two distinct rational roots, so the first weak quotient has two length-one rational points; blowing up their reduced union completes principalization. In characteristic two it is \((t+1)^2\), so the first weak ideal at the one rational point is \((x,(t+1)^2)\), of local colength two. Subsequent local lengths are two,one,zero,as in the monomial pair calculation. The total first weak length is two in all three cases, with different residue and nilpotent structures.

  1. Remove the gcd \(d\) from a generating tuple and start with its residual primary ideal \(J\). At each stage remove the full Cartier divisorial factor, and blow up the entire reduced finite support of the residual quotient. Divide its exceptional orders and repeat. The weighted integer BP10 decreases by at least the sum in BP11; initially it is \(\lambda_A(A/J)\), so this proves termination and the bound on the total number of individual point centres. Multiplying back the accumulated invertible factors gives principalization of \(I\), not merely of its residual ideal.

Every isomorphism preserving the ideal preserves this entire construction. A supplied finite group therefore preserves the full centre, and its automorphisms lift uniquely to each blowup. Their composition identities follow by uniqueness. No point of an orbit is chosen separately and no average is taken. For \((x^a,y^a)\) the first order is \(a\), and both weak chart ideals are the unit ideal. One point blowup principalizes it. The coordinate interchange lifts and exchanges the two charts. This remains valid in characteristic two, where its order two is not invertible; the proof uses the intrinsic centre and universal property.

  1. Embed the modification in \(\mathbf P^s_A\) and write its generic point as \([a_0:\cdots:a_s]\), with \(a_i\in F\). Clearing a common denominator places them in \(A\). The integral closed subscheme is the closure of this generic point, so it is the graph closure of these ratios. Its affine chart indexed by nonzero \(a_j\) has the actual subring \(A[a_i/a_j]\subset F\). These are precisely the blowup charts of the ideal \((a_0,\ldots,a_s)\), with the same overlap localizations. This proves the isomorphism, not just a map on generic points.

Multiplying or cancelling a common nonzero factor leaves all ratios unchanged; equivalently it gives an isomorphism of the two graded Rees algebras by the appropriate factor in each degree. Once the pullback ideal on the regular point-blowup sequence is invertible, NS2's cancellation proof gives the unique map to this actual blowup. Its composite to the base is the original sequence. An asserted birational equivalence without this extension would not prove domination.

  1. Choose finitely many affine opens \(U_i\) of the proper integral \(Y\), each with a closed affine-space embedding over \(A\). Close the joint rational graph in \(Y\times_A\prod_i\mathbf P^{n_i}_A\). The graph closure \(Z\) is integral and proper birational over \(Y\). Its projection to the product is proper because \(Y\) is proper. Over \(U_i\), the \(i\)-th projective coordinate is the given closed embedding into its affine chart, so that coordinate recovers the entire point of \(U_i\). The remaining graph equations give a locally closed immersion of \(Z|_{U_i}\) into the product. Thus a geometric fibre has at most one point in each of finitely many covering opens. The fibre is finite, and the actual proper finite-fibre theorem makes the projection finite. Finite over projective is projective by the previously proved construction 0F7. BP5 now dominates \(Z\), and hence \(Y\), by regular point blowups.

After cancelling the gcd of the projective blowup ideal for \(Z\), its residual ideal is primary. Hence \(Z_U=U\) on the punctured spectrum. The proper birational map \(Z\to Y\) is surjective; its restriction gives a surjective section \(U\to Y_U\). A separated section is a closed immersion. Its defining ideal lies in every prime of the reduced scheme \(Y_U\), hence is zero. Thus \(Y_U=U\). This part of the argument uses reducedness and separation, not an assumption that a proper map with one-point fibres is an isomorphism.

  1. A proper birational map onto a normal integral scheme pushes its structure sheaf to that of the target: on an affine normal chart, its global functions form a finite algebra inside the same fraction field, so integrality and normality identify it with the original ring. A regular point blowup also has zero positive structure-sheaf direct images by BP2 and local Čech comparison. Applying SC15 successively gives zero positive cohomology on the dominating regular sequence \(W\) over the affine base.

For \(g:W\to Y\), one has \(g_*\mathcal O_W=\mathcal O_Y\). Push a flasque resolution to get \(C^\bullet\), and put \(B^1=\operatorname{im}(C^0\to C^1)\), \(Z^1=\ker(C^1\to C^2)\). The exact sequence \(0\to\mathcal O_Y\to C^0\to B^1\to0\) gives

\[ H^1(Y,\mathcal O_Y) =\frac{\Gamma(B^1)}{\operatorname{im}\Gamma(C^0)} \hookrightarrow \frac{\Gamma(Z^1)}{\operatorname{im}\Gamma(C^0)} =H^1(W,\mathcal O_W)=0. \tag{BPX4} \]

This does not assert vanishing of all higher direct images for the arbitrary map \(g\). It proves the needed injection directly.

The regular base is essential to the exceptional-line geometry and the decreasing colength. A singular normal two-dimensional local ring may have embedding dimension three, as TN7 demonstrates; its maximal-ideal blowup need not have the regular charts BP1. Therefore the normal model TN5 is still to be resolved by a separate proved argument. The finite-cover boundedness,normal-surface termination and relevant completion or descent steps cannot be replaced by this regular-base vanishing. The full course objective and the further semiabelian and analytic constructions remain in force.

2AD. Finite covers of regular surfaces and normal modifications

A finite cover of a regular surface can be singular. The useful statement is that its proper birational models can be dominated by schemes finite over regular modifications of the base. Normalization is performed on those regular modifications, where TN1 applies. This gives finite normalization for the proper models themselves without assuming a general finiteness theorem for all algebras over a normal ring.

Throughout, \(A\) is a Noetherian regular integral domain of dimension at most two, \(F=\operatorname{Frac}A\), \(L/F\) is finite separable, and \(B\) is the integral closure of \(A\) in \(L\). Thus \(B\) is finite over \(A\), by TN1. A modification is an integral proper birational scheme over the specified integral base. For the local conclusions, \(C=B_{\mathfrak q}\) is a local ring of dimension two, \(\mathfrak m\) its maximal ideal, and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}C\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\).

The cohomological application belongs to the surface methods discussed in the freely accessible Stacks Project, §54.8. The final argument uses the projective-bundle construction of its Lemma 54.7.5. All the assertions needed here, including the finiteness of the normalizations in that construction, are proved below. The general Nagata hypothesis in the cited statement is replaced here by an explicit finite-cover construction. The prerequisites are BP1–BP7, TN1–TN3, the degree calculation CE1, proper coherent cohomology and the finite-fibre theorem of Lesson 3.

2AD.1. Principalization over a regular affine surface

FM1. Every nonzero coherent ideal on a regular Noetherian integral surface can be made invertible by a finite sequence of blowups at finite reduced sets of closed points. Each centre has local dimension two. For a stable ideal, the sequence can be chosen invariant under any given finite group of automorphisms. In particular every modification of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) is dominated by a regular scheme obtained by such point blowups, and

\[ H^j(W,\mathcal O_W)=0\quad(j>0) \tag{FM1} \]

for any such \(W\) over the affine regular base.

Proof. Regular local rings in dimension at most two are factorial, by NM2. For a coherent ideal \(I\), its common orders at the height-one points therefore define an effective Cartier divisor \(D\). This assertion is local: in a factorial neighbourhood take the gcd of a finite generating list. On overlaps the ratios of the two gcds have order zero at every height-one point, so both that ratio and its inverse are regular, by the height-one intersection in NM2. The local equations consequently differ by units. There are only finitely many height-one components, since each occurs in the divisor of any fixed nonzero local generator on a finite affine cover. The residual ideal

\[ J=I\mathcal O(D) \tag{FM2} \]

has no height-one support. Its nonunit locus is therefore a finite zero-dimensional closed set; at a point of local dimension zero or one the original ideal was already invertible.

Blow up the full reduced nonunit locus. Near each centre the calculation is precisely BP1–BP4: divide by the exceptional order, then remove the new common Cartier factor, and continue with the residual ideal. Write

\[ N=\sum_q\lambda_{\mathcal O_q}(\mathcal O_q/J_q), \tag{FM3} \]

where the sum ranges over its finite support. BP3 bounds the sum of the new colengths over a given old point after weighting them by their residue degrees over that point. Each degree is a positive integer. Hence the unweighted sum over the new points is no larger than that weighted sum, which is strictly smaller than the old colength. Thus \(N\) decreases by at least one for each individual point centre. The process terminates, and the Cartier factors show that the original ideal has become invertible. The centres and the residual divisorial factors are intrinsic. A finite group preserving \(I\) preserves each full centre, and the blowup universal property gives the action at every stage. No averaging is involved.

The graph construction in BP6 projectivizes an arbitrary proper modification. That part of its proof uses only an affine Noetherian integral base: embed a finite affine cover in projective spaces, close the joint graph, and apply the proved proper finite-fibre theorem to its projection to the product. A projective modification over the affine base is the blowup of an ideal, by the homogeneous-coordinate argument of BP5, which likewise does not require that the base be local. The preceding principalization therefore dominates it. Finally BP2 gives the vanishing of positive direct images of the structure sheaf for a point blowup, locally at its centres and trivially elsewhere. SC14 and SC15 compose these vanishings, giving (FM1) over the affine base. In particular a normal modification of this regular affine base has zero first structure-sheaf cohomology, by the explicit injection of BP7. \(\square\)

2AD.2. Finite graded invariants without division by the group order

FM2. Let \(R\) be a finitely generated nonnegatively graded \(A\)-domain and let a finite group \(G\) act by graded \(A\)-algebra automorphisms. Suppose \(R_0^G=A\). Then \(D=R^G\) is a finitely generated graded \(A\)-algebra, \(R\) is finite over \(D\), and

\[ \operatorname{Proj}R\longrightarrow\operatorname{Proj}D \tag{FM4} \]

is finite and surjective. Moreover \(\operatorname{Proj}D\) is projective over \(A\). These statements hold when the residue characteristic divides \(|G|\).

Proof. Choose finitely many homogeneous algebra generators \(r_i\), including generators of \(R_0\). The orbit equation

\[ \prod_{g\in G}(T-g(r_i)) =T^{|G|}+a_{i1}T^{|G|-1}+\cdots+a_{i,|G|} \tag{FM5} \]

has invariant homogeneous coefficients, with \(a_{ij}\) of degree \(j\deg r_i\). Let \(D'\) be the algebra generated by all these coefficients over \(A\). It is Noetherian, and the monic equations make \(R\) finite over \(D'\): bounded powers of the finitely many \(r_i\) span it. The submodule \(D\subset R\) is consequently finite over \(D'\). This proves its finite generation and also the finiteness of \(R\) over \(D\).

For a positive-degree homogeneous element of \(R\), every coefficient except the leading coefficient of (FM5) has positive degree. Its equation implies

\[ R_+\subset\sqrt{D_+R}. \tag{FM6} \]

Thus the homogeneous inclusion defines (FM4) everywhere. Here are the local finiteness details when degrees are not all one. For a positive integer \(e\), a finitely generated graded algebra \(H\) is finite over its Veronese algebra \(H^{(e)}=\bigoplus_nH_{ne}\). Indeed it is finite over the algebra generated by the \(e\)-th powers of a homogeneous generating list together with \(H_0\). That smaller algebra is Noetherian; \(H^{(e)}\), a submodule of the finite module \(H\), is finite over it and hence Noetherian. Now choose \(f\in D_e\). The algebra \(R^{(e)}\) is finite over \(D^{(e)}\): \(R\) is finite over \(D^{(e)}\), and its Veronese submodule is stable under that Noetherian ring. Choose homogeneous module generators \(s_j\) in degrees \(n_je\). Regrade by \(e\). In the degree-zero localized algebra the finitely many elements \(s_j/f^{n_j}\) span over \(D_{(f)}\). This proves finiteness on every affine chart \(D_+(f)\).

For surjectivity, take a homogeneous prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(D\) not containing \(D_+\). Lying over for the integral extension gives a prime \(P\) of \(R\) over it. The ideal \(P^{\mathrm h}\) of its homogeneous elements is a homogeneous prime: products of homogeneous elements satisfy the prime condition, and highest nonzero homogeneous terms then give the prime condition for arbitrary elements in the quotient. Its contraction is \(\mathfrak p\). An element of \(D_+\setminus\mathfrak p\) stays outside \(P^{\mathrm h}\), so this gives a point of \(\operatorname{Proj}R\) above \(\mathfrak p\). Lying over is the integral-extension argument already proved in TN3.

Finally choose positive-degree generators \(x_i\) for \(D\) over \(A\), and a common multiple \(e\) of their degrees \(d_i\). The algebra

\[ S=A[x_i^{e/d_i}:i] \tag{FM7} \]

has generators all of degree \(e\), and \(D\) is finite over \(S\). The same argument gives a finite map \(\operatorname{Proj}D\to\operatorname{Proj}S\). Regrading makes the latter a closed subscheme of an ordinary projective space. The explicit finite-over-projective construction of Lesson 3, Theorem 0F7, proves projectivity of \(\operatorname{Proj}D\). At no step was an invariant obtained by dividing an orbit sum by \(|G|\). \(\square\)

2AD.3. An orbit product of blowup ideals

FM3. Let \(E/F\) be a finite Galois extension containing \(L\), let \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\), and let \(\widetilde B\) be the integral closure of \(A\) in \(E\). For every projective modification \(Y\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\), there is an integral scheme \(Y_1\) mapping to \(Y\), and a projective modification \(X_0\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), with a finite surjection \(Y_1\to X_0\) whose extension of generic fields is \(E/F\).

Proof. By TN1, \(\widetilde B\) is finite over \(A\). Its invariants are \(A\): an invariant lies in \(E^G=F\), is integral over \(A\), and hence lies in the normal ring \(A\). BP5's homogeneous-coordinate construction writes \(Y=\operatorname{Bl}_I B\) for a nonzero ideal \(I\). Put

\[ I_0=I\widetilde B,\qquad J=\prod_{g\in G}g(I_0),\qquad Y_1=\operatorname{Bl}_J\widetilde B. \tag{FM8} \]

The ideal \(J\) is \(G\)-stable.

We will use a local fact about ideals in a domain. If the product \(HK\) of two nonzero finitely generated ideals in a local domain is principal and invertible, say \(HK=(s)\), write \(s=\sum h_i k_i\). Some \(h_i k_i/s\) is a unit. For this index and every \(h\in H\), the element \(hk_i/s\) belongs to the ring, so

\[ \frac{h}{h_i}=\frac{hk_i/s}{h_i k_i/s} \tag{FM9} \]

belongs to it. Thus \(H=(h_i)\), and likewise \(K\) is invertible. Induction gives the assertion for any finite product. Apply it to the pullbacks of the factors of \(J\) on \(Y_1\); its local rings are domains. Every \(g(I_0)\) becomes invertible. The actual blowup universal property NS2 gives \(Y_1\to Y\).

The Rees algebra \(R=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}J^nT^n\) is a finitely generated graded \(A\)-domain. Let \(G\) fix \(T\). Its degree-zero invariants are \(A\), so FM2 supplies the finite surjection to

\[ X_0=\operatorname{Proj}(R^G). \tag{FM10} \]

This target is integral and projective over \(A\). After inverting the nonzero elements of \(A\), one has \(\widetilde B\otimes_A F=E\), \(J\otimes_A F=E\), and \(R_F=E[T]\). Invariants commute with this localization: the denominators are fixed, and a nonzero denominator cannot annihilate a difference in the domain. Therefore \((R^G)_F=F[T]\), and the generic fibre of \(X_0\) is \(\operatorname{Spec}F\). This is the claimed birational modification, with the specified generic cover. \(\square\)

2AD.4. Finite-cover domination

FM4. For every modification \(Y\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\), there exist a regular point-blowup modification \(W\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) and its normalization \(M\) in \(L\), such that \(M\to W\) is finite and \(M\to Y\) is a proper birational surjection. In particular \(M\) is normal and projective over \(A\); regularity of \(M\) is not asserted.

Proof. First projectivize \(Y\) by the graph argument used in FM1. It is enough to dominate that projective modification. Apply FM3 and then FM1 to obtain \(W\to X_0\), with \(W\) regular. On each affine chart of \(W\), TN1 makes its integral closure in \(E\) finite. The localization statement TN2 glues these rings to a finite normalization \(N\to W\).

The unique component of \(Y_1\times_{X_0}W\) dominating \(W\), taken with its reduced scheme structure, is finite over \(W\). Its affine rings are finite subalgebras of \(E\), integral over the corresponding rings of \(W\). They are contained in those rings' integral closures in \(E\). The inclusions give a canonical map \(N\to Y_1\), and hence a map \(N\to Y\). This construction uses normalization only on regular affine charts.

To obtain the desired generic field \(L\), consider the map

\[ N\longrightarrow Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}W. \tag{FM11} \]

It is finite: its graph is closed since the target is separated over \(W\), and the projection from its product with \(N\) is finite since \(N\to W\) is finite. Let \(Z\) be its scheme-theoretic image. This is integral, proper over \(W\), and has generic fibre \(\operatorname{Spec}L\). Its geometric fibres have finite underlying sets. Indeed the finite map \(N\to Z\) is surjective (its closed image is its scheme-theoretic image), remains so after field extension, and \(N\to W\) has finite fibres. The proper finite-fibre theorem of Lesson 3 makes \(Z\to W\) finite.

Let \(M\) be the normalization of \(W\) in \(L\), finite by TN1. On an affine chart of \(W\), the ring of \(Z\) is a finite algebra inside \(L\), and thus is contained in the integral closure defining \(M\). These inclusions give \(M\to Z\to Y\). Its generic field is \(L\), so it is birational over \(B\). It is proper: \(M\) is proper over \(A\), \(Y\) is separated over \(A\), and the closed-graph argument applies. Its closed image contains the generic point of \(Y\), so it is surjective.

All schemes dominating \(Y\) in this construction have dimension at most two: \(W\) does by BP1 and FM1, and \(M\) does by the integral dimension argument TN3. The proper surjection \(M\to Y\) also bounds the dimension of \(Y\): given a chain of integral closed subsets of \(Y\), take a component dominating the largest, then successively a component of its inverse image dominating the next. Properness makes these images closed, and dominance and the distinct images make the lifted chain strict. The required dominating component exists because a finite union of proper closed subsets cannot cover an integral scheme. A finite normalization of a regular scheme in a larger separable field may be singular, as TN7 illustrates. No resolution of such singularities is hidden in this domination. \(\square\)

2AD.5. Finite normalization of proper birational models

FM5. The normalization of every modification of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) is finite. The same conclusion holds over every localization \(C=B_{\mathfrak q}\). It includes successive normalized blowups and proper birational models that are not projective.

Proof. By FM4 a normal \(M\) properly and birationally dominates a given model \(Y\); write \(q:M\to Y\). For an affine open \(V=\operatorname{Spec}H\subset Y\), proper coherent cohomology makes

\[ H'=\Gamma(q^{-1}V,\mathcal O_M) \tag{FM12} \]

a finite \(H\)-module. Since \(M\) is integral and has function field \(L\), it is a ring inside \(L\). Every element of \(H'\) is integral over \(H\), by the finite-module determinant argument. Conversely an element of \(L\) integral over \(H\) is integral over each local ring of \(q^{-1}V\). Normality makes it regular in every such local ring, and these regular rational functions glue on \(q^{-1}V\). Thus \(H'\) is exactly the integral closure of \(H\) in \(L\). Localization of integral closure, TN2, glues these finite algebras. This proves the assertion over \(B\).

For a modification \(Y\) over \(C\), first projectivize it. Its projective dominating model is \(\operatorname{Bl}_I C\) by the generic-coordinate construction. Choose finitely many generators of \(I\), and clear a common denominator in \(B\setminus\mathfrak q\). The resulting ideal \(I_B\subset B\) localizes to a nonzero scalar multiple of \(I\); scalar multiplication does not change the blowup, since it identifies the degree-\(n\) Rees pieces by the \(n\)-th power of that scalar. Normalize \(\operatorname{Bl}_{I_B}B\), whose normalization is finite by the first paragraph, and localize over \(\operatorname{Spec}C\). This gives a normal proper birational model dominating \(Y\). Apply (FM12) to this domination over \(C\). It proves finite normalization of \(Y\) itself. A composite of successive blowups and finite normalizations is still a proper birational model, so the assertion applies at each stage.

This is a finiteness assertion for these proper models in the fixed function field. It does not assert a general Nagata property for arbitrary finite-type algebras and arbitrary field extensions, nor normality of completed local rings. \(\square\)

2AD.6. An exceptional divisor with ample negative

FM6. Every modification \(X\) over the local surface \(C\) is an isomorphism over \(U\). It is dominated by a normal projective modification \(W\) with an effective Cartier divisor \(F\) supported on its closed fibre such that \(\mathcal O_W(-F)\) is ample over \(\operatorname{Spec}C\). If the modification is nontrivial, the construction has \(F\ne0\).

Proof. Every height-one local ring of the normal Noetherian domain \(C\) is a DVR, by the general normal one-dimensional local argument of RC1; it did not require a coefficient field. Projectivize \(X\) as \(\operatorname{Bl}_I C\to X\). At each point of \(U\), the ideal \(I\) is principal and invertible. Hence that blowup is \(U\) there. Its proper surjection to \(X\) restricts to a surjective section \(U\to X_U\). A section of a separated morphism is a closed immersion; its defining ideal in the reduced \(X_U\) is zero because its underlying image is all of \(X_U\). Thus \(X_U=U\).

Regard

\[ I^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_C(I,C) =\{z\in\operatorname{Frac}C:zI\subset C\}, \qquad J=II^\vee\subset C. \tag{FM13} \]

The Hom module is finite, since \(C\) is Noetherian and \(I\) is finitely presented. To check the displayed equality, choose \(i_0\ne0\) in \(I\). For a linear map \(f:I\to C\), the equality \(i_0f(i)=if(i_0)\) shows that it is multiplication by \(f(i_0)/i_0\). Localization of a finite presentation shows that Hom commutes with localization here. At a height-one prime the ideal \(I\) is an invertible DVR ideal, so \(J\) is the unit ideal there. Consequently \(J\) is a unit or is \(\mathfrak m\)-primary.

The product argument (FM9) makes \(\operatorname{Bl}_J C\) dominate \(\operatorname{Bl}_I C\). Normalize the former. FM5 makes this a finite map, so the resulting normal \(W\) is projective, by Theorem 0F7. The nonzero ideal \(J\mathcal O_W\) is invertible, hence

\[ J\mathcal O_W=\mathcal O_W(-F) \tag{FM14} \]

for an effective Cartier divisor \(F\). It is supported on the closed fibre since \(J\) is a unit on \(U\). It is the pullback of the ample tautological ideal on the blowup.

Here is the ampleness fact used in this last step. For a finite map \(h:W\to V\) of projective schemes over an affine Noetherian base, and an ample invertible sheaf \(L_0\) on \(V\), any coherent \(G\) on \(W\) has \(h_*G\otimes L_0^n\) globally generated for large \(n\), by PF7 and PF8. The evaluation \(h^*h_*G\to G\) is surjective, as is seen for a finite algebra on an affine open. Hence \(G\otimes h^*L_0^n\) is globally generated. Take \(G=H^{-1}\) for a fixed very ample \(H\) on \(W\). Then \(h^*L_0^n=H\otimes M_n\) with \(M_n\) globally generated. The graph of the maps given by \(H\) and \(M_n\), followed by the Segre embedding, is a closed immersion and realizes this tensor product as very ample. This proves the claimed ampleness.

If \(J\) is a unit, (FM9) says that \(I\) is invertible already, so the projectivizing blowup is \(\operatorname{Spec}C\); the surjective-section argument makes \(X\) the base as well. If \(J\) is proper, it vanishes over the nonempty closed fibre of the proper surjection \(W\to\operatorname{Spec}C\), and \(F\ne0\). The identity modification itself may be taken with \(F=0\), since its structure sheaf is ample on the affine base. \(\square\)

2AD.7. Vertical Cartier intersection and trivial conormal

FM7. On a normal modification \(X\) of the local surface \(C\), a nonempty effective Cartier divisor supported on the closed fibre cannot have trivial conormal.

Proof. First work on the projective \(W\) of FM6 with its divisor \(F\). If \(T\) is an effective vertical Cartier divisor, then some power of \(\mathfrak m\) annihilates \(\mathcal O_T\). Indeed its radical ideal contains \(\mathfrak m\mathcal O_W\) on a finite affine cover; finite generation gives a uniform power. Thus coherent cohomology on \(T\) has finite \(C\)-length, by proper coherent cohomology. It vanishes in sufficiently high degrees by the finite affine Čech computation. Put

\[ \chi_C(T,L)=\sum_{j\geq0}(-1)^j \lambda_C H^j(T,L). \tag{FM15} \]

If \(C_i\) are the reduced curve components of \(T\), and \(m_i\) is the length of \(\mathcal O_T\) at the generic point of \(C_i\), then

\[ \chi_C(T,L)-\chi_C(T,\mathcal O_T) =\sum_i m_i\deg_{\kappa(\mathfrak m)}(L|_{C_i}). \tag{FM16} \]

Zero-dimensional components or embedded subquotients contribute zero to this difference.

We give the dévissage behind (FM16). Filter a coherent sheaf first by powers of \(\mathfrak m\), then by powers of the nilradical on the resulting curve. The quotients live on reduced proper curves over \(\kappa(\mathfrak m)\). For a coherent sheaf on a reduced curve, restriction to its components modulo torsion changes it only by kernel and cokernel with finite support. This follows by checking at each generic point; a closed subset of a Noetherian curve omitting those finitely many points has dimension zero and is finite. On one integral component, twist a rank-\(r\) sheaf by a high power of an ample sheaf so that it is generated. Choose \(r\) generating sections that are linearly independent over the function field. They give a map from \(r\) copies of a fixed invertible sheaf which is an isomorphism at that generic point; its kernel and cokernel have finite support. Tensoring an invertible sheaf does not change the length of a finite-support module, and such modules have no higher cohomology. For clarity, CE1 makes the product of two operators of the form tensor-by-a-line minus identity zero on the curve support filtration. Applying Euler characteristic shows both degree additivity and independence of the initial invertible twist. This degree additivity therefore gives \(r\deg L\) for this quotient. Adding the filtrations gives (FM16); the sum of the generic ranks in them is exactly \(m_i\). This argument uses neither normalization of the components nor algebraic closedness of the residue field. A length-one sheaf at a closed point of residue degree \(d\) contributes \(d\) to the curve degree, as required.

For effective vertical Cartier divisors \(T,S\), define

\[ (T,S)=\sum_i m_i\deg_{\kappa(\mathfrak m)} (\mathcal O_W(S)|_{C_i}). \tag{FM17} \]

The exact product sequences

\[ \begin{aligned} 0&\longrightarrow\mathcal O_T(-S) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{T+S}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_S \longrightarrow0,\\ 0&\longrightarrow\mathcal O_S(-T) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{T+S}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_T \longrightarrow0 \end{aligned} \tag{FM18} \]

follow locally by multiplication by the local equation of the second divisor. Equations (FM15)–(FM16) make both \((T,S)\) and \((S,T)\) equal to

\[ \chi_C(T,\mathcal O_T)+\chi_C(S,\mathcal O_S) -\chi_C(T+S,\mathcal O_{T+S}). \tag{FM19} \]

This proves symmetry with all multiplicities and residue degrees included.

Suppose \(Z\ne0\) is vertical Cartier and \(\mathcal O_Z(-Z)\simeq\mathcal O_Z\). For a component of \(F\) contained in \(Z\), the restriction of \(\mathcal O_W(Z)\) is trivial and has degree zero. On a component not contained in \(Z\), its canonical section is nonzero and its zeros form an effective finite Cartier divisor, so its degree is nonnegative. Consequently

\[ (F,Z)\geq0. \tag{FM20} \]

In contrast \(\mathcal O_W(-F)\) is ample. Its restriction to every proper integral curve component of \(Z\) has positive degree. To see the positivity directly, a power embeds the curve projectively. At a closed point choose a homogeneous polynomial vanishing at that point but not identically on the curve. It yields a nonzero section of a positive power with a nonempty finite zero divisor. The divisor exact sequence and degree additivity make that power's degree strictly positive, and therefore the degree of the original ample sheaf is strictly positive. Since a nonempty Cartier divisor on this two-dimensional integral scheme has a curve component, (FM17) now gives

\[ (Z,F)<0, \tag{FM21} \]

contradicting symmetry.

For an arbitrary normal \(X\), choose a normal \(W\to X\) as in FM6 and pull \(Z\) back to it. The pullback is Cartier, since its local equation is nonzero in the common function field and \(W\) is integral. It is nonempty by surjectivity, vertical, and its conormal remains trivial by restriction of the pulled-back line bundle. The preceding contradiction applies on \(W\). If \(X\) is the identity modification, there is no nonzero Cartier divisor supported at its closed point: a nonzero principal ideal in a two-dimensional domain has height-one support, by the principal ideal theorem. This also covers the identity case in the argument. \(\square\)

2AD.8. Restriction of first cohomology to the punctured surface

FM8. For every normal modification \(X\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}C\), the restriction map

\[ H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\longrightarrow H^1(U,\mathcal O_U) \tag{FM22} \]

is injective.

Proof. We identify \(X_U=U\) by FM6. On a finite affine cover of the separated scheme \(X\), the affine-intersection Čech computation SC11–SC12 represents a class by an additive cocycle \(a_{ij}\). Glue trivial projective lines over the cover by

\[ z_j=z_i+a_{ij}. \tag{FM23} \]

The cocycle condition gives a projective-line bundle \(P\to X\), equivalently the projectivization of the rank-two vector bundle glued by the corresponding triangular matrices. It is proper over \(X\). The points at infinity glue to a section \(D\simeq X\). This section is Cartier. In the local parameters \(w_i=1/z_i\),

\[ w_j=\frac{w_i}{1+a_{ij}w_i} \equiv w_i\pmod{w_i^2}. \tag{FM24} \]

Thus its conormal is the trivial line bundle on \(D\).

Suppose the class restricts to zero on \(U\). Its restricted cocycle is a coboundary after an affine refinement, and the corresponding local functions give a second section over \(U\), disjoint from \(D\). Let \(T\) be its scheme-theoretic closure in \(P\). This is integral and proper birational over \(X\), and hence a proper modification over \(C\).

If \(T\) misses \(D\), then \(T\to X\) is affine, since \(P\setminus D\to X\) is an affine-line torsor, hence an affine morphism. An affine proper morphism of Noetherian schemes is finite: over an affine open its algebra of functions is a finite module by proper coherent cohomology. Since \(T\to X\) is finite birational and \(X\) is normal, each such finite algebra inside the function field equals the base ring. Hence \(T=X\). It gives a global section of the affine-line torsor. In the coordinates (FM23) that section is precisely a global coboundary, so the original class was zero.

Otherwise \(T\) meets \(D\). FM5 makes the normalization \(T^\nu\to T\) finite; it is a normal proper modification over \(C\). Pull back \(D\) to \(T^\nu\). Its local equation is nonzero generically, so the pullback \(Z\) is an effective Cartier divisor. It is nonempty since normalization is surjective, and it is supported on the closed fibre since the section over \(U\) misses \(D\). The conormal calculation (FM24) pulls back to

\[ \mathcal O_Z(-Z)\simeq\mathcal O_Z. \tag{FM25} \]

This contradicts FM7. The only remaining possibility was the zero class, proving (FM22).

These assertions justify finite-cover domination, finite normalization and restriction injectivity. For a complete DVR with perfect residue field, §2AE bounds the lengths of \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) on the local normal finite covers specified there. Regular models require a terminating resolution argument in addition to these cohomological assertions. \(\square\)

Exercise 2AD — finite covers, exceptional divisors and cohomology (100 points)

Each part is worth 10 points. Use the notation of §2AD. Assertions about lengths must include residue degrees when lengths over different local rings are compared.

  1. Explain why the unweighted sum in (FM3) terminates global principalization, although BP3 is a residue-degree-weighted inequality. Explain why a global gcd element is unnecessary.
  2. Prove finite generation of the graded invariant algebra without an averaging operator. For an invariant homogeneous element of degree \(e\), explain why Veronese regrading proves finiteness of the induced affine Proj chart.
  3. In a local domain prove that invertibility of a product of nonzero finite ideals implies invertibility of each factor. State exactly where locality and the domain hypothesis enter.
  4. For the orbit product \(J\) in (FM8), determine the generic Rees algebra and its invariant algebra. Explain why their Proj schemes give a finite cover of a birational model over \(A\).
  5. Give the domination construction with a Galois closure \(E/F\), and then recover the required field \(L\). Explain why replacing \(L\) permanently by \(E\) would not give a birational modification over \(B\).
  6. Prove finite normalization for proper models over \(B_{\mathfrak q}\). Distinguish this from a general finiteness theorem for all finite-type algebras and from a statement about normality after completion.
  7. Let \(A=\mathbf Z_2[t]\), \(B=\mathbf Z_2[\theta]\) with \(t=\theta^2\), and let the involution send \(\theta\) to \(-\theta\). For \(I=(2,\theta)\), compute the invariant Rees algebra for \(J=I\,g(I)\). Exhibit a singular quotient chart and principalize the corresponding base ideal by regular point blowups.
  8. Derive symmetry of (FM17) from (FM18), including nonreduced divisors. For a \((-1)\)-curve \(E\simeq\mathbf P^1_k\) over the closed residue field \(k\), compute \((aE,bE)\) and \(\chi_k(aE,\mathcal O_{aE})\).
  9. For the gluing \(z_j=z_i+a_{ij}\), calculate the conormal of the infinity section. Explain why a closure of a punctured section that misses infinity makes the original cohomology class zero.
  10. Prove the restriction injection (FM22) using finite normalization and the exceptional-divisor contradiction. Identify the further statements still needed to obtain resolution of the normal surface.

Complete solution.

  1. Over an old point \(q\), write \(r_q\) for the residual order. The BP3 calculation says
\[ \sum_{q'\mapsto q}[\kappa(q'):\kappa(q)]\, \lambda_{\mathcal O_{q'}}(\mathcal O_{q'}/J_{q'}) \leq\lambda_{\mathcal O_q}(\mathcal O_q/J_q) -\frac{r_q(r_q+1)}2. \tag{FMX1} \]

Each coefficient on the left is at least one. Sum over the finitely many old points to bound the new unweighted sum by the old sum minus a positive integer for each centre. The initial sum bounds the total number of individual point blowups. The common divisorial factor is a Cartier divisor whose local equations differ by units, rather than necessarily the divisor of one global element. Removing that divisor leaves the finite-support ideal to which (FMX1) applies. This also explains why nontrivial divisor class groups on the affine regular surface do not obstruct the procedure.

  1. A finite homogeneous generating list satisfies its orbit polynomials. Their finitely many invariant coefficients generate a Noetherian subalgebra \(D'\). Bounded powers of the generators span \(R\) over \(D'\); the invariants are a submodule of this finite module, so are finite over \(D'\). This proves finite generation even if the group order is zero in the residue field. For \(f\in D_e\), use
\[ D^{(e)}=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}D_{ne},\qquad R^{(e)}=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}R_{ne}. \tag{FMX2} \]

The \(e\)-th powers of algebra generators make the first Noetherian and make \(D\) finite over it. Hence \(R^{(e)}\) is a finite graded module over it, since it is a submodule of the finite module \(R\). If its homogeneous generators have degrees \(n_je\), their quotients by \(f^{n_j}\) generate the degree-zero localization. This is the finite ring map on \(D_+(f)\). The orbit equations for positive-degree generators also show that these inverse-image charts cover Proj.

  1. Write the invertible product locally as \(HK=(s)\) and \(s=\sum h_i k_i\). Then \(\sum h_i k_i/s=1\). In a local ring at least one summand is a unit. For this \(i\), equation (FM9) puts every \(h/h_i\) in the ring, so \(H=(h_i)\). The argument for \(K\) is identical. The domain hypothesis makes cancellation and these fractions legitimate, and makes the nonzero generators nonzerodivisors. Locality supplies a unit among the finitely many summands. Apply this result with one factor and the product of the others to handle any finite product.

  2. After tensoring with \(F\), the nonzero ideal in the field \(E\) becomes the unit ideal. Consequently

\[ R_F=E[T],\qquad (R^G)_F=F[T]. \tag{FMX3} \]

The second equality holds because denominators from \(A\) are fixed and multiplication by them is injective in the domain. Thus the generic Proj schemes are \(\operatorname{Spec}E\) and \(\operatorname{Spec}F\). FM2 proves the finite surjection and projectivity of its target over \(A\). Since that target is integral with the indicated generic fibre, it is a birational modification. Invertibility of the product on its blowup makes each orbit factor invertible by part 3; the blowup universal property therefore gives the map to the chosen \(B\)-model.

  1. First dominate the projectivized \(B\)-model by the orbit-product blowup over the integral closure in \(E\). Principalize the invariant Proj model over \(A\) to obtain a regular \(W\). Its normalization \(N\) in \(E\) is finite by TN1 and maps to that blowup by inclusions of integral subalgebras of \(E\). It hence maps to the original \(Y\). Take its scheme-theoretic image \(Z\) in \(Y\times_A W\). This is proper over \(W\) with finite geometric fibres, and thus finite. Its generic field is \(L\), since \(Y_F=\operatorname{Spec}L\). The finite rings of \(Z\) lie in the normalization \(M\) of \(W\) in \(L\), so \(M\to Z\to Y\) is the desired map. If one stopped at \(N\), the map over \(B\) would have generic degree \([E:L]\), rather than be birational when that degree exceeds one. Neither \(N\) nor \(M\) is asserted regular.

  2. Projectivize a local model, write the projective model as \(\operatorname{Bl}_I B_{\mathfrak q}\), and clear a common denominator of its ideal generators outside \(\mathfrak q\). The resulting ideal of \(B\) has a proper blowup. Its finite normalization, already proved over \(B\), localizes to a normal proper domination of the original local model. For an affine chart \(\operatorname{Spec}H\) of that model, the functions on its proper normal inverse image form a finite \(H\)-module inside the fraction field. Every integral rational function belongs to all the normal local rings upstairs and is therefore one of these global functions. Thus this finite module is exactly the integral closure. The proof concerns proper models in one fixed function field. It supplies no theorem for an arbitrary finite-type quotient ring or arbitrary further field extension, and it makes no claim that a completed local ring is normal.

  3. The rings \(A\) and \(B\) are polynomial rings over the complete DVR and hence regular and normal, by TN2 and the regular-parameter calculation. The field extension is separable of degree two, and \(B\) is the integral closure of \(A\): it is finite integral over \(A\), and any element of its fraction field integral over \(A\) is integral over the normal ring \(B\). The stable ideal has

\[ J=(2,\theta)^2,\qquad (J^n)^G=(4,t)^n,\qquad R^G=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}(4,t)^nT^n. \tag{FMX4} \]

Indeed the invariants in \(\mathbf Z_2[\theta]\) are the even polynomials: an odd coefficient fixed by sign change would satisfy \(2c=0\), so is zero. A coefficient of \(\theta^{2j}\) in \((2,\theta)^{2n}\) must be divisible by \(2^{\max(2n-2j,0)}\). This is exactly the coefficient condition for \(t^j\) in \((4,t)^n\). There is no division by two.

The \(t\)-chart of the invariant blowup is

\[ A[v]/(tv-4). \tag{FMX5} \]

At \((2,t,v)\) it has dimension two but cotangent dimension three, since its equation lies in the square of that maximal ideal. It is the normal singular chart of NS3 with thickness two. The ideal \((4,t)\) in \(A_{(2,t)}\) has colength two and order one. Blow up \((2,t)\). On the \(2\)-chart write \(t=2s\): the weak ideal is \((2,s)\), of colength one. The \(t\)-chart has unit weak ideal. Blow up the remaining point \((2,s)\); both of its weak charts are units. Thus the residual colengths are \(2,1,0\). Elsewhere the ideal was already invertible. The regular two-blowup base dominates the singular quotient model, just as FM1 requires.

  1. Taking Euler characteristics in the two product sequences gives
\[ \begin{aligned} \chi_C(T+S,\mathcal O_{T+S}) &=\chi_C(T,\mathcal O_T)-(T,S) +\chi_C(S,\mathcal O_S)\\ &=\chi_C(S,\mathcal O_S)-(S,T) +\chi_C(T,\mathcal O_T). \end{aligned} \tag{FMX6} \]

Cancellation proves symmetry. The generic lengths in (FM16) retain multiplicities for nonreduced divisors. At a closed intersection point, dimension over the base residue field is local length times residue degree. For the \((-1)\)-curve, \(\mathcal O_W(E)|_E=\mathcal O_E(-1)\), and hence

\[ (aE,bE)=-ab. \tag{FMX7} \]

The successive kernels in the thickening \(aE\) are \(\mathcal O_E(j)\) for \(0\leq j<a\), so the projective-line Čech calculation gives

\[ \chi_k(aE,\mathcal O_{aE}) =\sum_{j=0}^{a-1}(j+1)=\frac{a(a+1)}2. \tag{FMX8} \]

Substitution in (FM19) again gives \(-ab\). Thus the symmetry is an Euler identity for the actual thickenings, not an assumption that they are reduced.

  1. Near infinity, \(w_j=w_i/(1+a_{ij}w_i)\), so the transition on \((w_i)/(w_i^2)\) is the identity. The conormal is therefore trivial. If the closure \(T\) of a section over \(U\) misses infinity, it is closed in the affine-line torsor. Its map to \(X\) is both affine and proper, hence finite by the proper-cohomology argument in FM8. It is birational, and normality of \(X\) makes the finite algebra equal to \(\mathcal O_X\). Thus the closure is a global section, represented in the gluing charts by functions whose differences are \(a_{ij}\). They express the original cocycle as a coboundary.

  2. If the cohomology class in the kernel were nonzero, part 9 forces the section's closure to meet infinity. Normalize that closure; finiteness follows from part 6 because it is a proper birational model over \(C\). The pulled-back infinity divisor is a nonempty effective vertical Cartier divisor with trivial conormal. Dominate this normal model by the projective model of FM6, pull back the divisor, and use symmetry to get simultaneously \((F,Z)\geq0\) and \((Z,F)<0\). This contradiction proves injectivity. One still needs a uniform bound on the first-cohomology lengths, an argument reaching the appropriate rational-singularity case, and a terminating resolution procedure with the required local and descent properties. Finite-cover domination alone provides none of those conclusions. Semilinear actions and the later semiabelian and analytic-cover constructions likewise require their own proofs. \(\square\)

2AE. Uniform coherent-cohomology bounds over a complete valuation ring

Let \(R\) be a complete discrete valuation ring, with uniformizer \(\pi\), perfect residue field \(k\), and fraction field \(K\). Put \(A=R[t]\), \(F=K(t)\), and let \(L/F\) be finite separable. Write \(B\) for the integral closure of \(A\) in \(L\). It is finite by TN1. Fix a prime \(\mathfrak q\) such that

\[ C=B_{\mathfrak q},\qquad \dim C=2,\qquad U=\operatorname{Spec}C\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \quad \mathfrak m=\mathfrak qC . \tag{HB1} \]

A normal modification means an integral normal scheme proper and birational over the specified base. The result below bounds the \(C\)-length of \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) for every normal modification of \(\operatorname{Spec}C\). The bound depends on \(C\), not on \(X\).

The regularity of \(R[t]\) can be seen locally. Away from \(\pi\) its local rings are localizations of the principal ideal domain \(K[t]\). Over \(\pi\), the height-one local ring is the DVR with uniformizer \(\pi\); at a closed point its maximal ideal is generated by \(\pi\) and a monic lift of the irreducible residue polynomial. Modulo \(\pi\) the second generator is a parameter in \(k[t]\). These two generators are independent modulo the square of the maximal ideal: reduce modulo \(\pi\) for the second, and modulo the monic polynomial for the first. The latter quotient is finite free over \(R\). The integral dimension calculation TN3 gives dimension two at these closed points. Thus the base satisfies the hypotheses of FM1–FM8. Proper coherent cohomology, finite-pushforward cohomology and localization of cohomology are the results proved in Lesson 3.

2AE.1. Normal local algebra and reduced principal cuts

HB1. Let \(S\) be a Noetherian normal domain. Each height-one localization is a DVR, and inside its fraction field

\[ S=\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=1}S_{\mathfrak p}. \tag{HB2} \]

For \(0\ne a\in S\), the associated primes of \(S/aS\) all have height one. In particular, in a normal local domain of dimension two, a principal quotient is reduced exactly when the order of its defining element at every height-one prime containing it is one.

Proof. We give the module and local-ring arguments used here. A finite module over a Noetherian ring has a finite prime filtration. To construct one, choose a nonzero element whose annihilator is maximal among annihilators of nonzero elements. That annihilator is prime: if \(xyv=0\) and \(yv\ne0\), maximality applied to \(yv\) forces \(xv=0\). Insert this cyclic submodule and repeat in the quotient. The ascending chain condition on submodules makes the process finite.

An associated prime of a finite module occurs among the primes of such a filtration. Indeed, for a cyclic submodule isomorphic to \(S/\mathfrak p\), choose the first filtration term having nonzero intersection with it. The intersection has zero intersection with the preceding term. A nonzero element of it therefore has the same annihilator before and after passage to the corresponding prime-filtration quotient, namely \(\mathfrak p\). This proves finiteness of the set of associated primes. The zero divisors on the module are their union: apply the maximal-annihilator argument to the nonzero kernel of multiplication by a zero divisor.

We also use the resulting injection of a finite module into the product of its localizations at its associated primes. If a nonzero element belonged to the kernel, its cyclic submodule would have an associated prime, and an element with that prime annihilator would remain nonzero there, a contradiction. Minimal primes of the support are associated. To see this, localize at such a prime; the localized module has finite length and has a nonzero element killed by the maximal ideal. Clearing denominators for a finite list of generators of the prime gives an element of the original module with precisely that annihilator.

Here is the local normality argument. Suppose \((T,\mathfrak n)\) is a Noetherian normal local domain and

\[ x\notin T,\qquad \mathfrak n x\subset T . \tag{HB3} \]

If \(\mathfrak n x\subset\mathfrak n\), multiplication by \(x\) on a finite generating tuple for the nonzero ideal \(\mathfrak n\) gives a matrix over \(T\). Its characteristic polynomial annihilates the tuple, by the adjugate identity. The ideal is faithful in a domain, so the polynomial vanishes at \(x\). Normality would give \(x\in T\), a contradiction. Otherwise there is \(u\in\mathfrak n\) with \(ux\) a unit, and

\[ v/u=(vx)/(ux)\in T\quad(v\in\mathfrak n). \tag{HB4} \]

Thus \(\mathfrak n=uT\).

A Noetherian local domain with nonzero principal maximal ideal \(uT\) is a DVR. For completeness, \(J=\bigcap_{r\ge0}u^rT\) is a finite ideal and cancellation gives \(J=uJ\). The finite-module determinant proof of Nakayama gives \(J=0\). Hence every nonzero element is a unit times a finite power of \(u\), and the least such order in a nonzero ideal generates that ideal. The only nonzero prime is the maximal ideal, so the dimension is one.

If \(T\) is a normal local domain of dimension one, choose \(0\ne a\in\mathfrak n\). The radical of \(aT\) is \(\mathfrak n\), so choose the least \(r\) with \(\mathfrak n^r\subset aT\), and \(b\in\mathfrak n^{r-1}\setminus aT\). Then \(x=b/a\) satisfies (HB3); the preceding argument makes \(T\) a DVR. This applies to height-one localizations; normality under localization is the denominator-clearing argument of TN2.

If an associated prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(S/aS\) had height at least two, localization would produce (HB3) in \(S_{\mathfrak p}\): take the quotient of a representative of an element with maximal-ideal annihilator by \(a\). Formula (HB4) would make its maximal ideal principal and its dimension one, a contradiction. Height zero is impossible because \(a\ne0\). Thus all these associated primes have height one. The module-localization injection just proved then gives (HB2): for \(b/a\) regular at all height-one points, \(b\) is zero in every relevant localization of \(S/aS\), hence belongs to \(aS\).

Finally \(S/aS\) injects into the product of its height-one localizations. Each is a DVR quotient by a power of its uniformizer. It is reduced exactly for power one. This proves both directions of the reducedness criterion. \(\square\)

HB2. In a normal Noetherian local domain \(C\) of dimension two, finitely many prescribed height-one primes are contained in the zero locus of an element \(c\ne0\) for which \(C/cC\) is reduced. Consequently, for every \(0\ne a\in\mathfrak m\) there are such a \(c\) and an integer \(n\ge1\) with

\[ c^n/a\in C . \tag{HB5} \]

Proof. We first spell out finite prime avoidance in the form needed here. If \(I\) is not contained in any of the pairwise incomparable primes \(\mathfrak p_j\), choose \(b_j\in I\setminus\mathfrak p_j\) and \(v_j\in\bigcap_{i\ne j}\mathfrak p_i\setminus\mathfrak p_j\). The latter element is a product of elements chosen from the other primes outside \(\mathfrak p_j\). Then \(\sum b_jv_j\) is in \(I\) and outside every \(\mathfrak p_j\).

For \(f\ne0\) in \(\mathfrak m\), let \(t(f)\) be the number of height-one primes containing \(f\). Choose \(g\in\mathfrak m\) outside those finitely many primes. Then \((f,g)\) is \(\mathfrak m\)-primary, and \(g\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(C/fC\), by HB1. We claim

\[ t(f)\le \lambda_C(C/(f,g)). \tag{HB6} \]

For a finite module \(N\) supported on \(V(f)\), set

\[ \chi_g(N)=\lambda_C(N/gN)-\lambda_C(N[g]), \qquad N[g]=\ker(g:N\to N). \tag{HB7} \]

Both lengths are finite: away from the closed point, the primes of \(V(f)\) are its height-one generic points and \(g\) is invertible. The kernel-cokernel sequence for multiplication by \(g\) makes \(\chi_g\) additive in short exact sequences. Apply a prime filtration of \(C/fC\). A factor \(C/\mathfrak p\) of dimension one contributes \(\lambda_C(C/(\mathfrak p,g))\ge1\), and a residue-field factor contributes zero. Every minimal prime of \(C/fC\) occurs. Since the kernel on \(C/fC\) is zero, (HB6) follows.

Let \(I\) be the intersection of the prescribed primes, and choose \(0\ne f_0\in I\). Choose \(g\) as above and \(N\) with \(\mathfrak m^N\subset\mathfrak m(f_0,g)\). For \(h\in\mathfrak m^N\), write \(h=uf_0+vg\) with \(u,v\in\mathfrak m\). Since \(1+u\) is a unit,

\[ (f_0+h,g)=(f_0,g). \tag{HB8} \]

Thus (HB6) bounds \(t(f_0+h)\) independently of \(h\). Among \(h\in I\cap\mathfrak m^N\), choose one maximizing this integer and replace \(f_0\) by \(f=f_0+h\). Write the height-one divisor of \(f\) as \(\sum_j m_j\mathfrak q_j\). Each prescribed prime occurs among the \(\mathfrak q_j\).

For each \(j\) we can choose \(a_j\in\mathfrak q_j\) of order one there and outside the other \(\mathfrak q_i\). Here is a construction using only the prime avoidance already proved. First choose \(a\in\mathfrak q_j\) outside all the other primes. If its order at \(\mathfrak q_j\) is one, take it. Otherwise choose \(b\in\mathfrak q_j\) of order one, by writing a uniformizer of \(C_{\mathfrak q_j}\) as a fraction. Among the other primes, call those not containing \(b\) good, and those containing \(b\) bad. For each good prime choose an element in it outside \(\mathfrak q_j\) and all bad primes, and multiply these choices to obtain \(v\). Then \(b+av\) has order one at \(\mathfrak q_j\), and is outside every other prime: reduce modulo good and bad primes separately.

Choose \(w\in\mathfrak m\) outside all the \(\mathfrak q_j\), and set

\[ h'=w^N \prod_{m_j=1}a_j^2 \prod_{m_j>1}a_j . \tag{HB9} \]

This belongs to \(I\cap\mathfrak m^N\). At every old prime, \(f+h'\) has order one. A new height-one prime containing it would strictly increase the maximal number \(t(f)\). Thus there are no new primes, and HB1 makes \(C/(f+h')\) reduced. This proves the first assertion.

For the second, prescribe all height-one primes in the divisor of \(a\), and choose \(c\) by the first assertion. Take \(n\) at least their largest order in \(a\). Every height-one order of \(c^n/a\) is nonnegative, so (HB2) gives (HB5). \(\square\)

2AE.2. Curve normalization in the special and generic directions

HB3. Let \(k\) be perfect and \(H\) an integral algebra finite over the polynomial ring \(k[t]\), with the latter embedded in \(H\). The normalization of \(H\) in its fraction field is finite over \(H\), even when the extension of \(k(t)\) is inseparable.

Proof. Write \(E=\operatorname{Frac}H\). In characteristic zero it is finite separable over \(k(t)\), so TN1 applies. In characteristic \(p>0\), Frobenius and the degree tower give

\[ [E:E^p]=p,\qquad [E:k(t^p)]=p[E:k(t)],\qquad [E^p:k(t^p)]=[E:k(t)] . \tag{HB10} \]

There is \(b\in H\setminus E^p\); otherwise every algebra generator, and hence the whole field \(E\), would belong to \(E^p\), since \(k\) is perfect. We have \(E=E^p(b)\). Every \(k\)-derivation of \(E\) is determined by its value on \(b\), and the derivation with value one exists: differentiate the unique expansion in \(1,b,\ldots,b^{p-1}\) over \(E^p\), whose defining relation has zero derivative.

Choose a monic relation \(b^m+\sum_{i<m}a_i(t)b^i=0\). Choose a power \(N=p^r\), with \(r\ge1\), such that

\[ \deg a_i < N(m-i)\quad(i<m),\qquad f=t^N+b. \tag{HB11} \]

Substitution \(b=f-t^N\) yields a polynomial equation for \(t\) over \(k[f]\), of degree \(Nm\) and leading coefficient \((-1)^m\). Every other term has smaller \(t\)-degree. Thus \(t\) is integral over \(k[f]\), and \(H\) is finite over \(k[f]\). The element \(f\) is transcendental over \(k\), since otherwise this integrality would make \(t\) algebraic. The derivation above sends \(f\) to one. Consequently the only \(k(f)\)-derivation of \(E\) is zero.

We justify the finite-field-extension criterion used in this conclusion. For a finite extension \(E/J\) in characteristic \(p\), let \(J_s\subset E\) consist of the elements separable over \(J\). Every element has a sufficiently high \(p\)-power in \(J_s\), by separating the \(p\)-power from its minimal polynomial. Thus \(E/J_s\) is purely inseparable of finite exponent. If it is nontrivial, then \(E\ne J_sE^p\): equality would iterate to \(E=J_sE^{p^r}=J_s\) for a sufficiently large \(r\). A finite extension of exponent one has a basis of monomials in successively chosen generators of degree \(p\). Differentiation in one generator, with the others and \(J_sE^p\) constant, defines a nonzero derivation; its defining \(p\)-power relations have zero derivative. This is a nonzero \(J\)-derivation of \(E\). Conversely a derivation over \(J\) kills every separable algebraic element by differentiating its minimal polynomial. Hence a finite extension has no nonzero derivations precisely when it is separable.

Apply this criterion to \(E/k(f)\). TN1 gives a finite normalization \(D\) of \(k[f]\) in \(E\). Since \(H\) is integral over \(k[f]\), transitivity of integrality identifies \(D\) with the normalization of \(H\). The same finite generating list over \(k[f]\) generates it over \(H\). \(\square\)

HB4. For a complete DVR \(R\) with perfect residue field, the integral closure \(R_E\) in every finite field extension \(E/K\) is a finite \(R\)-module, a complete DVR, and the valuation ring of the unique valuation extending that of \(K\).

Proof. First suppose the extension is separable. TN1 makes \(S=R_E\) finite and normal. It is torsion-free over the DVR \(R\), hence finite free and complete. The freeness assertion follows directly by projecting a finite submodule of a finite free module onto one coordinate: its image is a principal ideal, split off an element generating that image and induct on the remaining rank. The containing free module here is the trace-dual module in TN1.

Every maximal ideal of \(S\) contracts to the maximal ideal of \(R\). Indeed a subring over which a field is integral is a field: apply a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element and rearrange. The finite-dimensional \(k\)-algebra \(S/\pi S\) is a product of local Artinian rings. One can obtain this decomposition by taking its finitely many minimal primes, which are maximal since a finite-dimensional domain over \(k\) is a field; the nilradical is nilpotent because it is a finite ideal of nilpotent elements. Chinese remainders for powers of these maximal ideals give the product.

Every idempotent of \(S/\pi S\) lifts to \(S\). Starting with a lift \(e\), the element \(2e-1\) is a unit, since its square is in \(1+\pi S\). Newton's correction

\[ e\longmapsto e-\frac{e^2-e}{2e-1} \tag{HB12} \]

squares the order of the error; completeness gives the idempotent lift. An element of \(1+\pi S\) is a unit by its convergent geometric series. Since \(S\) is a domain, it has only the idempotents zero and one. The product therefore has only one factor, so \(S\) is local. It has dimension one: after inverting \(\pi\) it is the field \(E\), and primes over \((\pi)\) are incomparable by integrality. HB1 makes it a DVR. If \(u\) is its uniformizer, then \(\pi\) is a unit times \(u^e\) for some \(e\ge1\), so its \(\pi\)-adic completeness is also its valuation completeness. Its residue field is finite over \(k\).

Any valuation ring of \(E\) extending \(R\) contains \(S\). An element integral over \(R\) cannot have negative valuation, because the leading term of its monic equation would have uniquely smallest valuation. Every unit of \(S\) has value zero, and \(\pi\) is a unit times \(u^e\), so the valuation of every element is forced by its \(u\)-order. This proves uniqueness in the separable case.

It remains to treat positive-characteristic inseparability. Let \(E_s\) be the separable part of \(E/K\), so \(E/E_s\) is purely inseparable of some exponent \(r\). Its valuation ring \(S\) just constructed has residue field \(l\) finite over \(k\). This field is perfect: Frobenius preserves its finite degree over the perfect field \(k\), and the degree tower gives \([l:l^p]=1\). We construct a coefficient field in \(S\), rather than assuming one. For \(a\in l\), choose any lift \(a_n\) of \(a^{p^{-n}}\) and put

\[ [a]=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{p^n}. \tag{HB13} \]

Successive differences have valuation at least \(p^n\), and changing the lifts has the same vanishing effect. In characteristic \(p\), the formulas for \(p^n\)-th powers of sums and products show that this map preserves addition and multiplication and is a section of the residue map. Recursively subtracting residue coefficients gives a unique convergent expansion in a uniformizer \(u\). Thus \(S=l[[u]]\) and \(E_s=l((u))\).

Inside a fixed algebraic closure,

\[ E_s^{1/p^r}=l((u^{1/p^r})),\qquad T=l[[u^{1/p^r}]] =\bigoplus_{i=0}^{p^r-1}S\,u^{i/p^r}. \tag{HB14} \]

These equalities follow by taking the unique roots of coefficients in the perfect field \(l\). The ring \(T\) is the integral closure of \(S\) in that field: it is finite over \(S\), and any integral element has nonnegative valuation. Since \(E\subset E_s^{1/p^r}\), its integral closure over \(R\) is \(T\cap E\). This is an \(S\)-submodule of the finite module \(T\), hence finite. The equality follows in both directions from the monic valuation test and transitivity of integrality. Multiplying an element of \(E\) by a large power of \(\pi\) puts it in \(T\cap E\), so its fraction field is \(E\). Apply the complete-local and normal-DVR arguments of the preceding paragraphs to this finite normal \(R\)-algebra. The same uniformizer argument proves uniqueness of the valuation. \(\square\)

HB5. For \(C\) in (HB1) and \(0\ne c\in\mathfrak m\) with \(H=C/cC\) reduced, its normalization \(D_c\) in its total quotient ring is finite. Moreover

\[ \delta_C(c):=\lambda_C(D_c/H)<\infty . \tag{HB15} \]

Proof. The prime \(\mathfrak q\) contains \(\pi\), since \(B[1/\pi]\) is finite over the one-dimensional ring \(K[t]\). Each minimal prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(C/cC\) has height one by HB1. It is induced by a height-one prime \(P\subset\mathfrak q\) of \(B\); localization preserves all chains below \(P\). Its contraction to \(A\) is nonzero: for \(0\ne b\in P\), the nonzero constant term of its minimal polynomial belongs to \(P\cap A\). The coefficients belong to \(A\), by the integral-conjugate argument in TN1.

If \(\pi\in P\), this contraction is \((\pi)\). A larger contraction would give a finite algebra over a field as \(B/P\), so \(P\) would be maximal and would equal \(\mathfrak q\), contradicting its height. Hence \(B/P\) is integral and finite over \(k[t]\). HB3 gives its finite normalization.

If \(\pi\notin P\), then \((B/P)[1/\pi]\) is a field \(E\) finite over \(K\): it is an integral finite algebra over the quotient of \(K[t]\) by a nonzero prime. The element \(\pi\) is not a unit in \(B/P\), because \(P\subset\mathfrak q\). Let \(S\) be the finite valuation ring in \(E\) furnished by HB4. We claim \(B/P\subset S\).

Suppose \(b\in B/P\) had negative extended \(K\)-valuation \(v(b)\), normalized by \(v(\pi)=1\). All roots of its minimal polynomial have that same valuation, by uniqueness in a finite splitting field. For a monic polynomial \(\sum_{i=0}^m a_iX^i\), this gives

\[ v(a_0)=m v(b),\qquad v(a_i)\ge(m-i)v(b)>v(a_0)\quad(i>0). \tag{HB16} \]

The inequality includes the leading coefficient. Dividing its value at \(b\) by \(a_0\) gives \(1+\sum_{i>0}(a_i/a_0)b^i=0\), with every displayed coefficient in \(\pi R\). This would make \(\pi\) a unit in \(B/P\), a contradiction. Thus all its elements lie in \(S\). The ring \(S\) is integral over \(B/P\), normal in \(E\), and finite over it: its finite \(R\)-generating list suffices. It is exactly its normalization.

By TN2 these normalizations localize to finite normalizations \(D_i\) of \(C/\mathfrak p_i\). The total quotient ring of the reduced ring \(H\) is the product of the fraction fields of these domains. To see the product idempotents explicitly, choose \(b_i\in\bigcap_{j\ne i}\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i\) in \(H\). Then \(s=\sum b_i\) is a nonzerodivisor, and \(b_i/s\) has component one at \(i\) and zero elsewhere. Fractions in each component are obtained by clearing its denominator with these idempotents. Thus \(\prod_iD_i\) is a finite \(H\)-algebra inside this total quotient ring. Coordinatewise integrality and normality show it is precisely \(D_c\).

At every minimal prime of \(H\), normalization is the identity on the fraction field. The finite module \(D_c/H\) is consequently supported only at the closed point of this local one-dimensional ring. A finite module with that support is killed by a power of the maximal ideal and has finite length. This proves (HB15). \(\square\)

2AE.3. One annihilator for all normal modifications

HB6. Choose an integral \(F\)-basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\) of \(L\), as in TN1, and put

\[ G=(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/F}(b_i b_j))_{i,j},\qquad d=\det G\in A\setminus\{0\}. \tag{HB17} \]

For every normal modification \(X\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}C\),

\[ d\,H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)=0 . \tag{HB18} \]

Proof. First let \(Y\) be a modification over \(B\). FM4 dominates it by the normalization \(M\) of a regular point-blowup model \(W\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) in \(L\). The map \(g:M\to W\) is finite. Trace sends an element integral over a normal affine chart of \(W\) into that chart, by TN1's integral-conjugate proof. The basis elements are regular on \(M\). We therefore have sheaf maps
